# Architecture Decisions

This ledger records the rulings that shape the design system and the reason behind each one, in no strict order of date.

**Names.** Each ruling carries a permanent short name of two to five lower-case words joined by hyphens, and the name heads its entry, so `DECISIONS.md#focus-ring` opens the focus-ring ruling. A new ruling takes a new name, and no name changes or returns to use after its ruling leaves. Entries cite one another as links. Stories, code and the other documents cite a ruling as `[[focus-ring]]`.

**Tags.** Each entry opens with one to three tags and the date of the ruling, or with `No date recorded.` when the ruling carries no date. The tags are `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`, `COMPONENTS`, `CONTRIBUTING`, `DOCUMENTATION`, `FOUNDATIONS`, `INSTALL`, `LAYOUT`, `MOTION`, `SIZING`, `TOKENS` and `TYPOGRAPHY`. The sections below group the rulings by the part of the system they first concerned, and the tags cross those sections.

**Reading an entry.** Entries name the source files that carry each rule. The paths are relative to the system's repository, and the npm package ships only the build, so outside the repository read a path as provenance: this rule lives somewhere, and here is where. The ledger is self-contained. No entry depends on a document outside this repository.

## Substrate & architecture

### radix-themes-substrate

**Tags.** `FOUNDATIONS`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**The system takes Radix Themes as substrate, not a fork, and adds its own token and component layer on top.**

**What you see.** `@radix-ui/themes` is a peer dependency at `3.3.x`, the 3.3 line only, because the package stylesheet already contains the Radix Themes 3.3 stylesheet. An app imports that one stylesheet.

**Why.** Accessibility, maintenance and re-skinning are free with the substrate. A fork would carry the whole maintenance burden of Radix Themes.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling. On 2026-10-03 the peer range narrowed from 3.3 or later to `3.3.x`, the line the bundled stylesheet comes from.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Radix Themes as substrate, not a fork.** Consume `@radix-ui/themes` as a dependency; add a thin token + component layer on top. Rationale: accessibility, maintenance, and re-skinning come for free; a fork would inherit the maintenance burden.

> **What you see**, before 2026-10-03: `@radix-ui/themes` is a peer dependency at version 3.3 or later. The package stylesheet already contains the Radix Themes stylesheet, so an app imports one stylesheet.

### brand-props-on-provider

**Tags.** `FOUNDATIONS`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**The brand, the neutral and the radius are props on `Provider`, and no token file holds a brand value.**

**What you see.** `accentColor` defaults to `iris`, `grayColor` defaults to `auto`, which pairs a neutral with the accent, and `radius` defaults to `medium`. One change to `accentColor` re-skins every component, because the `--ds-*` roles read the accent scale.

**Brand values.** `accentColor` takes one of the 26 Radix colours, the `oxblood` preset, or `{ seed }` with a colour of your own.

**Not exported.** The package does not export Radix's `Theme`, so `Provider` is the one place to set these props.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset) adds the `oxblood` preset as a brand value.
- [seeded-brand-collisions](#seeded-brand-collisions) rules the `{ seed }` brand and moves its status families when they collide with it.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Brand & neutral are runtime `<Theme>` props, never in token files.** `accentColor` (default `iris`), `grayColor="auto"`, `radius`. One swap re-skins the whole product. The role layer (`semantic.css`) stays brand-agnostic.

### one-accent

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `FOUNDATIONS`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**The theme has one accent, and it is both the brand colour and the default colour of every interactive element.**

**What you see.** Links, solid fills, selected states and the focus ring all read the accent scale. The four status families carry scales of their own, so no status colour serves as a second accent.

**Part colour.** A single part may take another colour through its `color` prop. Its focus ring stays the page accent.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved, on 2026-09-27, one focus colour for every part, so a part given its own colour keeps the page accent on its focus ring, and one exported colour type for the `color` prop of every wrapper ([part-colour-parity](#part-colour-parity)).

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [colour-prop-and-high-contrast](#colour-prop-and-high-contrast) and [part-colour-parity](#part-colour-parity) let a single part take its own colour, and [part-colour-parity](#part-colour-parity) keeps one focus colour for every part.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **No secondary accent.** `accent == interactive == brand`. Semantic families carry their own hues.

### status-colour-defaults

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Each status family takes a fixed default colour, distinct from the brand accent.**

| Family | Default scale |
|---|---|
| Error | `red` |
| Warning | `amber` |
| Success | `green` |
| Info | `cyan` |

**Why.** Info uses a hue apart from the accent, so an info message keeps its meaning after a brand change.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) and [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate) move a family to another scale when a named brand colour collides with it.
- [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset) adds oxblood as the error scale for a brand in the red family.
- [seeded-brand-collisions](#seeded-brand-collisions) applies the same move to a seeded brand.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Semantic families:** error→`red`, warning→`amber`, success→`green`, info→`cyan`. Info is kept a distinct hue from the accent so info messaging survives a brand swap.

### light-and-dark-token-set

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `FOUNDATIONS`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Light and dark resolve from one set of tokens on the theme root, and only a value that differs by appearance takes a dark override.**

**What you see.** The `--ds-*` roles are declared on `.radix-themes`, so they resolve again when the appearance changes. A role with a dark override holds a value that must differ by appearance, such as the raised, overlay and sunken surfaces and the inset shadow.

**Dark selectors.** Every dark override carries two selectors, so it applies whether the dark class sits on the theme root or on the page root.

**Rejected.** Two parallel token sets, one per appearance.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [elevation-model](#elevation-model) adds the sunken surface to the dark overrides.
- [dark-override-selectors](#dark-override-selectors) requires both dark selectors on every dark override.
- [scrim-value](#scrim-value) deletes the dark scrim override, so one scrim value serves both appearances.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Light/dark via appearance + `.radix-themes` scoping**, not two parallel token sets. Tokens are declared on `.radix-themes` (the element carrying the appearance class) so they re-resolve per mode from one block. Only genuinely mode-dependent tokens (raised/overlay surfaces, scrim) are overridden in `.dark`.

### content-on-solid-fills

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Content on a solid fill takes its paired `--on-*` token, and an inverted section flips the appearance with `Contrast`.**

**What you see.** Text, icons and strokes on a solid accent or status fill use `--on-accent`, `--on-error`, `--on-warning`, `--on-success` or `--on-info`. A section wrapped in `Contrast` renders in the opposite appearance, so its roles flip with the page.

**Rejected.** A fixed inverse palette.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [scrim-foreground-tokens](#scrim-foreground-tokens) adds `--ds-on-scrim` and `--ds-on-scrim-light` for content drawn on a scrim.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Content on solid fills uses `--on-*` contrast tokens**; inverted neutral sections use the `<Contrast>` appearance-flip wrapper. No fixed inverse palette.

### one-scoped-stylesheet

**Tags.** `FOUNDATIONS`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Components are styled with one scoped stylesheet, custom properties and data attributes, and their icons are Phosphor glyphs.**

**What you see.** Component rules live in `src/tokens/components.css`, scoped under `.radix-themes` and keyed on `rt-ds-` class names and data attributes such as `data-tone`. Paint comes from custom properties, chiefly the `--ds-*` roles.

**Rejected.** styled-components, Tailwind and CVA.

**Icons.** Component icons are imported from `@phosphor-icons/react`.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Styling for components: CSS Modules + custom properties + data-attributes.** No styled-components, Tailwind, or CVA. Icons: Phosphor.

### catalog-as-specification

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-07-08.

**A component may follow Astryx's catalog entry, API and behaviour, and it is still built on Radix Themes and the `--ds-*` roles under this system's rulings.**

**What you see.** No component takes Astryx's styling or colour rules. Where this system and Astryx disagree on a foundation, this system wins.

**Names.** A component that wraps a Radix Themes component keeps the Radix name, such as `Callout`, `Separator` and `DataList`. A component with no Radix Themes counterpart may keep its Astryx name.

**Notice.** A file that reuses MIT code begins with a copyright line and one notice per source file, naming its path, its commit and the licence. Every such source and its commits also appear in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved, on 2026-10-01, the gathering of every third-party notice in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`, with the Astryx portions in its first section beside the four upstream commits that their file notices cite ([package-licence](#package-licence)).

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered a component, an API or code taken from another design system. The component layer held the wrappers that [system-wrapper-layer](#system-wrapper-layer) places in `src/components/ui/`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-07-08.

- [package-licence](#package-licence) corrects the file notices against their sources and gathers every third-party notice in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Astryx port doctrine (2026-07-08).** The component layer expands to the breadth of Meta's Astryx catalog (~93 components) via blueprint + selective MIT logic lifts: Astryx supplies the catalog, API reference, and behavior spec; every component is built on the Radix Themes substrate + the `--ds-*` role layer under this system's existing rulings — no StyleX, no Astryx styling, no new color rules. All foundations conflicts resolve in favour of this system. Component naming: the Radix Themes name wins for wrapped components (Callout not Banner, Separator not Divider, DataList not Metadata List); Astryx's name applies only where no Radix equivalent exists. Lifted logic pins the consulted Astryx version and carries a header notice: `Portions derived from facebook/astryx <path> @ <commit> (MIT, © Meta Platforms)`.

### headless-primitives-declared

**Tags.** `FOUNDATIONS`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-07-08.

**A headless `@radix-ui/react-*` primitive that a component imports is a declared dependency, and the docs and the tests pre-bundle it.**

**What you see.** Each such primitive appears in `package.json` `dependencies`, never only as a dependency of another package. Each also appears in the pre-bundle lists of `.storybook/main.ts` and `vitest.config.ts`, so every primitive shares one copy of React.

**Applies to.** Today these are the accordion, collapsible, popover, toast, toggle, toggle group and toolbar primitives.

**Why.** A dependency that arrives only through another package breaks without warning when that package changes how it installs. These primitives belong to the same family as Radix Themes, so declaring one adds no new vendor.

**Changed from.** No ruling covered a headless primitive. `@radix-ui/themes` already installs each one through its own `radix-ui` dependency, so a component could import a primitive that `package.json` never declared.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-07-08. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **@radix-ui headless primitives are first-class dependencies (2026-07-08).** A primitive a System component builds on (`@radix-ui/react-popover`, `-toggle`, `-toast`, …) is declared explicitly in `package.json` `dependencies` — never ridden transitively — and pre-bundled in both `.storybook/main.ts` `viteFinal` and `vitest.config.ts` `optimizeDeps` (the single-React constraint). Same substrate family as [radix-themes-substrate], so no new-dependency stress. Rationale: a transitive-only dep breaks silently when upstream hoisting changes.

## Tooling & verification

### package-manager-and-storybook

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**The project uses npm as its package manager and Storybook 10 on React and Vite for its documentation.**

**Tools.**

- Package manager: npm.
- Documentation: Storybook 10, with the React and Vite framework.

**Package name.** The package is the unscoped `dsiab` on public npm, as [package-name-and-release-line](#package-name-and-release-line) records.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [package-name-and-release-line](#package-name-and-release-line) replaces the private unscoped package name `design-system` with the public `dsiab`, and records the release line.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Package manager npm; Storybook 10 (React + Vite).** Private unscoped package `design-system`. **[Update 2026-09-24 ([package-name-and-release-line](#package-name-and-release-line)): superseded for the package. It publishes on public npm as the unscoped `dsiab`, and [package-name-and-release-line](#package-name-and-release-line) records the name and the release line.]**

### story-tests-in-browser

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Every change is verified twice: by eye, and by automated story tests that run in a real browser.**

**What runs.** The Storybook Vitest addon runs every story test in browser mode. `getComputedStyle` resolves a `--ds-*` role only in a live `.radix-themes` DOM, so a simulated DOM cannot check the tokens.

**Which browser.** The story suite and `test:publish` find the browser through one shared module, `scripts/browser.mjs`, in this order:

- `DS_BROWSER_PATH`, when it names an existing file
- Playwright's own Chromium, installed once per machine with `npx playwright install chromium`

**Startup wait.** Both gates wait until the ad blocker that some Chromium builds include finishes its startup, because that blocker reloads tabs while it starts.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- An update of 2026-09-24 in this entry makes the browser a lookup in `scripts/browser.mjs`, shared by the story suite and `test:publish`, where the entry first named the browser installed on the system, through the Playwright `chrome` channel.
- [test-browser-order](#test-browser-order) sets the order to `DS_BROWSER_PATH`, then Playwright's own Chromium, and removes the `chrome` channel and any named maintainer browser from it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Verification = visual + automated story tests** via the Storybook Vitest addon in **browser mode** (getComputedStyle only resolves `--ds-*` in a live `.radix-themes` DOM). Browser is **system Google Chrome** via Playwright `channel: "chrome"` — no Chromium download. **[Update 2026-09-24: the browser is found, not assumed. The story suite and `test:publish` resolve it through one shared module, `scripts/browser.mjs`, in this order: `DS_BROWSER_PATH`, then Helium, then Playwright's Chrome channel on other machines. Both gates also wait out the ad blocker built into Helium, which reloads tabs while it starts.]** **[Update 2026-09-28 ([test-browser-order](#test-browser-order)): the order is `DS_BROWSER_PATH`, then Playwright's own Chromium. Neither the Chrome channel nor a named maintainer browser sits in it.]**

### wcag-aa-enforcement

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**The system meets WCAG 2.2 AA, and an automated check fails a story that breaks it.**

**Enforced by.**

- `@storybook/addon-a11y` runs axe on every story with `parameters.a11y.test` set to `"error"`, so a violation fails the story test.
- The `Swatches` play on `Foundations/Colors` asserts contrast for every accent in the light and dark appearances.

**Accents.** The contrast matrix covers the 26 Radix accents and the oxblood preset, 27 in all.

**Changed from.** Nothing. This is a founding ruling.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset) adds oxblood as a 27th accent, and the `Swatches` play sweeps it with the other 26.
- [srgb-contrast-checks](#srgb-contrast-checks) runs the contrast ratios only in an sRGB context, and the collision and hue checks run everywhere.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **WCAG 2.2 AA, enforced.** `@storybook/addon-a11y` (axe, mode=error) on every story + custom contrast assertions across light/dark × **all 26 Radix accents** (the Foundations/Colors **Swatches** play).

### srgb-contrast-checks

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-21.

**Contrast ratio checks run only in an sRGB context, and colour parsing reads a colour from any gamut.**

**Parsing.** `parseColor` in `src/foundations/_assert.ts` paints the computed colour on an sRGB 2d canvas and reads the pixel with `getImageData`. A `color(display-p3 …)` value from a wide-gamut display parses like any other.

**sRGB gate.** WCAG ratios are defined in sRGB, and on a P3 display `getComputedStyle` returns the P3 variant of a Radix colour, which measures lower, so orange-11 on white reads 4.27 against 4.40 in sRGB. The ratio checks run only where `matchMedia('(color-gamut: p3)')` does not match, and on a P3 display a `console.info` line reports the skip.

**Always run.** The collision and hue checks hold on any gamut, so they run on every display.

**Source of truth.** CI and headless runs decide the WCAG floors.

**Accepted.** On a P3 display the shifted step-11 warning and link text renders about 0.1 below its sRGB ratio. It is accepted on the same colour-not-alone basis as the step-11 ruling in [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table).

**Changed from.** `parseColor` matched `rgb()` with a regular expression and threw on the `color(display-p3 …)` value a P3 display reports. CI and headless runs never showed the failure.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-21. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Contrast checks are sRGB-gated; colour parsing is gamut-safe (2026-06-21).** `parseColor` (`_assert.ts`) rasterises the computed colour on an sRGB 2d canvas and reads `getImageData`, rather than regex-parsing `rgb()` — so a P3 display's `color(display-p3 …)` (which the old regex threw on, a real interaction failure on a P3 monitor, invisible to non-P3 CI/headless) parses fine. But WCAG ratios are **sRGB-defined**, and on a P3 display `getComputedStyle` hands back Radix's P3 *variant*, which maps to slightly lower sRGB contrast than the sRGB fallback (e.g. orange-11 on white is 4.40 in sRGB but **4.27 on P3**) — and the sRGB fallback can't be read back on a P3 monitor. So the contrast-**ratio** checks run **only in an sRGB context** (CI / headless, detected via `matchMedia('(color-gamut: p3)')` in the Swatches play; a `console.info` notes the skip); the gamut-robust **collision + hue** checks always run. CI/headless is the source of truth for the WCAG floors. *(Implication: on a P3 display the shifted step-11 warning/link text renders ~0.1 below its sRGB ratio — accepted under the same colour-not-alone basis as [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table)'s step-11 ruling.)*

### component-registry

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-07-08.

**`registry.json` is the roster of record for the system's components, and a component it does not list as ported is never improvised as a system component.**

**What it records.** One entry per component: its `status`, its build `wave`, its documentation `tier`, the `buildingBlock` it composes and its `storyPath`. The `status` is `ported`, `planned`, `external` or `out-of-scope`, and the `tier` is `full` or `lite`.

**Kept current.** An entry changes in the same commit as the component it describes. `src/foundations/registry.node-check.ts` fails when an entry is malformed, when a ported `storyPath` does not exist, or when a `Components/*` story file maps to no ported entry.

**Agent gap.** A component the registry does not list as `ported` never gets a hand-built `Components/*` equivalent. Use the raw Radix Themes component under the documented conventions, or surface the gap.

**In the package.** The package ships a projection of the file, also named `registry.json`. Each entry keeps its name, status, tier and export names, `ported` reads `available`, and the fields that record how the system was built are absent.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-07-08.

- [registry-module-paths](#registry-module-paths) lets the `module` of an entry name a path under `src/`, so any module can publish its exports.
- [docs-page-header](#docs-page-header) makes the registry spelling of a component the subject of every page title it has.
- [prior-art-required](#prior-art-required) adds a `priorArt` field, required on every entry added after 2026-09-20.
- [sidebar-order](#sidebar-order) renames the `System` story root to `Components`.
- [contribution-threshold](#contribution-threshold) records the outcome of a proposal in the registry, as `planned`, or as `out-of-scope` with its reason.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Port registry + agent-gap rule (2026-07-08).** `registry.json` (repo root) is the machine-readable state of the Astryx port: per catalog component — `status` (`ported | planned | external | out-of-scope`), `wave` (0–5), docs `tier` (`full | lite`), `buildingBlock`, `storyPath`. It is updated in the same commit as the component it describes, and enforced by `src/foundations/registry.node-check.ts` (well-formed entries; every ported `storyPath` exists; every `System/*` story file maps to a ported entry). The agent-gap rule (`AGENTS.md`): a component not `ported` in the registry must not be improvised as a `System/*` equivalent — use the raw Radix Themes component under documented conventions, or surface the gap.

### missing-provider-warning

**Tags.** `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**In a development build, the package warns once when a page lacks the Provider or the stylesheet.**

**What you see.** One `[dsiab]` console warning per missing piece per page. A correct install prints no warning, and a production build prints none at all.

- **No `Provider`.** Size and colour attributes are absent, so every `calc()` fails. Components still render at a usable size.
- **No stylesheet.** Every `--ds-*` role resolves to an empty value.

**Why.** Both failures are silent otherwise: the page renders wrong and raises no error.

**Not checked.** A Radix stylesheet loaded after this one. Both sheets set the same properties at equal strength, so no wrong value exists to report.

**Changed from.** A page without the `Provider` or the stylesheet rendered wrong and printed no warning and no error.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **The two silent consumer failures are detected and reported (2026-09-17).** `src/theme/detectAndWarn.ts`. Rationale, measured 2026-09-02: rendering with `class="radix-themes"` alone — what anybody writes without React — leaves `--ds-fill-accent`, `--ds-space-8`, `--ds-radius-3` and `--ds-text-sm-size` all computing to the EMPTY STRING, and `--ds-text-strong` falling off slate to `#202020`. `--scaling` comes from `[data-scaling]`, radius from `[data-radius]`, the accent ramp from `[data-accent-color]`, greys from `[data-gray-color]`, all written by `Provider`, so without it every `calc()` is invalid at computed-value time. Nothing errored and nothing warned: the page painted wrong and the reader had no thread to pull. **Two causes, two seams.** (1) NO PROVIDER is detected in `useResolvedSize` — the one seam 74 sized components already pass through, which is why the check is not repeated in each of them. It needs its own sentinel context, `ProviderPresenceContext`, because `SizeContext` cannot answer the question: its default is a real tier, indistinguishable from a Provider that set it. The component still renders a usable step, so the failure is loud rather than fatal. (2) NO STYLESHEET is detected in a `Provider` `useEffect` reading `--ds-fill-accent` off `.radix-themes` — the element Provider renders and the selector `semantic.css` declares the whole role layer on — because the library build extracts CSS out of the JS, so importing `Provider` alone paints nothing. It is the same property the publish acceptance test reads, which keeps both checks pointed at one fact. **One warning per cause per page**, since the size seam runs on every render of 74 components and a per-instance warning buries the signal it exists to raise. **Radix's stylesheet loaded AFTER ours is deliberately NOT detected:** both sheets set `--default-font-family` and the root `font-size` on `.radix-themes` at equal strength, the loser is decided by source order, and the winner's value is legitimate either way — there is nothing to compare against, so a check would be a guess. That stays a documented trap. Guard: `src/foundations/detect-and-warn.node-check.ts`, which asserts the render half through `renderToString` (the check runs in render, not an effect, so it needs no DOM), that a wrapped tree is SILENT, and that the canary property is declared on `.radix-themes` in `src/tokens/` — a renamed canary would tell every correctly-installed consumer their stylesheet was missing, which is worse than the silence it replaced. All three perturbations were driven red before the guard was trusted. The runtime half was verified in real Chrome both directions (`#5b5bd6` with the sheet, `""` without), and the publish gate now asserts a correct install emits no `[dsiab]` line at all. **Surfaced gap, not fixed here:** fourteen components under `src/components/ui/` carry a byte-identical private copy of the `DEV_WARN` IIFE and its comment (Avatar, Badge, ChatMessageList, CommandPalette, DateInput, DateRangeInput, NumberInput, PowerSearch, TextArea, TextField, TimeInput, Token, Tokenizer, Typeahead). That is the [container-size-seeding] shape; `detectAndWarn.ts` is the one definition they should reach for, and migrating them belongs to a diff that says so.

### registry-module-paths

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**A registry `module` may be a path under `src/`, so any module in `src/` can publish, and a bare name still resolves under `src/components/ui/`.**

**What you see.** In `scripts/gen-barrel.mjs` a bare `module` resolves under `src/components/ui/`, the form every component entry uses. A `module` that contains a slash resolves relative to `src/`, and the barrel reaches it with `../../<path>`. The slash is the whole signal, so the registry takes no new field.

**Why.** A hook, a util or a date helper had no supported route into the public surface. Each workaround was worse than a path:

- moving a general-purpose file into a components directory where it does not belong
- listing it by hand beside the theme exports, in a section whose subject is `Provider` and the types a wrapper needs
- leaving a settled decision half done because of a limit in the generator

**Published.** `useMediaQuery` publishes from `hooks/useMediaQuery`. `useAnnounce` publishes with `AnnouncePoliteness`, because that type appears in the signature of the function the hook returns, and a public signature needs its types public too.

**Withheld.** `useIsMobile`, `NAV_BREAKPOINTS` and `NavBreakpoint` stay in `internalExports`. They encode where this system's navigation collapses, a ruling a consumer should not inherit by importing a media-query helper. An export added later is safe, and an export removed later breaks consumers.

**Changed from.** The barrel generator read modules from `src/components/ui/` alone and threw on a module with no file there, so only a file in that directory could publish.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A registry `module` may be a PATH, so any `src/` module can publish (2026-09-17).** `scripts/gen-barrel.mjs`: a bare `module` still resolves under `src/components/ui/`, which is what all 104 component entries use and nothing about them changed. A `module` CONTAINING A SLASH resolves relative to `src/`, and the barrel reaches it with `../../<path>` — the slash is the whole signal, so there is no new registry field. Rationale: the public surface was reachable only from `src/components/ui/`, because `UI_DIR` was the only directory the generator looked in and it threw on a module with no file there. A hook, a util or a date helper therefore had no supported route out, and the three available answers were all bad: move a general-purpose file into a components directory it does not belong in, hand-list it beside the theme exports in a section whose stated subject is `Provider` and the types needed to write a wrapper, or leave a settled decision half-done because of a generator limitation. **The first two entries to use it export the withheld hooks**, because adding an export later is safe and removing one is breaking: `useAnnounce` (`AnnouncePoliteness` ships with it, because the type appears in the returned function's signature and a type withheld from a public signature is a wart) and `useMediaQuery` at `hooks/useMediaQuery`. The system's own nav ladder — `useIsMobile`, `NAV_BREAKPOINTS`, `NavBreakpoint` — is WITHHELD via `internalExports`: it encodes where THIS system's navigation collapses, which is a ruling a consumer should not inherit by importing a media-query helper. Verification: a unit test cannot prove this, because it resolves source rather than the tarball — so the publish acceptance app imports `useMediaQuery` from the installed package and asserts it rendered `"true"` for `(min-width: 600px)` in real Chrome. An unresolved import fails the consumer's Vite build; a broken one reaches the page and renders nothing.

### dsiab-command

**Tags.** `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**`dsiab` is the one command a consumer runs, and `ds-check` stays a supported alias for `dsiab check`.**

**What you see.** `bin/dsiab.mjs` routes subcommands: `dsiab check [path]`, `dsiab rules`, `dsiab init` and `dsiab docs`. Help names `ds-check` as an alias, kept rather than deprecated because the shipped README, the agent rule files that `--init` writes and a consumer's CI may call it, and removing it gains nothing.

**Why.** The package first shipped one binary, `ds-check`, and its `--init` flag installed agent instruction files and hooks, which checks nothing. A setup flow under a binary named for checking needs an explanation every time.

**Delegation.** The router runs `bin/ds-check.mjs` in a child process and exits with its status, so the alias and the subcommand are one code path. Rewriting the checker into modules the router imports would put the tool consumers run every day at risk for a cosmetic gain. A child killed by a signal reports no status, and the router then exits 1, because the check did not pass.

**Help.** Help lists only commands that run. A listed command that prints "coming soon" teaches a reader to expect something, while an absent one is honest, so `eject` remains absent from the router until it works.

**Guarded by.** Three publish-gate checks on a real install: `dsiab --version` matches the installed manifest, `dsiab check` and `ds-check` print byte-identical output, and every command the help text lists is in the router's command table.

**Changed from.** The package shipped one binary, `ds-check`, which checked code and, with `--init`, installed agent instruction files and hooks.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17.

- [project-init-command](#project-init-command) defines `dsiab init`, which prints its plan by default and writes only with `--write`.
- [docs-hosting](#docs-hosting) adds `dsiab docs`, which prints the documentation URL for the installed version and opens it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`dsiab` is the consumer's front door; `ds-check` stays a working alias (2026-09-17).** `bin/dsiab.mjs`, a subcommand router: `dsiab check [path]`, `dsiab rules`, `dsiab init [--force]`. Rationale: the package shipped one binary named `ds-check`, and it had already outgrown its name — `ds-check --init` installs agent instruction files and hooks, which is not checking anything, and the commands added after it (serve the docs locally, copy a component out into a consumer's repo) are further from it still. A setup flow under a binary called "check" is a name that needs explaining every time. **The alias is kept rather than deprecated:** it is in the shipped README, in the agent rule files `--init` writes into a consumer's project, and plausibly in somebody's CI. Removing it would buy nothing. **DELEGATION IS BY PROCESS, and that is the decision, not an implementation detail.** `bin/ds-check.mjs` is 443 lines with no exports: it reads `process.argv` and runs at import. Refactoring a shipped checker into importable modules to satisfy a router would put the one tool consumers run daily at risk for a cosmetic gain, so the router spawns it and propagates its exit status. One process start, and the alias and the subcommand are provably the same code path rather than two that agree today. A child killed by a signal reports a null status and the router exits 1, because "it did not pass" is true where 0 would claim it did. **HELP LISTS ONLY WHAT RUNS.** A command printing "coming soon" is worse than an absent one: absence is honest, a listed command teaches a reader to expect something. `docs` and `eject` are designed and are not in the router until they work. Guarded from a REAL install by three publish-gate checks: `dsiab --version` matches the installed manifest, `dsiab check` and `ds-check` produce byte-identical output, and every command the help text advertises resolves rather than reporting unknown-command — that last arm is what keeps the honesty rule mechanical instead of remembered. **It caught two defects on its first run**, which is the argument for putting it in the gate: a help parser that read the `USAGE` line as a command name, and `.claude/skills/design-system/SKILL.md` silently dropped from `files[]` while the bin entries were inserted beside it. The second would have shipped a tarball whose own `--init` fails on a missing file, and no type check or unit test can see it.

### project-init-command

**Tags.** `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**`dsiab init` prints a plan and the exact diff for wiring a project to the package, and writes only when given `--write`.**

**Steps.** Each step answers a failure measured on a real install:

- The stylesheet import, `dsiab/styles.css`. Without it every `--ds-*` role resolves to an empty value.
- The `Provider`. It writes the size, radius and colour attributes, so without it every `calc()` fails.
- The peer dependency ranges. A mismatched React resolves twice and fails with *Invalid hook call* far from its cause. The plan names only the peers that are absent.
- A token override file, `dsiab-tokens.css` at the project root, which directs a new consumer to the override seams that section 10 of `docs/GUIDELINES.md` documents, in place of a `.rt-Button { … }` rule that no guard can see.
- The agent instruction files, which the command hands to `ds-check --init` rather than reimplementing them.

**Print first.** The default prints the plan and the exact diff, and `--write` applies it. A run with no terminal shows no prompt: every question has a flag, and the command takes the defaults and prints them. Two publish-gate checks read the filesystem and confirm that a dry run changes no byte of the entry file, creates no token file and names both imports it would add.

**Insertion.** The imports land after a leading directive such as `"use client"` and after any leading comment block, so the directive stays first. The token file specifier comes from the directory of the importing file, so a file in `app/` imports `../dsiab-tokens.css`. A second `--write` run changes nothing.

**Not done.** The command never mounts the `Provider`. Wrapping a tree is a structural edit, so the command prints a snippet built from the four answers (accent, neutral, size and radius) and leaves that edit to the consumer.

**Why.** People stop trusting a setup tool that edits an entry file without asking, and a prompt with no terminal to read from hangs an agent or a CI job. The command depends on nothing beyond `node:readline`, so a consumer accepts no dependency tree for a setup script.

**Changed from.** No command wired a project to the package. `ds-check --init` installed the agent instruction files alone, and nothing directed a new consumer to the token override seams.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`dsiab init` wires a project up, and prints before it writes (2026-09-17).** `bin/dsiab-init.mjs`. **Every step is a MEASURED failure, not a wishlist.** (1) The stylesheet import: without it every `--ds-*` role computes to the empty string, because the library build extracts CSS out of the JS. (2) The `Provider`: `--scaling`, `[data-radius]`, `[data-accent-color]` and `[data-gray-color]` are written by it, so without it every `calc()` is invalid at computed-value time. Both measured 2026-09-02, both silent. (3) The peer ranges, because a mismatched React resolves twice and surfaces as *Invalid hook call* far from its cause. (4) A token override file, because GUIDELINES §10 documents two sanctioned seams and nothing pointed a new consumer at them, so people reach for `.rt-Button { … }` instead — which no guard, including `dsiab check`, can see. (5) The agent layer, delegated to `ds-check --init` rather than reimplemented. **PRINT FIRST, WRITE ONLY WHEN ASKED.** The default prints a plan and the exact diff; `--write` applies it. An init that silently edits a consumer's entry file is a tool people run once and then distrust, and this mirrors the restraint the agent-layer installer already had — it refuses to overwrite a CLAUDE.md, which is why it is safe to run twice. **NO TTY MEANS NO PROMPTS.** This package ships agent hooks, so an agent will run this command and so will CI. A prompt with nowhere to read from is a hang, and a hang in the tool built to help agents is the worst available failure. Every question therefore has a flag, and with no TTY the defaults are taken *and printed* so the choice is visible rather than assumed. **WHAT IT REFUSES TO DO:** mount the `Provider`. Wrapping a tree is a structural edit and guessing where a root renders is how a setup tool corrupts a file, so it prints a snippet tailored to the four answers and says the part is yours. The imports are mechanical; that is not. **Zero dependencies**, on `node:readline` rather than a prompt library, because the alternative is asking a design-system consumer to accept a dependency tree for a setup script. **Two defects the first dry run exposed, both of which would have reached a consumer:** the plan told people to `npm i react react-dom @radix-ui/themes` when only one of the three was missing, and it wrote `./dsiab-tokens.css` into `src/main.tsx` — a resolve error at the consumer's next build, since the token file sits at the project root. The specifier is now computed from the importing file's directory. **The insertion point is the dangerous part and is handled explicitly:** a directive prologue (`"use client"`) has to stay first or it stops being a directive, so imports land after it and after any leading comment block. Verified on a Next-shaped project: the directive remained line 1, the specifier resolved as `../dsiab-tokens.css` from `app/`, and the framework was detected well enough to print the client-boundary note. **Idempotent, proven rather than claimed:** a second `--write` run left both files exactly as they were and the entry still carried exactly two imports. Guarded from a REAL install by two publish-gate checks that read the FILESYSTEM rather than the command's own output — the dry run changes no byte of the entry and creates no token file, and the plan names both imports it would add.

### prior-art-required

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**A new component or a large edit to one requires research into how other design systems solve the same problem.**

**What it asks.** The registry entry of the component carries a `priorArt` field. The field names at least two sources, cites at least one URL, and says what was taken and what was deliberately rejected, because a reasoned rejection is worth as much as a borrowing.

**Why.** This is the reuse rule of `AGENTS.md` one level out. A pattern that every mature system shares is prior art too, and a private re-derivation of it yields something subtly wrong that internal review cannot catch, because every reviewer shares the blind spot.

**Guard.** `prior-art.node-check.ts` holds three arms:

- every entry added after the rule carries a substantive field
- the grandfathered list still matches the registry it came from
- the gate still has entries to check

**Grandfathered.** The 107 entries that predate the rule are listed and counted, as the files over the 400-line cap in `AGENTS.md` are. They take no retroactive prior art. Each gains the field at its next substantial change.

**Not checked.** Whether the research was any good. That stays a review obligation.

**Changed from.** Research into other design systems was a courtesy, and no registry field or guard recorded it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20.

- [contribution-threshold](#contribution-threshold) makes this prior art one part of the written proposal that a new component needs.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Prior art is a requirement, not a courtesy (2026-09-20).** For any new component or large component edit, researching other design systems is a requirement. **This is `AGENTS.md`'s reuse rule one level out.** That rule governs assets inside this repository and treats repetition of a shipped asset as consistency rather than laziness. A pattern that every mature system has converged on is prior art too, and re-deriving it privately yields something subtly wrong in ways internal review cannot catch, because everyone reviewing shares the blind spot. A reader who has used other tools feels it in seconds. **Mechanism:** a `priorArt` field on the registry entry naming at least two sources, citing at least one URL, and saying what was taken AND what was deliberately rejected, because a reasoned rejection is worth as much as a borrowing. **Guard:** `prior-art.node-check.ts`, three arms — the field is substantive on every post-rule entry, the grandfathered list still matches the registry it was taken from, and the gate still has something to check. **107 entries predate the rule and are grandfathered and counted**, the same call `AGENTS.md` makes for the 400-line cap and `regression-cover.node-check.ts` makes for measured rulings. They are not to be retro-documented because the guard exists; the field lands when one is next substantially changed, which is the second half of the rule. What it deliberately does not assert is whether the research was any GOOD: that stays a review obligation.

### agents-md-context-file

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**`AGENTS.md` is the agent context file, and the documentation assumes no particular agent harness.**

**What you see.** The rules for agents live in `AGENTS.md`, the cross-tool convention that many agent harnesses read with no configuration. The root `AGENTS.md` holds the rules for work in this repository and does not ship, and `npx ds-check --init` writes the consumer rules from `skills/dsiab/references/rules.md` into a consumer project as `AGENTS.md`.

**Enforcement.** Three harness-neutral commands are the floor the project guarantees: `npx ds-check`, `npm run test:tokens` and `npm test`. An agent gate sits above that floor, and its binding to one harness, such as the files under `.claude/`, is one adapter and never the mechanism.

**Documentation.** Tooling may be tuned for the harness in use. The documentation never assumes one.

**Why.** The documentation described the hook binding of one harness as the enforcement mechanism, so a reader in any other harness found no true account of what binds the code.

**Changed from.** The rules lived in `CLAUDE.md`, and the documentation described the Claude Code hook binding as the enforcement mechanism.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20.

- [agent-files-and-docs-layout](#agent-files-and-docs-layout) keeps the root `AGENTS.md` for contributors, moves the consumer rules into `skills/dsiab/references/rules.md`, and has `--init` write no `CLAUDE.md`, because Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` when a project holds no `CLAUDE.md`.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`AGENTS.md` is the context file, and the documentation is harness-neutral (2026-09-20).** The law lived in `CLAUDE.md`. `AGENTS.md` is the cross-tool convention and is discovered automatically by many agent harnesses, so the rules now live there and 26 operational references were updated with it. The dated plan records were deliberately left saying `CLAUDE.md`, because they are a log of what was true when they were written, and rewriting history to match the present is how a record stops being worth keeping. **The deeper point is which harness the documentation assumes.** The repo had drifted into describing Claude Code's hook binding as though it were the enforcement mechanism. It is not. Enforcement is three harness-neutral commands — `npx ds-check`, `npm run test:tokens`, `npm test` — and those are the floor this project actually guarantees. The agent gates sit on top: the gate LOGIC is `python3` reading JSON on stdin and is portable, while the BINDING is per-harness because every harness announces its events differently. `.claude/` is therefore **one adapter, not the mechanism**, and the prose now says so. Tooling may be tuned for the harness in the chair; documentation may never assume it. **[Update 2026-10-01 ([agent-files-and-docs-layout](#agent-files-and-docs-layout)): Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` natively from v2.1.277 when the project holds no `CLAUDE.md` (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#agents-md), so `--init` writes no `CLAUDE.md`. The root `AGENTS.md` now holds the rules for contributors to this repository and does not ship. The consumer rules live in `skills/dsiab/references/rules.md`, and `--init` writes them into a consumer project as `AGENTS.md`.]**

### governance-model

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**Governance here is written down and checked by machine, because no second team exists to hold the conversations a standard governance model runs on.**

**Why.** The reference governance model for a design system assumes a design system team and a product team who talk, and its pivot is the conversation in which they agree whether a need belongs to one product or to the system. This project is a small maintainer group with agents, and its product team is an unknown future consumer who installs a package and meets nobody, so each step that runs on a conversation becomes an artefact or does not happen.

**Translated.**

- Ask and talk: the registry answers in writing first, through an entry with `status: out-of-scope` and its reason, so the question "why is there no X" finds its answer when it arises.
- One product or the system: a consumer who needs to own one component copies its source file from the release tag on GitHub, and a need that belongs in the system becomes a surfaced gap.
- Review gates: guard lanes, because a review that depends on memory is the step an unattended agent skips. axe runs on every story in two appearance lanes, beside the control box check, registry parity and `ds-check` over consumer code.
- Trial in an application before release: `npm run test:publish` packs the real tarball, installs it in a throwaway app and reads computed values in a browser.

**Kept as written.** Governance exists to stop entropy, it fits the organisation rather than a copied template, and it deserves a fresh look when users grow frustrated, because frustration is the signal that the process no longer holds. For that reason this ledger records each rule together with the defect that produced it.

**Handover.** Artefact-first is a floor, because a system in a box exists to pass to an engineer or a team. Each guard states the defect it prevents and how to satisfy it, each ruling records its reasoning, `docs/REFERENCES.md` records what was adopted and rejected, and when a second party exists the conversation steps of the reference model return and take precedence. The test for any addition to this process is whether an engineer who joined this week can follow it, disagree with it and change it.

| Handover shape | What the model owes |
|---|---|
| One engineer inherits it | Legibility: the reasoning travels with the rule. |
| A designer and an engineer share it | Both surfaces stay first class. A change to what a component looks like owes a rendered specimen, and a change to what it promises owes a guard. |
| A suite of systems absorbs it | The system works as one layer among several: every token is a `--ds-*` name, every rule sits under `.radix-themes`, `!important` is banned, and brand and neutral are runtime props, so a host system can re-skin it without touching it. |

**Gaps.** Recorded on 2026-09-20, and not fixed by this ruling:

- No stated release cadence.
- No support protocol or intake channel for a consumer who meets a gap. The repository was private, so the `homepage` and `bugs` URLs led nowhere.
- No cross-browser testing, because the suite runs in one Chromium engine.
- No governance inheritance. Under a parent system this ledger would need to record which rulings are its own to make and which it inherits.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20.

- [docs-hosting](#docs-hosting) points the `homepage` URL at the hosted documentation.
- [agent-files-and-docs-layout](#agent-files-and-docs-layout) removes `dsiab eject` from the package, so the one-off route is a component file copied from the release tag.
- [contribution-threshold](#contribution-threshold) adds the written contribution route with its three-use threshold, the private security route and a code of conduct, which answers part of the missing intake channel.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Governance here is written down and machine-checked, because there is no second team to talk to (2026-09-20).** The reference governance model for a design system assumes two parties, a design system team and a product team, who TALK. Its pivot is a conversation: a product team cannot find a component, reaches out through a support channel, and the two sides agree whether the need is a snowflake for one product or a change to the system, then prototype, review, build, review again, document, release, and the product team adopts and reports back. **That process is sound and most of it does not transfer, for one structural reason: this project has no second team.** It is a small maintainer group plus agents, and the product team is a future consumer, unknown, who installs a package and never meets anybody. Every step of the reference model that runs on a conversation therefore has to become an ARTEFACT, or it does not happen at all. **What is adopted, translated.** *Reach out and talk* becomes the registry answering in writing before anybody asks, through `status: out-of-scope` carrying a reason, so "why is there no X" is answered at the moment the question occurs rather than in a thread. *Agree snowflake or system* becomes two shipped routes: `dsiab eject` records a consumer's one-off in `dsiab.json`, and "surface the gap" covers anything that should come back into the system instead. *The internal review gates* become the guard lanes, because a review that depends on somebody remembering to look is exactly what an unattended agent skips, so axe runs on every story in two appearance lanes, alongside the box law, registry parity and `ds-check` over consumer code. *Trial in applications before release* already exists as `npm run test:publish`, which packs the real tarball, installs it into a throwaway app and reads computed values out of a browser. **What is adopted without translation, because it concerns temperament rather than team shape:** governance exists to stop entropy, it must fit the organisation rather than be copied, and it should be revisited when users get frustrated, because frustration is the signal that the process has stopped holding. That is the argument for this ledger recording the rule AND the defect that produced it. **THE GAPS IT EXPOSES, recorded rather than quietly carried.** There is no stated release cadence, so releases happen whenever work happens. There is no support protocol or intake channel for a consumer who hits a gap, and the repository is private, so the `homepage` and `bugs` URLs resolve to nothing: a consumer today has no route back at all, which is the weakest point in this model. Cross-browser testing does not exist, because the suite drives a single Chromium engine. Each is a real hole in the loop the reference model closes, and none is fixed here. **AND THE MODEL MUST SCALE PAST THE PEOPLE CURRENTLY IN IT.** The adaptation above is written for how this system is maintained today, which is a small group working with agents, but a system in a box exists to be handed over: the realistic future is an engineer, or a team of them, picking it up and extending it. So artefact-first is a FLOOR rather than a ceiling, and two obligations follow from that. First, every mechanism has to explain itself to a human who was not here: a guard states the defect it prevents and how to satisfy it, a ruling records the reasoning and not only the outcome, and `REFERENCES.md` says what was adopted or rejected so a newcomer inherits the research instead of repeating it. A gate whose only rationale is institutional memory fails the day the memory leaves. Second, the process has to DEGRADE GRACEFULLY UPWARD: when a second party does exist, the conversation steps of the reference model become available again and should be used, because a real conversation beats an artefact whenever one is actually possible. Nothing recorded here forbids that, and the artefacts stay useful underneath it, because they are what a conversation would otherwise have to reconstruct from scratch. The test for any future addition to this process is therefore not whether an agent can follow it, but whether an engineer who joined this week can follow it, disagree with it, and change it. **THREE HANDOVER SHAPES ARE PLAUSIBLE AND THE MODEL HAS TO SURVIVE ALL THREE.** *One engineer inherits it.* This is the case the paragraph above is written for, and the obligation is legibility: the reasoning has to travel with the rule. *A designer and an engineer share ownership.* This is the healthiest shape and the artefacts already split along that seam, but only if both halves stay first class. The design language, the rendered specimens and the token layer are the designer's surface, and Storybook is the source of truth there precisely because a running page is reviewable by somebody who does not read the source. The API, the guards and the types are the engineer's surface. Shared ownership fails when one of those decays into a by-product of the other, so a change that alters what a component LOOKS like owes a rendered specimen, and a change that alters what it PROMISES owes a guard, and neither substitutes for the other. *It is absorbed into a suite of systems.* Then this stops being the top-level authority and becomes one layer among several, which is a harder constraint than either of the others and is already partly designed for: every token is namespaced `--ds-*`, every rule is scoped under `.radix-themes`, `!important` is banned so a parent layer can always win, and brand and neutral are runtime props rather than a build-time fork, so a host system can re-skin this one without touching it. What is NOT yet designed for is governance inheritance: this ledger currently reads as final authority, and under a parent system it would need to record which rulings are ours to make and which we inherit. That is unresolved and is named here rather than assumed away. **[Update 2026-10-01 ([agent-files-and-docs-layout](#agent-files-and-docs-layout), [contribution-threshold](#contribution-threshold)): `dsiab eject` left the package, so the one-off route is now a component file that a consumer copies from the release tag on GitHub and owns in their own project. The surface-the-gap route stays for anything that belongs in the system. [contribution-threshold](#contribution-threshold) adds the written contribution route with its three-use threshold, the private security route and a code of conduct, which answers part of the missing intake channel that this entry records.]**

- The first public release is `0.9.0` on the `latest` dist-tag.
- Release candidates publish to the `next` dist-tag.
- A release tag is the bare version with no "v", because the changelog uses the tag name as its section heading.

It publishes on public npm and stays pre-1.0. The first public release is `0.9.0` on the `latest` dist-tag, and release candidates publish to `next`.
