### changelog-regeneration

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**The changelog regenerates after every commit on `main`.**

**What runs.** A `post-commit` hook, `scripts/git-hooks/post-commit`, the sibling of `post-merge`, runs `scripts/gen-changelog.mjs` after a commit on `main`. It commits `CHANGELOG.md` and `src/foundations/changelog.generated.ts` by pathspec, so nothing else in the index moves.

**No loop.** The generator keeps only feat, fix and breaking commits. The chore commit the hook makes changes nothing the next pass reads, so that pass finds no difference.

**Skipped.**

- on any branch other than `main`
- during a rebase
- when `DS_CHANGELOG_HOOK=off` is set

**No prepack step.** The package has no `prepack` step on purpose. A pack from a shallow clone or a clone with no history would regenerate an empty changelog and ship it.

**Changed from.** Only the `post-merge` hook regenerated the changelog, so it covered work that arrived by merge and missed direct commits on `main`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The changelog regenerates after every commit on `main` (2026-09-24).** A `post-commit` hook, the sibling of `post-merge`, runs `scripts/gen-changelog.mjs` after a commit on `main` and commits `CHANGELOG.md` and `src/foundations/changelog.generated.ts` by pathspec, so nothing else in the index moves. It cannot loop: the generator keeps only feat, fix and breaking commits, so the chore commit it makes changes nothing the next pass reads, and that pass finds no difference. It skips work off `main`, during a rebase, and when `DS_CHANGELOG_HOOK=off` is set. There is deliberately no `prepack` step, because a pack from a shallow or history-free clone would regenerate an empty changelog and ship it.

### internal-hooks

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**Five internal hooks stay unexported, and every module under `src/hooks` needs a registry entry or a recorded reason to stay internal.**

**Applies to.** `useGridFocus`, `useListFocus`, `useScrollOverflow`, `useFieldGroupControl` and `useGroupItemDescribedBy`. Each ships inside the bundle because a shipped component calls it, and none is exported.

**Why.** The test is the one [registry-module-paths](#registry-module-paths) applies: an export added later is safe and an export removed later breaks consumers, so a name ships when a consumer need is shown, not because its code already sits in the package. Libraries whose product is the behaviour, such as React Aria, Floating UI and Ariakit, publish these primitives, and styled systems built on primitives, Radix among them, keep them inside. This system is the second kind, and a consumer who builds a composite of their own is directed to the first.

**Each hook.**

| Hook | Decision | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `useFieldGroupControl`, `useGroupItemDescribedBy` | Withheld with `FieldGroup` | Both read the group context that only `FieldGroup.Root` provides, and `FieldGroup` does not ship. Outside one, the first throws and the second only joins two id strings. The `Field` entry in `registry.json` lists both in `internalExports`. |
| `useGridFocus` | Withheld | Its one caller, `Calendar`, shaped its API: Page Up and Page Down call back with no event, and the caller passes the writing direction as an argument. Publishing it would freeze both. |
| `useListFocus` | Withheld | It is about a hundred lines of index arithmetic with no right-to-left handling, and Astryx ([catalog-as-specification](#catalog-as-specification)) publishes a different hook under the same name. |
| `useScrollOverflow` | Deferred | It is generic, and `Carousel` ships the pattern it serves. It is published the first time a consumer needs edge-overflow state on a scroller of their own, as the hook and `ScrollOverflowState` only. |

**Guard.** Arm D of `src/foundations/barrel.node-check.ts` walks `src/components/ui` and `src/hooks` from one `WALKED_DIRS` list. `INTERNAL_MODULES` maps each internal module, keyed by a path such as `hooks/useGridFocus`, to a one-line reason. A new module under `src/hooks` with no registry entry and no line fails, and the failure prints a registry entry ready to paste. Arm C fails a line whose file is gone, whose module is now registered, whose reason is empty, or whose directory arm D does not walk.

**Gap.**

- `useResizable` is internal, but the published `ResizeHandle` takes its `separatorProps` and `onDragStart` from that hook, so a consumer has no supported way to use `ResizeHandle` outside `Layout` and `SideNav`. The hook's `SeparatorProps` type also shares a name with the published `Separator` props. Publishing the hook or narrowing `ResizeHandle` is a separate decision.
- Arm D does not walk `src/utils`, `src/dates`, `src/palette`, `src/powersearch` or `src/theme` yet.
- Whether the `Field` and `FieldGroup` shell ships stays an open gap.

**Changed from.** Three of the five hooks carried no record either way, and arm D walked only `src/components/ui`, so sixteen of the eighteen modules under `src/hooks` had no decision behind them.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Five internal hooks stay internal, and `src/hooks` can no longer hold an undecided module (2026-09-24).** `useGridFocus`, `useListFocus`, `useScrollOverflow`, `useFieldGroupControl` and `useGroupItemDescribedBy` ship inside the bundle because shipped components call them, and none is exported. Three of them carried no record either way, and this entry is that record. The test applied to each is the one [registry-module-paths](#registry-module-paths) applied: adding an export later is safe and removing one breaks, so a name ships when a consumer need is shown, not because its bytes are already in the package. **The two group hooks follow `FieldGroup`.** Both read the group context that only `FieldGroup.Root` provides, and `FieldGroup` does not ship. Outside one, `useFieldGroupControl` throws and `useGroupItemDescribedBy` reduces to joining two id strings, so publishing either alone ships a name that is broken or trivial for every consumer. The `Field` entry withholds both in `internalExports`. If `FieldGroup` is published to close the group-validation gap, `CheckboxGroup` and `RadioGroup` already wire themselves to it, and these two stay withheld unless a hand-built group becomes a supported extension point. The `Field` entry rules that out for hand-built inputs. This entry rules on the two hooks only. Whether the `Field` and `FieldGroup` shell ships stays an open gap. **`useGridFocus` is withheld because one caller shaped its API.** Page Up and Page Down call back with no event, so `Calendar` intercepts Shift+Page Up before the hook sees it, and right-to-left has to be passed in rather than detected. Publishing it would freeze both. **`useListFocus` is withheld because it is small, has no right-to-left handling, and its name is taken.** It is about a hundred lines of index arithmetic over `querySelectorAll`, and it only moves focus, leaving the tab stop to its caller. Astryx ([catalog-as-specification](#catalog-as-specification)) publishes a different hook under the same name, with a vertical default, a menu-item default selector, boundary scoping, Escape handling, optional roving-tabindex ownership and automatic right-to-left detection, so a reader who knows one would misuse the other. **`useScrollOverflow` is deferred, not refused.** It is generic and reaches nothing private except the shared `ResizeObserver`, and `Carousel` ships the pattern it serves. It is published the first time a consumer needs edge-overflow state on a scroller of their own, as the hook and `ScrollOverflowState` only. `computeOverflow`, `scrollByViewport` and `prefersReducedMotion` stay withheld, the last because `useMediaQuery("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)")` already answers it and updates when the setting changes. **Prior art sets the default.** Libraries whose product is the behaviour publish these primitives with documentation and tests of their own: React Aria (`useGridList`, `useFocusManager`), Floating UI (`useListNavigation`, `Composite`) and Ariakit (`Composite`). Styled systems built on primitives keep them inside. Radix ships `RovingFocusGroup` only as a package whose readme calls it an internal utility not intended for public usage, and Ark UI and Zag document no roving-focus utility. This system is the second kind, and a consumer building a composite of their own is pointed at the first. Sources are in `REFERENCES.md` under this entry. **Guard.** Arm D of `barrel.node-check.ts` walked only `src/components/ui`, so a module under `src/hooks` that no entry names reached no arm, and sixteen of the eighteen modules there sat in that state. Arm D now walks `src/components/ui` and `src/hooks` from one `WALKED_DIRS` list. `INTERNAL_MODULES` is now a record from module to a one-line reason, and it takes path keys such as `hooks/useGridFocus`, resolved under `src/` the way a registry `module` is ([registry-module-paths](#registry-module-paths)). All sixteen carry a reason drawn from their real callers. The next module added to `src/hooks` with no entry and no line fails, and the failure prints a paste-ready path-module entry. Arm C keeps its two rot checks, a missing file and a module that is now registered, and adds two more: a line with an empty reason and a line whose directory arm D does not walk. Each arm was red-probed in a scratch copy of the repository. Dropping the `hooks/useGridFocus` line failed arm D on that module. A throwaway unregistered hook failed arm D with its entry printed, and pasting that entry and running `npm run barrel` turned it green. The previous guard stayed green against the same throwaway hook. **Recorded, not closed.** Two gaps surfaced during the classification. `useResizable` is allowlisted because nothing public exports it today, but `ResizeHandle` is published, takes its `separatorProps` and `onDragStart` from this hook, and its own docs page tells the consumer to own the `useResizable` call. As a result, a consumer has no supported way to use `ResizeHandle` outside `Layout` and `SideNav`, and the hook's `SeparatorProps` type shares a name with the published `Separator` props. Publishing the hook or narrowing `ResizeHandle` is a separate decision. The other directories [registry-module-paths](#registry-module-paths) made publishable, `src/utils`, `src/dates`, `src/palette`, `src/powersearch` and `src/theme`, are not walked by arm D yet.

### docs-hosting

**Tags.** `DOCUMENTATION`, `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**The documentation is hosted on Cloudflare Pages at one permanent URL per release, and the `dsiab-docs` package is retired.**

**Addresses.** `bin/docs-url.mjs` is the one source for every docs URL.

- The latest stable release: `https://dsiab.pages.dev`, also the `homepage` in `package.json` and the Documentation line of the README.
- One release: `https://v<version>.dsiab.pages.dev`, where every run of characters other than a lowercase letter or a digit becomes one hyphen, so 0.9.0 is at `https://v0-9-0.dsiab.pages.dev`.

**Deploy.** `.github/workflows/docs.yml` builds the Storybook on a bare semver tag or a manual run, deploys it to the release address, then to the latest address, and stops unless the tag equals the manifest version. A release candidate deploys only to its own address, because it publishes to the npm `next` tag, and a manual run can promote one with the `latest` input.

**The CLI.** In a source checkout after `npm run build-storybook`, `dsiab docs` serves the built bundle locally from `bin/dsiab-docs.mjs`. Anywhere else it prints the address for the installed version and opens it, and `--no-open` prints the address only, with no server and no network request.

**Why.** A consumer could not reach the docs by any route, because the docs were not hosted and the `dsiab-docs` package was never published. Pages keeps the version pinning of the package plan with no 23 MB download, serves static requests free, deploys a private repository with Direct Upload, and takes a custom domain with one CNAME (canonical name) record.

**Rejected.**

- GitHub Pages needs a public repository or a paid plan, and puts the account in the URL.
- The Netlify free tier stops at a hard credit limit.
- The Vercel free tier is for non-commercial use only, and puts the username in preview URLs.
- Chromatic charges for a custom domain.

**Changed from.** An earlier plan held that hosting was not needed and shipped the docs as a separate `dsiab-docs` package. `dsiab docs` from an install ran `npx dsiab-docs@<version>` and printed the npm 404, and a build script of its own, run by `npm run pack:docs` and `npm run build:docs`, built that package, all retired by this ruling.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The docs are hosted on Cloudflare Pages, with one permanent URL per release, and the `dsiab-docs` package is retired (2026-09-24).** This supersedes the installed-package and registry-fetch routes of the earlier `dsiab-docs` package plan, and that plan's framing that hosting was not a need. `bin/docs-url.mjs` is the one source for every docs URL. The latest release is at `https://dsiab.pages.dev`. Each release is at `https://v<version>.dsiab.pages.dev`, where every run of characters other than a lowercase letter or a digit becomes one hyphen, so 0.9.0 is at `https://v0-9-0.dsiab.pages.dev`. `.github/workflows/docs.yml` builds the Storybook on a bare semver tag or a manual run. It deploys `storybook-static` to the Pages project `dsiab` with `cloudflare/wrangler-action`, first to the branch `v<hyphenated version>` for the permanent alias, then to `main` for latest. A release candidate deploys only its own alias, because it publishes to npm `next` and must not replace the pages a `latest` install reads. A manual run can promote one with the `latest` input. The workflow reads the branch name from the same module the CLI reads, and the run stops unless the tag equals the manifest version. Rationale: a consumer could not reach the docs by any route. The README said the docs were not hosted. `dsiab docs` from an install fell through to `npx dsiab-docs@<version>` and printed npm's raw 404, because the package was never published. Every link on the npm page led to a private repository. The registry-fetch route never ran, and it was the only route an installed user had. Hosting gives the same version pinning the package plan wanted, with no 23 MB download and no second package to publish at every release, and each publish needs the maintainer's approval. The second manifest also copied the author and repository fields into a second public artefact. Pages was chosen over GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel and Chromatic. Static requests are free with no bandwidth meter. Direct Upload never reads the repository, so it works while the repository is private. A later custom domain is one CNAME (canonical name) record from any DNS provider. Every branch keeps a permanent alias served with `noindex`. The default URL carries the project name and no account name. GitHub Pages needs a public repository or a paid plan and puts the account in the URL. The Netlify free tier stops at a hard credit limit. The Vercel free tier is for non-commercial use only and puts the username in preview URLs. Chromatic charges for a custom domain. **The CLI.** `dsiab docs` keeps the source-checkout route unchanged: with `bin/dsiab-docs.mjs` and a built `storybook-static/` beside it, it serves the bundle locally. Anywhere else it prints `dsiab <version> docs → <that version's URL>` and opens it, and `--no-open` prints the URL only. It starts no server and uses no network. Help lists `docs [--no-open]` as 'open the documentation for this exact version', because the old text, 'serve this system's Storybook locally, from disk', described a route no installed user had. **Retired:** `scripts/build-docs-package.mjs`, `npm run pack:docs`, `npm run build:docs`, the generated `dsiab-docs` manifest and its guard. `bin/dsiab-docs.mjs` stays as the checkout server, and it stays out of the tarball. **Guard:** `src/foundations/docs-url.node-check.ts` asserts the URLs for `0.9.0` and `0.9.0-rc.1`. It asserts that Pages' own alias normalisation returns every branch the module builds unchanged, because a mismatch would send installed users to a page that does not exist. It fails on a version whose alias Pages would cut at 28 characters. It holds `package.json` `homepage` and the README Documentation line to the constant, and it keeps the server out of `files[]`. A drifted homepage, a drifted README line and a removed length cap each turned it red. The publish gate runs `dsiab docs --no-open` from the real install with every socket connect and DNS lookup made fatal, and checks the printed URL. **Unverified, and stated as such:** no deploy ran yet. A deploy needs the Cloudflare project and the two repository secrets, and the first public deploy needs the maintainer's approval.

### sidebar-order

**Tags.** `DOCUMENTATION`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-25.

**The sidebar reads Index, Foundations, Components, UI examples, then `_internal`, and Index is the front door.**

**The order.**

- `Index` is the one page at the root of the sidebar.
- `Foundations` follows.
- `Components` holds the system's wrappers in twelve categories, as `Components/<Category>/<Name>`.
- `UI examples` holds the eight recreations, one leaf each, as `UI examples/<Name>`.
- `_internal` comes last and opens collapsed. Its first page, `About this section`, says the fixtures are tests that keep the docs honest and are not guidance.

**Index.** The page reads like `README.md`: what the system is, the install, how the sidebar is organised, the rules that bind consumer code, the accessibility scope, and where decisions and changes live. A live list of pages follows, read from Storybook's own index, and it omits `_internal`.

**Amends.**

- [system-wrapper-layer](#system-wrapper-layer) kept the `Components/*` name for raw Radix showcases. Those pages no longer exist, so the name now titles the wrappers.
- [showcases-and-fixture](#showcases-and-fixture), on placement only. Among the root pages the recreations read as eight more sections and pushed the component reference below them, so they move into one folder after Components. The rest of that ruling stands: at rest, full-bleed, axe off, exactly one story, no `play`.

**Enforced by.** The `storySort` order in `.storybook/preview.tsx`, the titles and `SHOWCASE_FOLDER` in `src/foundations/showcases.ts`, and three guards:

- `showcases.node-check.ts` holds each recreation's title to `UI examples/<Name>`, its story name to `<Name>`, and the `storySort` folder to the order of `SHOWCASES`.
- `story-category.node-check.ts` and `story-category-order.node-check.ts` hold every component to `Components/<Category>/<Name>`.

**Guidance.** The maintainer ruled this order on 2026-09-25.

**Changed from.** The eight recreations sat among the root pages, the component library was called "System", and Index was a raw list of links that included the test fixtures.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-25. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The sidebar reads Index, Foundations, Components, UI examples, then `_internal`, and Index is the front door (2026-09-25).** Ruled by the maintainer on 2026-09-25. The sidebar placed the eight recreations among the root pages, called the component library "System", and its Index was a raw link list that included the test fixtures. **The order.** `Index` is the one root-level page. `Foundations` follows, then `Components`, which is the old `System` root under the name a reader expects, with its twelve categories unchanged. `UI examples` holds the eight recreations, one leaf each: every file names its single story after its title, and Storybook shows a lone story whose name matches its component as a leaf. `_internal` comes last and opens collapsed. Its first page, `About this section`, says the fixtures are tests that keep the docs honest and are not guidance. **Index reads like `README.md`:** what the system is, the install, how the sidebar is organised, the rules that bind consumer code, the accessibility scope, and where decisions and changes live. The live page list follows, read from Storybook's own index, and it omits `_internal`. **This amends [system-wrapper-layer](#system-wrapper-layer).** That entry kept the `Components/*` name for raw Radix showcases. Those showcases no longer exist, so the name is free, and it now titles the opinionated wrappers. **This amends [showcases-and-fixture](#showcases-and-fixture) on placement only.** [showcases-and-fixture](#showcases-and-fixture) put the recreations at the sidebar root so a newcomer would find them without a click. Among the root pages they read as eight more sections and put the component reference below them, so they move into one folder after Components. Everything else [showcases-and-fixture](#showcases-and-fixture) ruled stands: at rest, full-bleed, axe off, exactly one story, no `play`. **Mechanism:** the storySort literal in `.storybook/preview.tsx`, the titles and `SHOWCASE_FOLDER` in `src/foundations/showcases.ts`, and three guards. `showcases.node-check.ts` holds a showcase title to `UI examples/<Name>`, its story name to `<Name>`, and the storySort folder to `SHOWCASES` order. `story-category.node-check.ts` and `story-category-order.node-check.ts` hold every component to `Components/<Category>/<Name>`. `isShowcaseStory` now slugs the whole title for its id fallback, because Storybook turns the `/` into a hyphen like any other punctuation.

### storybook-onboarding-card

**Tags.** `DOCUMENTATION`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-28.

**Storybook's onboarding card is off in the dev sidebar.**

**What you see.** The dev server's sidebar starts at the search box and Index, as the public build does. `.storybook/main.ts` sets `features: { sidebarOnboardingChecklist: false }`, and the public build needs no setting, because Storybook draws the card in development only.

**Why.** The card listed Storybook's own onboarding tasks, and none of them belong to this system.

**Not covered.** The gear menu keeps its "Onboarding guide" line. Storybook 10.4.6 has no flag for it, and the `menuOnboardingChecklist` flag of Storybook 10.6 needs an upgrade.

**Open tasks.** Of the card's 20 tasks that apply to this setup, checked on 2026-09-28, the system met 10 by its own means, five do not apply, and publishing is a release step under [docs-hosting](#docs-hosting). Four stay open, on three topics:

- No workflow runs the gates in CI.
- No test compares a rendered story against a stored image.
- No coverage report is configured.

**Deferred.**

- The image comparison uses the `toMatchScreenshot` assertion of Vitest browser mode, with its built-in pixelmatch comparator and no hosted service. It lands after 0.9.0 as an enhancement, and it depends on the CI question, because its reference images differ by browser and operating system.
- A coverage report lands after the image comparison, through `@vitest/coverage-v8` and a `coverage` block in both Vitest configurations.
- The "Run tests" widget at the foot of the dev sidebar cannot start Vitest, and a click ends the dev server. It ships in 0.9.0 as a known defect, with its fix after 0.9.0. `npx vitest run` does not use the widget and is unaffected.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved removing the card from the dev sidebar on 2026-09-28. After the task check that day, the maintainer ruled the image comparison and the coverage report enhancements after 0.9.0, deferred and not dropped, and accepted the "Run tests" widget in 0.9.0 as a known defect.

**Changed from.** The dev sidebar opened on a checklist card that read "Level up 56%" above the search box, with three open tasks.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-28. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Storybook's onboarding card is off in the dev sidebar (2026-09-28).** Approved by the maintainer as option B of decision 11. Storybook 10.4.6 draws a checklist card at the top of the dev server's sidebar with Storybook's own onboarding tasks, none of which belong to this system. `.storybook/main.ts` sets `features: { sidebarOnboardingChecklist: false }`. The public build needs nothing, because `storybook build` writes `CONFIG_TYPE = "PRODUCTION"` and Storybook draws the card only in development. **Measured before**, on the dev server: the card read "Level up 56%" above the search box, with three open tasks. **Measured after**, the same way: the sidebar starts at the search box and Index, as the public build does. The gear menu keeps its "Onboarding guide" line, because 10.4.6 has no flag for it, and the `menuOnboardingChecklist` flag of Storybook 10.6 waits on an upgrade. **The checklist, checked against the repository on 2026-09-28.** Of its 20 tasks that apply to this setup, 10 are done by the system's own means: 735 stories render, 91 pages sit under `Components`, 734 of 735 titles sit under a root, 91 story files switch Controls on for their Props page, 484 stories carry a play function, the Vitest and accessibility addons are registered, and `npx vitest run` runs every story in both appearance lanes with axe failing the test on a violation, bar the registered opt-outs. The checklist asks for those runs from the sidebar widget, and the command line does the same work. Five do not apply: the release notes page, the viewport toolbar tutorial, and the Docs addon, autodocs and MDX, because every page is a story on the shared `_storyKit` spine and the Props pages replace autodocs. Publishing is release step 4, through [docs-hosting](#docs-hosting). Four stay open, on three topics: no workflow runs the gates in CI, no test compares a rendered story against a stored image (the checklist's Chromatic install and run), and no coverage report is configured. **Found on the way, recorded and NOT FIXED:** the "Run tests" widget at the foot of the dev sidebar cannot start Vitest. Reproduced on 2026-09-28 with one click: the log reads `Project name "vitest.config.ts" is not unique` and `Failed to start test runner process`, and the dev server then exited with code 1. The same messages preceded an earlier exit of the dev server that day. `npx vitest run` does not use the widget and is unaffected. **Ruled by the maintainer on 2026-09-28, after that check.** The image comparison uses the `toMatchScreenshot` assertion that the installed Vitest browser mode ships, with its built-in pixelmatch comparator, and no hosted service. It lands after 0.9.0 as an enhancement, deferred and not dropped, so the release does not wait on it. Its reference images differ by browser and operating system, so the machine that takes them is the machine that checks them, which ties it to the CI question. The Run tests widget ships in 0.9.0 as a known defect, and its fix lands after 0.9.0: with the card off, no onboarding task links to it, and a click still ends the dev server. A coverage report lands after the image comparison, also as an enhancement, through `@vitest/coverage-v8` and a `coverage` block in both Vitest configurations.

### test-browser-order

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-28.

**The story suite and the publish gate run in the browser `DS_BROWSER_PATH` names, or else in Playwright's own Chromium, and no maintainer browser sits in the default order.**

**What you see.** `scripts/browser.mjs` picks the browser for `npm test` and `npm run test:publish`: `DS_BROWSER_PATH` when it names an existing file, otherwise Playwright's own Chromium. `npx playwright install chromium` installs that browser once per machine.

**Why.** Every machine then runs the same browser version, which the planned image comparison and CI need.

**Scope.**

- Playwright stays a development dependency, so a consumer who installs the package from npm receives neither Playwright nor a browser.
- The docs no longer promise that nothing downloads a browser.
- A maintainer names a personal browser in a local environment, outside the repository.
- The wait for a built-in uBlock Origin stays, as support for any Chromium build that bundles it, because `DS_BROWSER_PATH` may name such a build.
- `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, the skill, `vitest.config.ts`, `.storybook/main.ts` and `scripts/acceptance.mjs` state this order.

**Not verified.** The fallback to Playwright's own Chromium was checked as the launch options it returns, with no executable path and no channel. As of 2026-09-28 no run in that browser was made on the maintainer's machine.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved this order on 2026-09-28.

**Changed from.** The order was `DS_BROWSER_PATH`, then Helium, then Playwright's Chrome channel ([story-tests-in-browser](#story-tests-in-browser)).

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-28. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The test browser is `DS_BROWSER_PATH` or Playwright's own Chromium, and no maintainer browser sits in the default order (2026-09-28).** Approved by the maintainer as option B of decision 14, with three choices inside it. The story suite and `test:publish` resolve the browser through `scripts/browser.mjs`: `DS_BROWSER_PATH` when it names an existing file, otherwise Playwright's own Chromium. `npx playwright install chromium` installs that once per machine, and every machine then runs the same version, which the planned image comparison and CI need. The Chrome channel and the named Helium path leave the order, so the docs no longer promise that nothing downloads a browser. Playwright stays a development dependency, so a consumer who installs the package from npm receives neither Playwright nor a browser. The wait for a built-in uBlock Origin stays, described as support for any Chromium build that bundles it, because a machine that names such a build through `DS_BROWSER_PATH` still needs it. A maintainer names a personal browser in a local environment, outside the repository. `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, the skill, `vitest.config.ts`, `.storybook/main.ts` and `scripts/acceptance.mjs` state the new order. **Limits.** The fallback to Playwright's own Chromium was checked as the launch options it returns, with no executable path and no channel, and a run in that browser has not been made on the maintainer's machine.

### agent-files-and-docs-layout

**Tags.** `INSTALL`, `CONTRIBUTING`, `DOCUMENTATION`. **Ruled.** 2026-10-01.

**Public documents live in `docs/`, Agent Skills live in `skills/`, and `--init` writes seven marked files.**

**Layout.**

- `docs/` holds the public documents, `docs/GUIDELINES.md`, `docs/DECISIONS.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md` and `docs/AGENT-SETUP.md`, and nothing private.
- `skills/` holds four skills in the Agent Skills format (https://agentskills.io/specification): `dsiab`, the skill a consumer's agent reads, and the three reviewers `design-system-steward`, `docs-steward` and `pattern-steward`.
- The root `AGENTS.md` holds the rules for work in this repository and does not ship. The consumer rules live in `skills/dsiab/references/rules.md`, inside the skill.

**What ships.** Only the `dsiab` and `design-system-steward` skills ship, because `docs-steward` and `pattern-steward` review this repository's own documentation and patterns. The eject command left the package, so a consumer who needs to own one component copies its source file from the release tag on GitHub.

**What `--init` writes.** `npx ds-check --init [dir] [--force]` writes exactly these seven files, and no `CLAUDE.md`, no `GEMINI.md`, no settings file, no hook, and nothing under `.codex/`, `.github/` or `.gemini/`.

| File | Carries |
|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` | The consumer rules, under a one-line HTML comment header |
| `.agents/skills/dsiab/SKILL.md` and `.agents/skills/dsiab/references/rules.md` | The skill, for harnesses that read `.agents/skills` |
| `.claude/skills/dsiab/SKILL.md` and `.claude/skills/dsiab/references/rules.md` | The skill, for Claude Code |
| `.agents/skills/design-system-steward/SKILL.md` | The reviewer |
| `.claude/agents/design-system-steward.md` | The Claude Code agent generated from the reviewer skill, with the same name, description and body, plus a tool list and `model: inherit` |

**Ownership.** Every file init writes carries the marker `dsiab-managed`, in the header of `AGENTS.md` and as `dsiab-managed: "true"` under `metadata:` in the frontmatter of each skill and of the agent. Init reports each file in one of four states:

- `WROTE`: a new file.
- `ALREADY CURRENT`: a marked file that matches.
- `KEPT`: a marked file that differs, which `--force` replaces.
- `YOURS`: a file with no marker, which init never replaces, with or without `--force`. When `AGENTS.md` is `YOURS`, init prints a sentence any tool follows and an `@node_modules/dsiab/skills/dsiab/references/rules.md` import line.

**Limits.** The rules file and the init header together stay under 24,000 bytes, because Antigravity truncates a rule file above that size (https://antigravity.google/docs/rules) and drops its last rules with no warning. `npm run agents` gives contributors untracked copies of all four skills and the three reviewers, and the two contributor reviewers carry `readonly: true` and no Write or Edit tool.

**Why.** The Agent Skills format is open and more than one harness reads it, while an agent file belongs to one harness. Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` natively when a project holds no `CLAUDE.md` ([agents-md-context-file](#agents-md-context-file)), so a second context file would add one more copy to maintain.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved this layout and the seven-file init contract on 2026-10-01.

**Changed from.** `--init` wrote eight files, the reviewers were Claude Code agent files, the skill was named `design-system`, and the package shipped an eject command. This ruling amended [agents-md-context-file](#agents-md-context-file) and [governance-model](#governance-model).

**Status.** Ruled 2026-10-01. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Public documents live in `docs/`, Agent Skills live in `skills/`, and `--init` writes seven marked files (2026-10-01).** Approved by the maintainer on 2026-10-01. It supersedes the eight-file `--init` list of the earlier agent layer, and it amends [agents-md-context-file](#agents-md-context-file) and [governance-model](#governance-model). **The layout.** `docs/` holds the public documents, `docs/GUIDELINES.md`, `docs/DECISIONS.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md` and `docs/AGENT-SETUP.md`, and nothing private sits in it any more. `skills/` at the root holds four skills in the Agent Skills format (https://agentskills.io/specification): `dsiab`, the skill a consumer's agent reads, and the three reviewers, `design-system-steward`, `docs-steward` and `pattern-steward`. Each reviewer was a Claude Code agent file and is now a skill, because the Agent Skills format is open and more than one harness reads it, while an agent file belongs to one harness. The skill is named `dsiab`, after the package, in place of `design-system`. **What ships.** Only `dsiab` and `design-system-steward` ship. `docs-steward` and `pattern-steward` review this repository's own documentation and patterns, so they stay with contributors. The root `AGENTS.md` now holds the rules for work in this repository and does not ship. The consumer rules live in `skills/dsiab/references/rules.md`, which ships inside the skill. **The init contract.** `npx ds-check --init [dir] [--force]` writes exactly seven files. `AGENTS.md` carries the consumer rules under a one-line HTML comment header. `.agents/skills/dsiab/SKILL.md`, `.agents/skills/dsiab/references/rules.md`, `.claude/skills/dsiab/SKILL.md` and `.claude/skills/dsiab/references/rules.md` carry the skill twice, once for the harnesses that read `.agents/skills` and once for Claude Code. `.agents/skills/design-system-steward/SKILL.md` carries the reviewer, and `.claude/agents/design-system-steward.md` is the Claude Code agent generated from it: the name and description come from the skill, the file adds a Claude Code tool list and `model: inherit`, and the body matches the skill body byte for byte. Init writes no `CLAUDE.md`, no `GEMINI.md`, no settings file, no hook, and nothing under `.codex/`, `.github/` or `.gemini/`. Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` natively when a project holds no `CLAUDE.md` ([agents-md-context-file](#agents-md-context-file)), so a second context file would only add a copy to keep in step. **Ownership comes from a marker, never from a path.** Every file init writes carries `dsiab-managed`, in the header of `AGENTS.md`, and as `metadata:` frontmatter with `dsiab-managed: "true"` in the skills and the generated agent. Init reports each file in one of four states. WROTE is a new file. ALREADY CURRENT is a marked file that matches. KEPT is a marked file that differs, and `--force` replaces it. ### package-licence

**Tags.** `INSTALL`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-10-01.

**The package licence is `(MIT AND OFL-1.1)`, `LICENSE` holds plain MIT, and every third-party notice sits in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`.**

**What you see.**

- `package.json` `license` reads `(MIT AND OFL-1.1)`, the Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) expression for a package under two licences at once: the code is MIT, and the font files under `dist/assets` are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1.
- `LICENSE` holds the MIT text alone.
- `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` opens with the font paragraph and carries seven sections: the portions derived from Astryx, the Radix Themes stylesheet, Radix Colors, and the four font families Inter, JetBrains Mono, Schibsted Grotesk and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next.

**Why.**

- GitHub detects a licence by matching the file against known licence texts, and a font paragraph inside `LICENSE` blocks that match.
- The bundled Radix Themes stylesheet carries the Radix Colors scales, and their MIT licence names its own copyright holder.
- The Astryx section carries the upstream copyright line word for word, because MIT requires the notice as the holder wrote it.

**File headers.** Each source file derived from Astryx names its upstream path and commit, as [catalog-as-specification](#catalog-as-specification) requires. The headers cite four upstream commits, and section 1 of `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` lists them with their full hashes.

**Gap.** Review alone checks the headers. A guard would read each `Portions derived from facebook/astryx` line and confirm that the named path exists at the named commit, and no such guard exists yet.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved this licence arrangement on 2026-10-01.

**Changed from.** `LICENSE` held the MIT text and a paragraph on the fonts, `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` had no Radix Colors section, and the Astryx headers in 70 files did not match the upstream tree.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-10-01. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The package licence is `(MIT AND OFL-1.1)`, `LICENSE` is plain MIT, and every third-party notice sits in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` (2026-10-01).** Approved by the maintainer on 2026-10-01. The code is MIT and the font files under `dist/assets` are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, so `package.json` `license` reads `(MIT AND OFL-1.1)`, the Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) expression for a package under both licences at once. `LICENSE` holds the MIT text alone, because GitHub detects a licence by matching the file against known licence texts, and the font paragraph inside the old file blocked that match. The font paragraph moved to the top of `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`, which now carries seven sections: the portions derived from Astryx ([catalog-as-specification](#catalog-as-specification)), the Radix Themes stylesheet, Radix Colors, and the four font families, Inter, JetBrains Mono, Schibsted Grotesk and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next. The Radix Colors section is new, because the bundled Radix Themes stylesheet carries the Radix Colors scales, and their MIT licence names its own copyright holder. The Astryx section carries the upstream copyright line verbatim, because MIT requires the notice as the holder wrote it. **The per-file headers.** The [catalog-as-specification](#catalog-as-specification) headers in 70 files were corrected against the upstream tree, and they now cite four upstream commits, which section 1 of `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` lists with their full hashes. **Enforced by** review. No guard checks an [catalog-as-specification](#catalog-as-specification) header against the upstream tree, and that guard is a recorded gap: it would read each `Portions derived from facebook/astryx` line and confirm that the named path exists at the named commit.

### contribution-threshold

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-10-01.

**New surface needs an accepted written proposal and three real uses, a security report goes to a private channel, and the code of conduct is the Contributor Covenant 3.0.**

**Routes.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` sorts a change into four tiers.

| Change | Route |
| --- | --- |
| A bug fix, a docs correction or a token-value fix | A pull request directly |
| A small enhancement inside an existing component | A one-line issue first |
| A new component, token family or pattern, or a large edit to one | An accepted written proposal first |
| A system-wide change | The maintainer alone |

**Proposal.** A proposal names the need and the places that use it, what already exists, the prior art under [prior-art-required](#prior-art-required), what it leaves out, the cost to own it, the alternatives and the drawbacks. The threshold is three real uses, because one use is a snowflake for one product ([governance-model](#governance-model)) and three show a shared need that justifies the cost to own it, and review checks the count, since no guard does.

**Outcomes.**

- Pursue: the entry enters `registry.json` as `planned`.
- More evidence: the issue stays open with the evidence it needs.
- Not in the system: the entry enters `registry.json` as `out-of-scope` with its reason, so the next person with the same need finds the answer ([component-registry](#component-registry)).

**Security and conduct.** `SECURITY.md` sends a vulnerability report to GitHub private vulnerability reporting, from the Security tab of the repository, and never to a public issue, because a public report discloses the flaw before a fix exists. The current release and the current release candidate receive fixes on a best-effort basis, and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` adopts the Contributor Covenant 3.0 with reports to GitHub Support, because the project has no reporting address of its own yet.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved the three-use threshold, the private security route and the code of conduct on 2026-10-01. Review enforces all three files, which sit at the repository root.

**Changed from.** No written route took a contribution into the system, and [governance-model](#governance-model) recorded that intake gap. This ruling closes part of it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-10-01. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **New surface needs three real uses, security reports stay private, and the code of conduct is the Contributor Covenant 3.0 (2026-10-01).** Approved by the maintainer on 2026-10-01. **The contribution threshold.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` sorts a change into four tiers. A bug fix, a docs correction or a token-value fix arrives as a pull request directly. A small enhancement inside an existing component needs a one-line issue first. A new component, token family or pattern, or a large edit to one, needs an accepted written proposal first. A system-wide change belongs to the maintainer alone. The proposal names the need and the places that use it, what already exists, the prior art under [prior-art-required](#prior-art-required), what it leaves out, the cost to own it, the alternatives and the drawbacks. The threshold is three real uses, because one use is a snowflake for one product ([governance-model](#governance-model)), and three show a shared need that justifies the cost to own it. Review checks the count, and no guard does. A proposal ends in one of three recorded outcomes. Pursue puts the entry in `registry.json` as `planned`. More evidence keeps the issue open with the evidence it needs. Not in the system puts the entry in `registry.json` as `out-of-scope` with its reason, so the next person with the same need finds the answer ([component-registry](#component-registry)). This closes part of the intake gap [governance-model](#governance-model) recorded. **Security.** `SECURITY.md` sends a vulnerability report to GitHub private vulnerability reporting, from the Security tab of the repository, and never to a public issue, because a public report discloses the flaw before a fix exists. The maintainer enables private vulnerability reporting once the repository is public. The current release and the current release candidate receive fixes, on a best-effort basis. **Conduct.** `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` adopts the Contributor Covenant 3.0, and reports go to GitHub Support for now, because the project has no reporting address of its own yet. **Enforced by** review. The three files sit at the repository root.

### ruling-shape

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `DOCUMENTATION`. **Ruled.** 2026-10-01.

**A ruling reads as a headline that states the decision, then short labelled parts, and its earlier versions sit in a hidden Evidence part.**

**Applies to.** Every ruling in this file. The rewrite of 2026-10-01 put each earlier ruling into this shape, and each ruling written since takes it from the start.

**Shape.**

- The headline states the decision and carries no date.
- Each part is a labelled paragraph of one or two sentences, a short list when its items are parallel, or a table when its rows compare the same attributes.
- A Guidance part paraphrases the guidance the maintainer gave for the ruling, gives its date and attributes it to the maintainer. A ruling with no recorded guidance has no Guidance part.
- A Changed from part describes the state before the decision in one or two sentences. A founding ruling with no earlier state reads: Nothing. This is a founding ruling.
- The Status part comes last among the visible parts. It gives the date of the ruling, or says that none was recorded, and names every later ruling that amends or replaces it. It names no person.
- The sources of a ruling are the rows of `docs/REFERENCES.md` that cite it, and the Decisions page lists them under the ruling. A source is written once, in that file.
- The Evidence part follows the Status part and keeps every earlier version of the ruling as a block quote, with its measurements, test results and history. The page never shows it, and no earlier version leaves this file.
- No part of a ruling and no earlier version in its Evidence part is written in the maintainer's voice or quotes the maintainer.

**What you see.** The Decisions page and the package copy, `dist/DECISIONS.md`, omit the Evidence part. On the page a table uses the system `Table`, at least as wide as a paragraph and no wider than the column, and the reading width binds prose only, as `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 3 asks.

**Why.** A ruling written as one paragraph mixed the rule with its measurements, tests and history, and a reader could not find the rule in it. The Guidance and Changed from parts and the source rows let a reader audit the view behind a ruling, so a later change shows the state it replaced.

**Guidance.** The maintainer directed, on 2026-10-01, that each ruling record how its decision was reached, the way a reference list records its sources, so a reader can audit the view behind it and see the state that a later change replaces. The same direction kept the five sections, kept `docs/REFERENCES.md` as the one bibliography, and barred documentation in the maintainer's voice.

**Changed from.** Each ruling was one paragraph under a bold headline that often carried a date, and it mixed the rule with its measurements, tests and history. The Decisions page showed that paragraph whole and read no row of `docs/REFERENCES.md`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-10-01.

- [ruling-names-and-tags](#ruling-names-and-tags) adds the name heading and the tags line that open every entry.
- [ruling-names-and-tags](#ruling-names-and-tags) removed twelve rulings from this file, the one exception to the rule that no earlier version leaves it.
- Revised on 2026-10-02: the Applies to part names every ruling, because the rewrite of 2026-10-01 reached each one.

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **A ruling reads as a headline that states the decision, then short labelled parts, and its original text sits in a hidden Evidence part.**
>
> **Applies to.** Every ruling written or rewritten from 2026-10-01. The first wave is [radix-themes-substrate] to [headless-primitives-declared], [missing-provider-warning], [token-chip] and [brand-status-collision-gate]. The other rulings keep their old form until a later wave rewrites them.
>
> **Shape.**
>
> - The headline states the decision and carries no date.
> - Each part is a labelled paragraph of one or two sentences, a short list when its items are parallel, or a table when its rows compare the same attributes.
> - The Status part comes last among the visible parts. It gives the date of the ruling, or says that none was recorded, and names every later ruling that amends or replaces it.
> - The Evidence part quotes the ruling as first written, word for word, as a block quote. Measurements, test results and history stay there.
>
> **What you see.** The Decisions page and the package copy, `dist/DECISIONS.md`, omit the Evidence part. On the page a table uses the system `Table`, at least as wide as a paragraph and no wider than the column, and the reading width binds prose only, as `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 3 asks.
>
> **Why.** A ruling written as one paragraph mixed the rule with its measurements, tests and history, and a reader could not find the rule in it. The Evidence part keeps that record for contributors without putting it in front of every reader.

The other rulings keep their old form until a later wave rewrites them.

### ruling-names-and-tags

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `DOCUMENTATION`. **Ruled.** 2026-10-01.

**A ruling is known by a permanent short name and one to three tags, and it carries no section code.**

**Names.** A name is two to five lower-case words joined by hyphens, and it says what the ruling concerns. The name heads the entry, so `DECISIONS.md#focus-ring` opens it on GitHub, and the Decisions page opens it from `?ruling=focus-ring`.

**Citations.** Entries cite one another as links, such as `[focus-ring](#focus-ring)`. Stories, code and the other documents cite a ruling as `[[focus-ring]]`, a form that a guard can find and resolve.

**Tags.** The twelve tags are `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`, `COMPONENTS`, `CONTRIBUTING`, `DOCUMENTATION`, `FOUNDATIONS`, `INSTALL`, `LAYOUT`, `MOTION`, `SIZING`, `TOKENS` and `TYPOGRAPHY`. A ruling takes one to three, so a ruling on focus contrast appears under both `ACCESSIBILITY` and `COLOUR`.

**Left the ledger.** Six rulings on withdrawn package features and on the maintainer's own process left this file. Six rulings that a later ruling replaced in full left it too, and each place that cited one now names its successor or describes it in words. The reserved codes and the closing list of open commitments left with them. These departures are the one exception to the rule in [ruling-shape](#ruling-shape) that no earlier version leaves this file.

**Why.** A section code gave a reader the place of a ruling and nothing about its decision, so a reader without the code could not find the ruling. A name says what the ruling concerns, and the tags place one ruling under every topic it concerns.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved, on 2026-10-01, the name and tags of every ruling, the tag set, and the removal of the rulings that later ones replaced in full. The same approval deferred a grouping of the component rulings by family to a later pass.

**Changed from.** Each ruling carried a section letter and a number, cited across the system as a bare code, and the five sections were its only grouping. Rulings on withdrawn features, on the maintainer's process and rulings that a later ruling replaced in full sat beside the rulings in force.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-10-01. It amends [ruling-shape](#ruling-shape) with the name heading and the tags line. No later ruling amends it.

- Revised on 2026-10-02: the Left the ledger part says that the departed rulings left this file, and no longer names where they went or a phase of work.

**Evidence.** The entry before the revision of 2026-10-02, the earliest text on record:

> **A ruling is known by a permanent short name and one to three tags, and it carries no section code.**

>
> **Citations.** Entries cite one another as links, such as `[focus-ring](#focus-ring)`. Stories, code and the other documents cite a ruling as `[[focus-ring]]`, a form that a guard can find and resolve.

The reserved codes and the closing list of commitments for Phase 2 left with them. >

### icon-weight-axis

**Tags.** `FOUNDATIONS`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-18.

**The icon weight axis has two token steps, `regular` and `fill`, and fuller Phosphor usage stays guidance.**

**Tokens.** `icons.css` sets `--ds-icon-weight-base` to `"regular"` and `--ds-icon-weight-emphasis` to `"fill"`.

**Not tokenised.** Section 4 of `docs/GUIDELINES.md` documents the fuller Phosphor usage, such as bold in a primary call to action and duotone for an empty state. No token carries it.

### motion-tokens

**Tags.** `MOTION`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-18.

**`motion.css` holds the motion tokens, a short duration scale and one standard easing, and reduced motion collapses every duration.**

**Tokens.**

- `--ds-duration-instant`, 40ms.
- `--ds-duration-fast`, 120ms.
- `--ds-duration-overlay`, 150ms.
- `--ds-ease-standard`, the standard curve.

**Reduced motion.** Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, `motion.css` collapses every duration to near zero, so a consumer writes no reduced-motion rule of its own.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-18.

- [motion-duration-ladder](#motion-duration-ladder) keeps these three durations and widens the scale to eight, from 40ms to 400ms, with separate entry and exit curves.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`motion.css`** — `--ds-duration-*` (40/120/150ms) + `--ds-ease-standard`, with `prefers-reduced-motion` collapsing durations to ~0, baked in. *(Scale expanded in [motion-duration-ladder](#motion-duration-ladder).)*

### shadow-tokens

**Tags.** `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-18.

**`shadow.css` holds the shadow tokens, and `--ds-shadow-1` to `--ds-shadow-6` alias the composite shadows of Radix Themes.**

**What you see.** Each of `--ds-shadow-1` to `--ds-shadow-6` reads the matching Radix `--shadow-*`, an etched shadow built from a 1px alpha ring and layered drops. `--ds-shadow-overlay` serves floating surfaces such as popovers and menus.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-18.

- [elevation-model](#elevation-model) adds `--ds-shadow-inset` to `shadow.css`, a custom recess bevel with its own dark value, and draws the elevation levels from these shadows.
- [stacking-ladder](#stacking-ladder) keeps the stacking tokens out of `shadow.css`, in `stacking.css`, because stacking order and elevation are different axes.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`shadow.css`** — `--ds-shadow-1..6` alias Radix's composite (etched) shadows; `--ds-shadow-overlay` for floating surfaces.

### motion-duration-ladder

**Tags.** `MOTION`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-19.

**Motion durations form one ladder named by intent, from 40ms to 400ms, with separate curves for entrances and exits.**

**The ladder.** The steps are 40, 80, 120, 150, 180, 260, 320 and 400ms. A text change takes no animation, so it has no token.

**Curves.**

- An entrance decelerates on `--ds-ease-entry`.
- A closing state runs `--ds-ease-standard` at a longer duration than its entrance.
- `--ds-ease-exit` serves only a dismissal gesture the user makes, such as a toast swipe.
- A list stagger takes one step, `--ds-stagger-step`.

**Why.** Motion reads as intent, not decoration. The Radix Presence lifecycle needs an explicit exit and a reduced-motion stance, or an element vanishes at once or never unmounts.

**Detail.** Token names and values, exit keyframes, the `0.01ms` reduced-motion collapse, `transform-origin` and height from the Radix variable live in section 7 of `docs/GUIDELINES.md` and on the `Foundations/Motion` page.

**Changed from.** Three durations, 40, 120 and 150ms, and one curve, `--ds-ease-standard` ([motion-tokens](#motion-tokens)).

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-19.

- [motion-retiming](#motion-retiming) replaces the accelerate-out exit with the standard curve at a longer duration than the entrance, and keeps `--ds-ease-exit` for dismissal gestures alone. Token values did not change.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`motion.css` expanded — intent-named duration ladder + enter/exit easing asymmetry (2026-06-19).** Kept the original three durations (40/120/150) and added an intent-named ladder reaching 400ms — full scale 40/80/120/150/180/260/320/400; the 0ms "text change" tier is expressed by not animating, so it gets no token. Adopted enter/exit easing asymmetry (decelerate-in entrances, accelerate-out exits) over a single curve, plus a list-stagger step. **Rationale:** motion should read as intent, not decoration, and the Radix Presence lifecycle needs an explicit exit + reduced-motion stance or elements pop out / never unmount. The operational detail — token names/values, keyframes-for-exit, `0.01ms` reduced-motion, `transform-origin`, height-via-Radix-var — lives in GUIDELINES §7 and the live Motion story. **[Update 2026-07-28 ([motion-retiming](#motion-retiming)): the "accelerate-out exits" doctrine is superseded — closed states now run `--ds-ease-standard` at a LONGER duration than their entry (fast-in / slow-out); `--ds-ease-exit` survives only for user-initiated dismissal gestures. Token values unchanged.]**

### brand-collision-shift-table

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-20.

**When a brand accent sits close to a status colour, that status family moves to another Radix scale, automatically and by default.**

**What you see.** The four status families keep their default hues ([status-colour-defaults](#status-colour-defaults)) until a brand accent collides with one of them. Then that family alone takes a different scale, so an amber brand no longer makes the accent and the warning read as one colour.

**Mechanism.** Radix writes `data-accent-color="<name>"` on `.radix-themes`, and `theme.css` holds one block per colliding accent, `.radix-themes[data-accent-color="<accent>"] { … }`. Each block re-aliases only the colliding family (12 solid steps, 12 alpha steps and `-contrast`) to another Radix scale, at specificity `(0,2,0)` over the base `(0,1,0)`, with no `!important` and no new imports.

**Shift table.** `COLLISION_TABLE` names the shift for 20 of the 26 Radix accents, and the other 6 need no block. The Swatches play on the Colors foundations page reads its expected scales from the same table and checks all 27 accents, oxblood included, in both appearances, so the CSS and the test cannot diverge. A red-family brand moves error to the oxblood scale ([oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset)), because every named red sits too close to the others to read as a different colour.

**Foreground on a shifted fill.**

- White on vivid chromatic solids.
- Near-black `#21201c` on light scales: warning on yellow, success on lime, and warning on orange.
- An orange brand's own accent fill takes `#21201c` as `--accent-contrast`.

White on `orange-9` measured 2.97:1, under the 3:1 floor of 2026-06-20 for text on a solid fill, and `#21201c` measured about 5.5:1.

**Text floor.** Status and link text on step 11 is held to 4.39:1 on the page background, not 4.5:1, for `--ds-text-warning`, `--ds-text-success` and `--ds-text-link`. Radix tunes step 11 as its accessible text step, and several scales the shift can route through land just under 4.5, such as `orange-11` at 4.40. This extends [warning-text-tolerance](#warning-text-tolerance).

**Override.** A consumer can override a shift without a new API: declare `--<family>-*` in a sheet loaded after the system sheet, at `(0,2,0)` or higher, for example `.radix-themes[data-accent-color="amber"] { --warning-9: … }`. Only the overridden family moves, and the rest keep the automatic shift.

**Rejected.** Routing shifted warning and success text to step 12 clears 4.5:1 but renders near-black and loses the status hue. Step 11 was kept, with colour never the only signal.

**Changed from.** The four status families kept their fixed hues whatever the brand, so a brand accent close to one of them read as that status.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-20.

- [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset) routes error for red, ruby, crimson and tomato brands to the oxblood scale, in place of the in-family shift to crimson or tomato, and measures the brand and error pair by perceptual difference rather than by the 18 degree hue gap.
- [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate) replaces the 18 degree hue test for every family with a test on perceptual difference and hue together, and adds shifts to the table.
- [seeded-brand-collisions](#seeded-brand-collisions) applies the shift to a brand supplied as a seed colour, chosen at runtime, and corrects the count of accents with a block to 20.
- [dark-override-selectors](#dark-override-selectors) records nine table entries that move a family further than the later gate requires, which stay as ruled.
- [soft-fill-text-exception](#soft-fill-text-exception) states that the 4.39 floor holds on the page background only, never on a tinted fill.
- [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) raises the floor for text on a solid fill from 3:1 to 4.5:1.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Automatic brand→semantic collision avoidance (the headline feature, on by default, 2026-06-20).** The four semantic families default to fixed hues ([status-colour-defaults](#status-colour-defaults): error red, warning amber, success green, info cyan). When the client's brand `accentColor` is hue-close to a semantic, they read as the same colour (an amber brand makes the accent indistinguishable from the amber warning). **Mechanism:** Radix writes `data-accent-color="<name>"` on `.radix-themes` and remaps `--accent-1..12` per that attribute; `theme.css` piggy-backs on the *same* attribute with per-accent blocks `.radix-themes[data-accent-color="<accent>"] { … }` that re-alias **only the colliding family** (full 12 solid + 12 alpha + `-contrast`) to a non-colliding Radix scale. Specificity `(0,2,0)` beats the base `.radix-themes` `(0,1,0)` with **no `!important`**; Radix already ships every scale + alpha + dark variants, so **no new imports**. **The shift table** (20 accents; the other 6 already clear on one axis and need no block — the count was stated as 17 until [seeded-brand-collisions](#seeded-brand-collisions) re-measured it) was derived by OKLCH step-9 hue-distance optimisation and lives once as `COLLISION_TABLE` in `_assert.ts`; the single Foundations/Colors **Swatches** play sweeps all 26 accents — 27 with the oxblood preset ([oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset)) — under **both appearances** (on a hidden, detached clone of the theme root, so the visible page never flickers) and asserts (a) brand↔semantic and semantic↔semantic hue separation ≥ 18° — skipped for the neutral **gray** accent, whose ~0-chroma step-9 hue is meaningless (it reads distinct by chroma, not hue), (b) `--on-<family>` on `--ds-fill-<family>` ≥ 3.0, plus the per-accent text/link WCAG pairings — deriving expected scales from the same table, so CSS and test cannot drift. **The red family can't separate error inside the family** — every named red sits ~ΔE-OK 0.07 from the others, so the in-family shift reads "still red." **Resolved by [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset) (2026-06-21):** red / ruby / crimson / tomato route error to the **oxblood** preset (ΔE-OK 0.21, separation by lightness), and the brand↔error check moved from the 18° hue floor to a perceptual ΔE-OK floor to see it. *(Originally accepted as residuals — red→crimson ~22°, ruby→tomato ~20° — on the colour-not-alone basis; oxblood makes them cleanly distinct.)* **Contrast polarities:** white on vivid chromatic solids; near-black `#21201c` on light scales — warning→yellow, success→lime (a flip from the base `--success-contrast:#fff`), and warning→orange (Radix intends white on orange, but white drops to 2.97:1 under the 3.0 gate, so it's flipped to dark at 5.49:1 — empirically verified). **Override is possible (not built):** layer your own `--<family>-*` declarations after the system sheet at ≥ `(0,2,0)` specificity (e.g. `.radix-themes[data-accent-color="amber"] { --warning-9: … }` loaded later); only the family you override moves, the rest keep the auto-shift. **Side-effect ruling (extends [warning-text-tolerance](#warning-text-tolerance)):** Radix's step-11 "tuned accessible-text step" lands a hair under 4.5 on a near-white bg for several scales the feature can route warning/success text through (orange-11 4.40, teal-11 4.45, yellow-11 4.454); the `text-warning`/`text-success`-on-bg floor is set to 4.39 to accept the Radix step-11 reality, same basis as the amber-11 [warning-text-tolerance](#warning-text-tolerance) tolerance. **(extended 2026-06-21):** `--ds-text-link` (also accent-11) is held to the same 4.39 floor — light-scale brands land just under 4.5 (orange 4.43, teal 4.48, yellow 4.49); and an **orange brand** takes white on its own accent-9 fill at only 2.97:1 (Radix's choice), below the 3.0 gate — the same case as warning→orange — so orange's `--accent-contrast` is pinned to dark `#21201c` (~5.5:1). **Ratified 2026-06-20:** the alternative — routing shifted warning/success text to step-12 — clears 4.5 (≈11:1) but renders near-black and loses the status hue, so accepting the step-11 colour (reinforced by colour-not-alone) was chosen over tightening.

### elevation-model

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `FOUNDATIONS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-20.

**Elevation is one ladder of five levels in both light and dark: a raised surface moves toward the light and a sunken surface moves into shadow.**

**What you see.**

- Up: a lighter surface in dark and a deeper drop shadow in light. Shadows stay in dark, because Radix ships deeper dark `--shadow-*` values, so a dark raised surface is lighter and keeps its shadow.
- Down: a darker surface in both appearances, with an inset bevel at its edge.

**Levels.**

| Level | Surface | Shadow |
|---|---|---|
| Sunken | `--ds-bg-sunken` | `--ds-shadow-inset` |
| Base | `--ds-bg-base` | None |
| Raised | `--ds-bg-raised` | `--ds-shadow-2` |
| Overlay | `--ds-bg-overlay` | `--ds-shadow-overlay` |
| Modal | `--ds-bg-overlay` | `--ds-shadow-6` |

**Sunken.** `--ds-bg-sunken` is `--gray-2` in light and `--black-a6` in dark. A black alpha darkens below the base, while a `gray-a` step is a white alpha in dark and would lighten the surface.

**Inset bevel.** `--ds-shadow-inset`, in `shadow.css` with a light and a dark value, draws a shadowed top wall, a light bottom edge and a visible rim. It is a custom value rather than an alias of a Radix shadow, so the dark value can carve harder, because a recess reads weakest on a dark surface.

**Guarded.** The `Foundations/Elevation` story renders the five levels in both appearances side by side. Its tests hold the same level count in each appearance, each dark level above the base lighter than the one below and the sunken level darker than the base, the inset as a composite shadow, and `--ds-text-strong` at 4.5:1 or more on every surface.

**Changed from.** The dark sunken surface used a `gray-a` step, a white alpha in dark, so it read lighter than the base, and no inset shadow token existed.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-20. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Elevation model — one cross-mode ladder (2026-06-20).** Five levels in BOTH appearances: Sunken / Base / Raised / Overlay / Modal. **Transferable rule:** elevation displaces the surface relative to overhead light — up = toward light (lighter surface in dark, deeper drop in light); down = into shadow (darker surface in both modes + an inset bevel). **Shadows persist in dark** — Radix ships deepened dark `--shadow-*` variants, so dark = lighter surface AND a kept shadow. **Sunken goes darker, not lighter:** `--ds-bg-sunken` is overridden in `.dark` to `var(--black-a6)` (a black alpha darkens below base; `gray-a` is a *white* alpha in dark and would lighten — the inversion bug). **New token `--ds-shadow-inset`** (shadow.css, light + dark) — a recess bevel: shadowed top inner wall + light-catching bottom edge + an identifiable rim (a dark-on-dark edge vanishes in dark). Custom, not a Radix `--shadow-1` alias, so the dark variant carves harder (the recess is subtlest on dark). The six raw `--ds-shadow-*` are the palette the levels draw from (1 inset, 2 raised, 3 raised-hover, 5/overlay, 6 modal). The `Foundations/Elevation` story renders all five levels at both appearances side by side (nested `<Theme>` per cell); play-tests assert level-count parity (light === dark), the dark up-ladder steps lighter while sunken steps darker than base, the inset is a composite, and `--ds-text-strong` clears AA 4.5 on every surface (sunken composited over base). Modelled on Material 3 (a shared level set; tonal surface in dark + shadow in light) and Radix's own surface approach.

### weakest-neutral-fill

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-21.

**`--ds-fill-weaker` is the subtlest neutral fill, one step below `--ds-fill-weak`.**

**Use.** A faint fill for a row, a section or an inset.

**The neutral ladder.**

| Role | Radix step |
|---|---|
| `--ds-fill-weaker` | `--gray-a2` |
| `--ds-fill-weak` | `--gray-a3` |
| `--ds-fill-hover` | `--gray-a4` |
| `--ds-fill-press` | `--gray-a5` |

**Why alpha.** Every step of the ladder is an alpha, so each one composes on any surface.

**Changed from.** The neutral fill ladder started at `--ds-fill-weak`, `--gray-a3`, and had no fainter step.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-21. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`--ds-fill-weaker` — subtlest neutral fill (2026-06-21).** Added below `--ds-fill-weak` (gray-a3), mapping to `gray-a2` (~2.4% alpha) for faint row/section/inset fills. Alpha like the rest of the neutral ladder — weaker (a2) → weak (a3) → hover (a4) → press (a5) — so it composes on any surface.

### oxblood-preset

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-21.

**Oxblood is a 27th preset scale, a brand colour in its own right and the error scale for a brand in the red family.**

**Why.** The named reds, red, ruby, crimson and tomato, sit about 0.07 apart in perceptual difference (ΔE-OK), so no named red reads as a distinct error beside a red brand. Oxblood is a deep red that sits 0.21 to 0.24 from the whole red family, separated by lightness rather than hue.

**What you see.**

- `src/tokens/oxblood.css` holds one pre-generated scale from the seed `#8a2119`, in light and dark: 12 solid steps, 12 alpha steps, and `contrast`, `surface`, `indicator` and `track`.
- `.radix-themes:where([data-accent-color="oxblood"])` maps `--accent-*` onto it the way Radix maps its 26 built-in colours, so `accentColor="oxblood"` on `Provider` is a brand, and the Storybook accent toolbar lists it.
- An oxblood brand keeps the normal red error, 0.21 away, so no collision follows.
- When the brand is red, ruby, crimson or tomato, `theme.css` aliases `--error-*` to oxblood.

**Contrast.** White on oxblood step 9 reads 9.1:1 and APCA Lc 94, and error text at step 11 reads 12.3:1 in light and 9.7:1 in dark. White is the better foreground by both WCAG and APCA, so `contrast.css` holds no override for it.

**Gap.** The scale is a hand-curated interim patch. A full custom-palette generator is to regenerate it at higher fidelity under the same token names.

**Changed from.** A brand was one of the 26 Radix colours ([brand-props-on-provider](#brand-props-on-provider)). [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) moved error inside the red family, red to crimson and ruby to tomato, which still read as red, and its 18 degree hue test counted oxblood, about 2 degrees from red in hue, as a collision.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-21.

- This ruling moved the brand and error collision test to a perceptual floor of 0.10. [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate) absorbs that floor into one perceptual gate for all four status families, and routes error to oxblood for pink, orange, gold, yellow, amber and lime brands as well.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Oxblood — a 27th custom preset scale + the red-family error target (interim patch, 2026-06-21).** The red family (red / ruby / crimson / tomato) is too crowded to give a red brand a *distinct* error inside Radix's named scales — every named red is ~ΔE-OK 0.07 apart, so [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table)'s in-family shift (red→crimson, ruby→tomato) stays perceptually "still red." **Oxblood** (`src/tokens/oxblood.css`) is one pre-generated **deep-red** scale (OKLCH, seed `#8a2119`; 12 solids + 12 alphas + `contrast`/`surface`/`indicator`/`track`, light + dark; alphas by the Radix alpha-colour algorithm over white/black) that sits **ΔE-OK 0.21–0.24** from the whole red family — separation by **lightness**, not hue. **First-class + selectable:** a `.radix-themes:where([data-accent-color="oxblood"])` block maps `--accent-*` onto it exactly as Radix maps its 26 built-ins (so it's the first *custom* accent — extends [brand-props-on-provider](#brand-props-on-provider) from "brand = a Radix accent prop" to "…or a system preset"), the Provider's `accentColor` type widens to include it, and it's in the Storybook accent toolbar — an oxblood **brand** ships a full palette and keeps a normal red error (ΔE-OK 0.21, no collision, so no recursion). **As the error target,** the four red-family blocks in `theme.css` re-alias `--error-*` to it. **A11y (measured, an *upgrade*):** white on oxblood-9 is **9.1:1 / APCA Lc 94**, error text-11 is **12.3:1** light / **9.7:1** dark — well above the floors (the shifted bright-reds barely cleared 4.39); white is best by **both** WCAG and APCA, so **no `contrast.css` override and no new divergence** (the `apcaForegroundFails` guard validates it automatically). **Metric change (refines [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table)):** the brand↔error collision check moved from the 18° hue floor to a perceptual **ΔE-OK ≥ 0.10** floor (`MIN_DELTA_E_BRAND_ERROR`, `_assert.ts`), because oxblood separates by lightness while sitting ~2° from red in hue — invisible to a hue gate; the other three families followed in [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate) (the perceptual gate now covers all four). The Swatches play now sweeps **27** accents (oxblood-as-brand included). **Interim:** a hand-curated patch ahead of the full custom-palette generator, which will regenerate it at higher fidelity under the same token names.

### brand-status-collision-gate

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `ACCESSIBILITY`. **Ruled.** 2026-06-22.

**A brand colour and a status colour collide only when they are close in both perceived difference and hue.**

**Perceptual collision gate.** A pair collides when its perceptual difference (ΔE-OK) is under 0.135 and its hue gap is under 40 degrees, so a pair that clears either limit passes. The same test runs between two status families.

**Shifts added by this ruling.** The earlier table holds the rest.

| Brand | Family | New scale | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pink, orange | Error | Oxblood | The brand sits close to red. |
| Gold, yellow, amber, lime | Error | Oxblood | Warning moves to orange, which sits close to red. |
| Cyan, teal | Info | Indigo | The brand sits close to cyan. |
| Blue | Info | Iris | The brand sits close to cyan. |
| Teal, grass | Success | Lime | The brand sits close to green. |
| Lime | Warning | Orange | The brand sits close to amber. |

**Why.** A hue test alone passed pairs that read as one colour, such as teal and cyan, just under 40 degrees apart in hue. Every status also carries an icon and a label, so colour is never the only signal.

**Changed from.** A brand collided with warning, success or info when the two hues sat less than 18 degrees apart ([brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table)), and with error when their perceptual difference (ΔE-OK) fell below 0.10 ([oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset)).

**Status.** Ruled 2026-06-22.

- Replaces the 18 degree hue test of [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table), and absorbs the error floor of [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset).
- [seeded-brand-collisions](#seeded-brand-collisions) applies the test to seeded brands.
- Nine shifts in the table, four of them added by this ruling, move a family further than this test requires. They stay as ruled, per the note after [dark-override-selectors](#dark-override-selectors).

**Evidence.** The entry as first written:

> **Perceptual collision gate for all four semantic families + the cluster shifts (2026-06-22).** Completes the [oxblood-preset] migration. **The gate:** a brand↔semantic pair is "too close" only when **ΔE-OK < 0.135 AND hue < 40°** — it clears on *either* axis (`MIN_BRAND_DELTA_E` / `MIN_BRAND_HUE` + `brandCollides`, `_assert.ts`). This replaces the hue-only-18° check for warning/success/info (and absorbs [oxblood-preset]'s brand↔error ΔE floor), because hue alone missed pairs that are hue-apart yet perceptually close (teal/cyan: 40° hue but ΔE-OK 0.081). Calibrated from observed calls — green/cyan reads fine at ΔE 0.137 (hue 64°) and amber/orange at 0.20 (hue 39°), but pink/red collides at 0.128 (hue 37°). **Scope:** one `tooClose` rule covers **both** brand↔semantic and semantic↔semantic. That semantic↔semantic axis is what routes the four warning→orange brands' error to oxblood (gold / yellow / amber / lime): orange-9 sits only 16° from a ruby/red error in hue yet is perceptually distinct from the *deep* oxblood by lightness (ΔE-OK 0.28) — a separation the old hue-18° floor couldn't express.
