(bronze keeps error→ruby — no orange warning, no collision.) colour-not-alone (semantics carry an icon+label, WCAG 1.4.1) remains the general backstop. **Shifts the gate added** (each re-routed to a hue-distinct, mood-preserved target, ΔE-OK 0.18–0.31): pink & orange error→**oxblood**; cyan & teal info→**indigo** (a true different hue, not max-ΔE's lighter-cyan *sky*); blue info→**iris** (blue *is* the info hue, so iris is the only clear option, ΔE 0.14); teal & grass success→**lime** (they had been aliased to *each other* — the swap bug); lime warning→**orange**. **Contrast:** lime→orange takes dark on-solid (orange-9 white is 2.97:1) and joins the `contrast.css` APCA white-flip set (gold/yellow/amber/lime); indigo/iris take white, lime-success takes dark — all guarded by the APCA play. The Swatches play runs `brandCollides` over all four families × 27 accents.

### error-hover-fill

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-07-08.

**`--ds-fill-error-hover` is the hover paint of a solid error fill, and no other status family takes a hover role until a component needs one.**

**What you see.** The danger solid button of [destructive-tone](#destructive-tone) lays `--ds-fill-error-hover`, today `--black-a2`, over its rest fill `--ds-fill-error` while the pointer is over it. The label is white on every error scale, so the overlay is black on every brand.

**Parallel.** The role mirrors `--ds-fill-accent-hover`, the hover paint of the accent solid.

**Not covered.** Warning, success and info carry no hover role. One is added when a real consumer exists.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this. A solid error fill had no hover role.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-07-08.

- [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) replaces the first value, `var(--error-10)`, with a `--black-a2` overlay on the rest fill, so the label passes 4.5:1 on hover.
- [interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas) rules that every hover stacks a Radix alpha on the rest fill and never moves the fill to another step.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`--ds-fill-error-hover` (2026-07-08).** `var(--error-10)` — the hover step for solid error fills (the [destructive-tone](#destructive-tone) danger-solid button); structural parallel of `--ds-fill-accent-hover` (accent-10). No other family gains a hover step until a real consumer exists.

### light-scrim

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-07-09.

**`--ds-scrim-light` is a light scrim, `var(--white-a8)`, for dark media where the dark scrim would vanish.**

**What you see.** `Overlay` paints `--ds-scrim-light` when its `scrim` prop is `light`, so a reveal over a dark image reads as a pale veil rather than a black one ([overlay-hover-scrim](#overlay-hover-scrim)). The dark scrim, `--ds-scrim`, serves light media.

**Value.** `var(--white-a8)` in both appearances. A white alpha reads the same in light and dark, so the token takes no `.dark` override.

**Changed from.** The system had one scrim, `--ds-scrim`, a black alpha that vanishes over dark media.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-07-09.

- [scrim-foreground-tokens](#scrim-foreground-tokens) adds `--ds-on-scrim-light`, the near-black ink for content drawn on this scrim.
- [scrim-value](#scrim-value) deletes the dark override of `--ds-scrim`, so both scrims now hold one value in both appearances, and the contrast with `--ds-scrim` that this ruling drew no longer holds.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`--ds-scrim-light` (2026-07-09).** `var(--white-a8)` — a light scrim for DARK media where `--ds-scrim` (black-a8) would vanish; appearance-independent (a white alpha needs no `.dark` override, unlike `--ds-scrim`). Consumed by Overlay ([overlay-hover-scrim](#overlay-hover-scrim)).

### overlay-entry-duration

**Tags.** `MOTION`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-07-28.

**`--ds-duration-overlay` is `150ms`, the entry duration of the popper tier.**

**What you see.** A menu, popover, flyout or select opens in `150ms`, between `--ds-duration-fast` (`120ms`) and `--ds-duration-moderate` (`180ms`).

**Why.** [motion-retiming](#motion-retiming) makes an entrance quicker than its exit, and it added this step for the popper tier's entrance. The popper tier leaves in `--ds-duration-emphasis` (`260ms`).

**Changed from.** No duration step sat between `--ds-duration-fast` and `--ds-duration-moderate`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-07-28. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`--ds-duration-overlay` (2026-07-28).** `150ms` — the popper-tier ENTRY step (menu / popover / flyout / select in), minted by the motion retiming ([motion-retiming](#motion-retiming)) to sit between `fast` (120) and `moderate` (180). 

### seeded-brand-collisions

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-12.

**A brand given as `{ seed }` takes the same status-family shift as a named brand, chosen at runtime from the seed.**

**What you see.** When a seeded brand collides with error, warning, success or info, that family moves to another Radix scale, so a destructive button no longer paints the brand's own colour. The shift is written as `var()` references, so light and dark both resolve from the vendor scales.

**Mechanism.**

- `palette/collision.ts` chooses the scales from the seed, and `theme/customBrand.ts` writes them on the root as `--ds-brand-<family>-*`.
- A 21st block in `theme.css`, `.radix-themes[data-accent-color="ds-custom"]`, routes each family through those properties. It is unwrapped at (0,2,0), like the twenty named-brand blocks.
- The block lives in `theme.css` and not in `custom-brand.css`. That file loads first and wraps its selector in `:where()`, so a family block there loses to the bare `.radix-themes` declarations in `theme.css` and paints nothing.

**Choice.**

- Candidates are per family and nearest first, so error stays a red. A search that only maximised distance chose lime for error.
- The shift is the smallest move the gate allows.
- The search covers all 108 assignments, because one shift can cause another: an amber brand moves warning to orange, and orange then collides with the default red error.
- Candidate step 9 values come from a fitted static table, `SCALE_STEP_9`, because the generator runs in the CLI and on the server, where no live style read exists.
- The ink on a solid fill follows the shift. A family moved to a pale scale takes `#21201c`, as the named-brand blocks do.

**Exception.** Some seeds cannot be separated. `#C8102E` collides with red, ruby and oxblood, every scale error may take. The search scores violations, so it still clears the families it can, and `semanticShiftDiagnostics()` names the families it cannot clear. This degraded default is accepted: a client who supplies a custom brand is taken to know its own semantic constraints, and the override route of [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) stays open.

**Side effect.** `oxblood.css` publishes its scale at `:root` as well as on `.radix-themes`. `Provider` writes the brand properties on `document.documentElement`, where `var(--oxblood-9)` was undefined, so the error colour vanished.

**Changed from.** The shift of [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) was a fixed table keyed on named accents, so a seeded brand had no block and took no shift. Seed `#C8102E` sat at ΔE-OK 0.0963 from the default error.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-12.

- [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) raises the floor for text on a solid fill to 4.5:1 and records a seeded brand's error fill, which stays on its own step 9, as an open gap.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The semantic collision shift now fires for SEEDED brands, chosen at runtime (2026-08-12).** [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table)'s shift is a hand-ruled lookup: `theme.css` carries one static block per colliding *named* accent. A brand supplied as `{ seed: "#…" }` ([brand-props-on-provider](#brand-props-on-provider)'s custom-brand path) has no name, so **no block served it and no shift fired** — the headline feature was absent on the only route to a client's exact hex. Measured before the fix, seed `#C8102E`: `--accent-9` `#c8102e` against `--error-9` `#e5484d`, ΔE-OK **0.0963**, hue **0.71°** — `tooClose()` returns **true** on the shipped output, and nothing ever ran it on that path. A destructive button rendered the brand's own colour. **Mechanism:** `palette/collision.ts` chooses the shift from the seed and `theme/customBrand.ts` writes it as `--ds-brand-<family>-*`; a 21st block in `theme.css` routes the families through those properties. The block is UNWRAPPED at `(0,2,0)` like its twenty siblings and lives in `theme.css`, **not** `custom-brand.css`: that file loads first (`index.css:46` vs `:47`) and wraps its selector in `:where()` (0,1,0), so a family block there is outranked by `theme.css`'s own bare-`.radix-themes` declarations and silently does nothing. Values are `var()` references, so light and dark resolve from the vendor scales and this path needs no appearance arm. **Sub-decisions, named rather than defaulted silently:** (a) candidates are **per-family and nearest-first**, not one global pool — a first attempt maximising distance chose *lime* for error, and an error that is not red is not an error; the hand table never once routes error to a green, a constraint encoded twenty times and written down zero times. (b) The shift is the **smallest move the gate allows**; red falls through to oxblood only because ruby cannot clear a red brand (named reds sit ~ΔE-OK 0.07 apart). (c) **Exhaustive search over the 108 assignments**, not a per-family pass: shifts cascade — an amber brand moves warning to orange, which collides with the *default* red error, so error must vacate although it never collided with the brand; a greedy pass only moves the family that is itself in trouble and deadlocks there. (d) Candidate step-9 values are a **fitted static table** (`SCALE_STEP_9`), measured off a live theme root, the same posture as `generate.ts`'s `L_CURVE`/`C_CURVE` — a live `getComputedStyle` read was rejected because `generate.ts` must run in the CLI and `custom-brand.css` documents an SSR story a DOM read forfeits. (e) On-solid contrast **follows the shift**: a family routed to a pale scale takes `#21201c`, because white on `orange-9` is 2.97:1 against the earlier 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill — `theme.css` already does this for every warning→orange and success→lime block, and a shift that moved the fill and left the foreground would pass a separation check and still be unreadable. (f) **Some brands cannot be separated, and that is REPORTED rather than absorbed:** `#C8102E` collides with red, ruby AND oxblood — every red error may reach. The search scores violations instead of filtering on them, so the three families that *can* be solved stay solved, ranks unavoidable failures by how much separation they still buy, and `semanticShiftDiagnostics()` names the families it could not clear. Measured after: ΔE-OK **0.1299** (from 0.0963) — improved, still under the 0.135 gate, and now visible instead of silent. An ordinary brand clears comfortably: seed `#1A5FB4` measures **0.3355**. **Ruled 2026-08-12:** this degraded default is acceptable — a client supplying a custom brand is assumed aware of their own semantic constraints, and the [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) override route stays open (verified live: a consumer sheet at `(0,2,0)` loaded after ours moves `--error-9` and reaches the painted button). **Verified:** all 27 named accents byte-identical against `semanticBaseline.fixture.ts`, captured before the change; 91 node-lane assertions including a 27-seed parity sweep against the hand table. **Side-effect:** `oxblood.css` now publishes its scale at `:root` as well as `.radix-themes`. It was the one candidate scale not at `:root`, and since `Provider` writes onto `document.documentElement`, `var(--oxblood-9)` was undefined at that scope and the whole custom property went guaranteed-invalid — `--error-9` resolved to nothing and the error colour vanished. Every other candidate worked, which is what made it hard to see.

### dark-override-selectors

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `FOUNDATIONS`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-12.

**Every dark override in the token layer carries both dark selector shapes.**

**The rule.** Each dark override in `src/tokens/**` ships both selectors:

```
.radix-themes:where(.dark, .dark-theme),
:is(.dark, .dark-theme) :where(.radix-themes:not(.light, .light-theme)) { … }
```

**Why.** Radix's `appearance` defaults to `inherit`, and under it the `dark` class sits on `<html>` while the theme root carries none. A rule with the first selector alone never matches in that default, so the vendor scales turn dark and this layer stays light.

**Light subtree.** The `:not(.light, .light-theme)` clause in the second selector keeps an explicitly light subtree light inside a dark document.

**Symptoms.** With the first selector alone, `--ds-bg-raised` stayed `#fff` on a `#111113` page in `semantic.css`, the light inset shadow painted on a dark surface in `shadow.css`, and the oxblood scale stayed light in `oxblood.css` while the vendor scales turned dark.

**Shift table residual.** Nine entries of the shift table in [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table), for gold, bronze, brown, teal, lime, mint and sky, move a family that the gate in [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate) counts as clear. They stay as they are, pinned in `KNOWN_TABLE_DIVERGENCE` in `src/palette/collision.logic.test.ts`, which fails on a new divergence and on a pinned one that no longer diverges, and a separate task re-derives them.

**Changed from.** The rule was in the code and cited from `semantic.css`, `shadow.css` and `oxblood.css` before the ledger held an entry for it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-12. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A dark-mode override in the token layer carries BOTH selector shapes (2026-08-12, minted against three existing citations).** Radix's `appearance` defaults to **`inherit`**, and under it the `dark` class sits on `<html>` while the theme root carries none. A rule written only as `.radix-themes:where(.dark, .dark-theme)` therefore never matches in the default configuration — the vendor's own scales flip and this system's layer does not. Every dark override in `src/tokens/**` must ship both:
>
> ```
> .radix-themes:where(.dark, .dark-theme),
> :is(.dark, .dark-theme) :where(.radix-themes:not(.light, .light-theme)) { … }
> ```
>
> **Measured symptoms of shipping only the first shape**, each recorded at the site that hit it: `--ds-bg-raised` stayed `#fff` on a `#111113` page (`semantic.css`); the LIGHT inset shadow recipe painted on a dark surface (`shadow.css`); the oxblood layer stayed light while the vendor scales went dark (`oxblood.css`). The `:not(.light, .light-theme)` clause in the second shape is load-bearing — it keeps an explicitly-light subtree light inside a dark document. **Why this entry is dated after the code:** the rule was already implemented and already cited as [dark-override-selectors](#dark-override-selectors) in those three files, and no entry existed. It is minted here rather than renumbered so the citations keep resolving.
>
> **Re-derivation owed — [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table)'s shift table vs [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate)'s gate (raised 2026-08-12, deferred by ruling).** Seven accents' hand-ruled shifts do not reproduce under the current perceptual gate: **gold** (error, warning), **bronze** (error), **brown** (warning), **teal** (info), **lime** (error, warning), **mint** (success), **sky** (info) — nine entries in all. In each the table moves a family that [brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate)'s ΔE-OK + hue gate says was already clear. The likely cause is chronological rather than a defect: [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) derived the table by hue-distance optimisation against an 18° gate, and [oxblood-preset](#oxblood-preset)/[brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate) replaced that metric without re-deriving the table. These are grandfathered Radix palettes from the base system and stay as they are. They are pinned in `collision.logic.test.ts`'s `KNOWN_TABLE_DIVERGENCE`, which fails if a NEW divergence appears **and** if a pinned one silently heals, so the residual is a stated number rather than an allowance that can rot. Re-deriving them is a separate task.

### stacking-ladder

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `LAYOUT`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-12.

**Three `--ds-z-*` tokens publish the order of surfaces that stack against other components, and the gaps between them belong to the consumer.**

**The rungs.** `stacking.css` holds them apart from `shadow.css`, because stacking order and elevation are different axes: a skip link casts no shadow, and [shadow-tokens](#shadow-tokens) rules `shadow.css` as the shadow aliases.

| Token | Value | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `--ds-z-skip-link` | `10` | The AppShell skip link, above app chrome |
| `--ds-z-panel` | `50` | The five portaled panels of MultiSelect, Typeahead, DateInput, DateRangeInput and PowerSearch |
| `--ds-z-toast` | `60` | Transient notices, which stay readable over an open panel |

**The gaps.** App chrome sits at 11 to 49, a surface that must clear the system's panels at 51 to 59, and anything above 60 belongs to the consumer. An app that needs a sticky header above the panels and below the toasts has a number to design against.

**Not covered.** Order inside one component, the `0`, `1`, `2` and `auto` values that stack siblings within its own stacking context, stays a raw number, because a token name would claim a global relationship that does not exist. So `stacking.node-check.ts` flags any raw `z-index` of `10` or more, and a component with a real local need registers its selector in `INTRA_COMPONENT_ALLOW` rather than add a global rung.

**How the panel rung works.** The five panels compute `position: static`, where a `z-index` is normally inert, and the rung still holds, because `@radix-ui/react-popper` copies the content's computed `z-index` onto the floating wrapper at mount. A token change under an open panel takes effect at the next open, and `position: relative` on these panels is unnecessary and nests a redundant stacking context.

**Limits.** The guard scans declarations, so it proves the token is used, never that the value reaches the screen, and it misses an outranked rule, a raw value from 3 to 9 and a `z-index` written in TypeScript. The highest TypeScript value that ships is `1`, on the exported `interactiveLayer` of `ClickableCard`, which orders a control against that card's own overlay and stays off the ladder.

**Changed from.** The same three values shipped as raw numbers at seven sites in `components.css`. The ladder renumbered nothing, so no stacking relationship changed.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-12. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The cross-component stacking ladder (2026-08-12).** Three rungs in a new `stacking.css`, kept out of `shadow.css` because stacking order and elevation are different axes — a skip-link casts no shadow, and [shadow-tokens](#shadow-tokens) already rules `shadow.css` as the shadow aliases: `--ds-z-skip-link: 10` (the AppShell escape hatch, above app chrome) · `--ds-z-panel: 50` (the five hand-rolled portaled surfaces — MultiSelect, Typeahead, DateInput, DateRange, PowerSearch) · `--ds-z-toast: 60` (transient notices, which must stay readable over an open panel). **The values are the ones already shipping** — seven sites in `components.css` were re-pointed at tokens and nothing was renumbered, so no stacking relationship changed and the diff is inert at runtime. The decision the ladder records is that these three numbers are now a published contract: an app needing a sticky header above our panels and below our toasts has a number to design against, where before it had to read our CSS. **The gaps between the rungs are the interface** — app chrome at 11–49, surfaces that must clear our panels at 51–59, above 60 is the consumer's. **Intra-component z-index is excluded on purpose:** the other 24 `z-index` declarations in `components.css` are `0`, `1`, `2` or `auto` and order siblings inside a single component's own stacking context, so naming them would advertise a global relationship that does not exist — which is why `stacking.node-check.ts` discriminates by **value** (`>= 10`) rather than by selector name. That threshold is a chosen line, not a law (10 is merely the lowest cross-component value shipping today), so it carries an escape hatch: a component with a genuine local need registers its selector in `INTRA_COMPONENT_ALLOW` (empty at adoption) instead of being pushed into adding a global rung for a local problem. **HOW THE PANEL RUNG REACHES THE SCREEN, because it is not the obvious route and a reader who assumes the obvious one will conclude it is broken.** The five panel elements compute `position: static`, where a `z-index` would normally be inert — but the rung is nonetheless effective, and the mechanism is Radix's: `@radix-ui/react-popper` reads `window.getComputedStyle(content).zIndex` when the content mounts and copies that value onto the inline style of the floating wrapper it positions (`react-popper/dist/index.mjs:194,206`). `getComputedStyle` returns the declared value irrespective of `position`, so our token is what the wrapper ends up carrying. **Verified end to end in Chrome, not inferred:** with the default token the wrapper's inline `z-index` reads `50` and an open panel paints over a consumer plane at `z-index: 20`; with `--ds-z-panel` overridden to `5` *before* the panel opens, the wrapper reads `5` and the same panel then paints *under* that plane. The other two rungs take the ordinary route — `--ds-z-toast` on `position: fixed`, `--ds-z-skip-link` on `position: absolute`. **The one real limitation:** the copy happens at mount, so changing the token while a panel is already open does not restyle it; the next open picks it up. **Do not "fix" these panels by adding `position: relative`** — it is unnecessary, and it introduces a redundant nested stacking context inside a wrapper that is already at the same rung.
>
> **What a pass does not prove, in four parts.** (0) The guard is a DECLARATION scan: it proves the token is consumed, never that the value reaches the screen. The end-to-end behaviour above was established by hand and is not re-checked on every run; an effective arm would have to mount each portal and read the wrapper. (1) A rule that is present but OUTRANKED also passes it. (2) The `>= 10` threshold leaves **3–9 unpoliced** — a new floating surface written `z-index: 5` is invisible to both arms; tolerable only because nothing at 5 could clear the existing 50s. (3) A `z-index` written in TypeScript is invisible, and that set is bounded rather than open-ended: the highest in any shipped `.tsx` is `1` — `ClickableCard.tsx`'s **exported** `interactiveLayer` — plus `2` in `_storyKit.tsx` and `0`/`1` in story fixtures, all below 10. **`interactiveLayer` is deliberately NOT on the ladder:** it orders a nested control against that card's own stretched-link overlay, which is ordering inside one stacking context, and it is exported only because consumers compose children into the card — a contract about composition, not about global order. Both guard arms were falsified before being trusted: a comment carrying the token while the real rule carried a raw `3` fails the forward arm, and a raw `999` written without a trailing semicolon fails the reverse arm.

### icon-size-follows-leading

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `FOUNDATIONS`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-12.

**A standalone icon takes the line height of the text role it sits beside, not that role's font size.**

**Sizes.** `icons.css` aliases each icon size to a text leading. Every leading is `calc(Npx * var(--scaling))` in Radix, so all six follow the scaling setting.

| Token | Aliases | At `--scaling: 1` |
|---|---|---|
| `--ds-icon-xs` | `--ds-text-xs-leading` | 16px |
| `--ds-icon-sm` | `--ds-text-sm-leading` | 20px |
| `--ds-icon-md` | `--ds-text-md-leading` | 24px |
| `--ds-icon-h5` | `--ds-text-h5-leading` | 22px |
| `--ds-icon-h4` | `--ds-text-h4-leading` | 26px |
| `--ds-icon-h3` | `--ds-text-h3-leading` | 30px |

**Why.** The line box is the space the icon fills, so an icon matched to it sits in a row with no padding adjustment. An icon matched to the font size leaves every row in need of one.

**Applies to.** Standalone icons: icon buttons, navigation and status, with the heading sizes for dialog titles and similar. An inline icon takes none of these tokens, because Phosphor defaults to `size="1em"` and `color="currentColor"` and so already matches its text run.

**Load order.** `icons.css` loads after `typography.css` in `src/tokens/index.css`, because every icon size resolves through a text leading. The order is part of this ruling, not an implementation note.

**Weight and colour.** The weight tokens in `icons.css`, `--ds-icon-weight-base: "regular"` and `--ds-icon-weight-emphasis: "fill"`, belong to [icon-weight-axis](#icon-weight-axis), which also keeps the fuller Phosphor usage in `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 4 as guidance rather than tokens. An emphasised icon takes its colour from its parent's state through `currentColor`, so no icon emphasis colour token exists, and every icon colour role lives in `semantic.css`.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-12. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The icon foundation — size follows the paired text leading (2026-08-12).** `icons.css` sizes a standalone icon to the LINE BOX of the text role it sits beside, not to that role's font-size: `--ds-icon-xs/sm/md` alias `--ds-text-{xs,sm,md}-leading` (16 / 20 / 24 at `--scaling: 1`) and `--ds-icon-h5/h4/h3` alias the heading leadings for dialog titles and similar (22 / 26 / 30 at the same scaling — every one is `calc(Npx * var(--scaling))` in Radix, so all six track the dial). The line box is the decision: it is the space the icon actually has to fill, so matching it lets an icon drop into a row with no padding micro-adjustment, where matching the font-size leaves every row needing one. Inline icons take none of these — Phosphor defaults to `size="1em"` and `color="currentColor"`, so an icon inside a text run already matches that run — which is why these tokens are scoped to the standalone case (icon buttons, nav, status) rather than being a general icon-size scale. **Load order is part of this ruling, not an implementation note:** `icons.css` must be imported AFTER `typography.css`, because every size above resolves through a text leading; invert the order and all six silently become invalid. The weight axis in this file (`--ds-icon-weight-base: "regular"` / `--ds-icon-weight-emphasis: "fill"`) is **[icon-weight-axis](#icon-weight-axis)**'s two-step ruling rather than a new one; [icon-weight-axis](#icon-weight-axis) also settles that the fuller Phosphor usage in `GUIDELINES.md` §4 — bold in primary CTAs, duotone for empty states, thin/light only at 48px and above — stays documented guidance and is deliberately not tokenised. An emphasised icon takes its COLOUR from the parent's state through `currentColor` (a selected tab fills its icon and shares the tab's colour), which is why no icon-emphasis colour token exists; every icon colour role lives in `semantic.css`.

### spacing-and-radius-scales

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `LAYOUT`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-12.

**`spacing.css` holds a value-named spacing scale and a radius scale, and both alias Radix, so a system component and a raw Radix component share one scale.**

**Spacing.** A step's name is its value: `--ds-space-4` resolves to 4px at `--scaling: 1`.

| Steps | Source |
|---|---|
| `--ds-space-4`, `-8`, `-12`, `-16`, `-24`, `-32`, `-40`, `-48`, `-64` | Radix `--space-1` to `--space-9`, one for one |
| `--ds-space-2`, `-20`, `-56`, `-80`, `-96`, `-128` | `calc()` against `--scaling`, so they track the same dial |
| `--ds-space-0` | A literal `0`, with no dial to track |

**Radius.** `--ds-radius-1` to `--ds-radius-6` alias Radix `--radius-1` to `--radius-6`, each a factor of `--scaling` and the radius factor. The sharp or rounded character of a brand stays on the `radius` prop of `Provider`, where a consumer can change it.

**Exception.** `--ds-radius-full` takes a fixed `9999px`. Radix sets `--radius-full` to a pill only under `radius="full"` and to `0` under `none`, `small`, `medium` and `large`, so a shape that must stay a pill on every brand cannot follow the dial.

**Why.** Two scales that agree by coincidence diverge on the next vendor update. An alias keeps one scale.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-12. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The spacing and radius foundation (2026-08-12).** `spacing.css` owns two scales and this ruling covers both. **Spacing is value-named:** `--ds-space-4` resolves to 4px at `--scaling: 1`, so a canvas or a spec reads a step without a lookup table. Nine steps alias Radix's `--space-1..9` one-for-one — 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64 — and that aliasing is the decision: it is what lets a system component and a raw Radix component share one scale rather than two that agree by coincidence and drift on the next vendor bump. Six extension steps — `--ds-space-2`, `-20`, `-56`, `-80`, `-96`, `-128` — are `calc()`-ed against `--scaling` so they track the same dial as the aliased ones; `--ds-space-0` is a literal `0`, which has no dial to track. **Radius aliases Radix's `--radius-1..6`**, each of which is factor-based (`calc(Npx * var(--scaling) * var(--radius-factor))`). Aliasing rather than redeclaring keeps the sharp-versus-rounded brand distinction on the `<Theme radius>` prop, where a consumer can move it, instead of freezing it into this layer. `--ds-radius-full` is the one exception and takes a fixed `9999px`: Radix sets `--radius-full` to a pill value ONLY under `<Theme radius="full">` and to `0` under `none`, `small`, `medium` and `large`, so a shape that must stay a pill on every brand cannot ride the dial.

### type-ramp

**Tags.** `TYPOGRAPHY`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-12.

**The type ramp is Radix's own, and `typography.css` overrides no step of it.**

**Roles.** Each named role is a portable alias onto a native Radix step, reachable through `<Heading size>`, `<Text size>` and the `--ds-text-*` tokens.

| Role | Radix step | Leading |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | 8 | heading |
| H2 | 7 | heading |
| H3 | 6 | heading |
| H4 | 5 | heading |
| H5 | 3 | heading |
| Medium | 3 | text |
| Small | 2 | text |
| Extra small (XS) | 1 | text |

**Why.** Each role inherits Radix's `--scaling` and its letter-spacing per size, and this layer restates neither. A redeclared ramp would re-derive tables that Radix maintains and would silently stop tracking them.

**What the file changes.** Five things, and nothing else:

- a 600 Strong weight, which Radix does not ship ([type-and-target-density](#type-and-target-density))
- the typeface indirection: `Provider` writes `--ds-typeface-body`, `--ds-typeface-heading` and `--ds-typeface-code` on `document.documentElement`, because a portal renders into `<body>`, outside the theme root
- the serif `--ds-font-em` and `--ds-font-quote` set against the sans UI ([serif-em-and-quote](#serif-em-and-quote))
- `--ds-text-measure: 65ch`, a reading cap for prose only, as `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 3 asks
- the root body size, `--ds-ui-body-size`

**Body size.** `.radix-themes` takes Radix step 2, 3 or 4 at the small, medium and large tiers of `data-ui-size`. Default body copy is step 2 (14px), where Radix's own default is step 3 (16px), so body copy follows the global UI size like every other part.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-12.

- [measure-cap-scope](#measure-cap-scope) removes the 65ch cap from prose in a pane the reader resizes.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The type ramp is Radix's, deliberately (2026-08-12).** `typography.css` overrides no scale step. The named roles are portable aliases onto native Radix steps — H1=8, H2=7, H3=6, H4=5, H5=3, Medium=3, Small=2, XS=1 — so every role is reachable through both `<Heading size>` / `<Text size>` and the `--ds-text-*` tokens, and inherits Radix's `--scaling` and per-size letter-spacing without this layer restating either. Headings take the tighter heading line-heights; Medium takes text leading. **Not overriding is the decision:** a redeclared ramp would have to re-derive the letter-spacing and scaling tables Radix already maintains, and would silently stop tracking them. **This file changes five things, and nothing else.** (1) A 600 "Strong" weight, which Radix does not ship — it ships **300 / 400 / 500 / 700** — ruled at **[type-and-target-density](#type-and-target-density)(a)**, where 600 is the UI workhorse a 400/700 pair cannot cover without reading flat or shouty. (2) The typeface indirection: `Provider` writes `--ds-typeface-body` / `-heading` / `-code` onto `document.documentElement` rather than the theme root, because a portal renders into `<body>` and is not a descendant of the theme root, so a style set there would never reach portaled content; with no `typefaces` prop nothing is written, every `var()` falls through to its default, and rendering is identical to before the indirection existed. (3) The serif-italic `--ds-font-em` / `--ds-font-quote` set against the sans UI, ruled at **[serif-em-and-quote](#serif-em-and-quote)**. (4) `--ds-text-measure: 65ch`, a reading-measure cap for PROSE only — visual and data content is scanned rather than read and goes full width (`GUIDELINES.md` §3). (5) **The root body size**, the only item here that changes what an unstyled paragraph looks like: `.radix-themes` takes `--ds-ui-body-size`, which the `data-ui-size` tier sets to Radix step 2 / 3 / 4, so default body copy is step 2 (14px) where Radix's own `--default-font-size` is step 3 (16px). That is deliberate — body copy follows the global UI size like everything else.

### scrim-foreground-tokens

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `COLOUR`, `ACCESSIBILITY`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-02.

**`--ds-on-scrim` and `--ds-on-scrim-light` are the foreground for content drawn on a scrim, and their values derive from the scrim's worst case.**

**What you see.** Text on the dark scrim, `--ds-scrim`, takes `--ds-on-scrim`, which is `#fff`. Text on the light scrim, `--ds-scrim-light`, takes `--ds-on-scrim-light`, which is `#21201c`.

**Measured.** A scrim at an alpha of 0.6 or darker clamps the composite to one side whatever media sits beneath it, so a worst case exists even for unknown media.

| Scrim | Worst case | Composite | Foreground | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--ds-scrim`, a black alpha | Light appearance over pure white media | `#666666` | `#fff` | 5.74:1 |
| `--ds-scrim-light`, a white alpha with no dark override | Over pure black media | `#999999` | `#21201c` | 5.72:1 |

Both clear WCAG 1.4.3 AA at 4.5:1. The two scrims are opposites, and white on `--ds-scrim-light` measures 1.00:1, so each scrim needs its own token.

**Limit.** Both guarantees hold only while the scrim alpha stays at 0.6 or higher, and below about 0.53 each falls below 4.5:1. `--ds-scrim` is marked mutable in `semantic.css`, so a softer scrim forfeits this guarantee. `--ds-on-scrim-light` is the literal `#21201c` rather than an alias of `--warning-contrast`, because the brand collision blocks re-pin that token.

**Not covered.** A control border on a scrim, held to 3:1 by WCAG 1.4.11, is not certified by these tokens. A focus ring on a scrim follows [focus-ring](#focus-ring).

**Why a token.** axe reports no result when it cannot resolve the background a colour composites against, and a scrim always sits over an image. A named role and a written number are the only checks that reach this case, in this system or in a consumer's app.

**Scope.** A whole scrim surface the system owns, such as the Thumbnail remove control or the Lightbox chrome, keeps the permanently dark `<Theme>` idiom. These tokens serve a foreground on a scrim that cannot be wrapped, which is the consumer's case, because `Theme` is not exported. They sit in `DS_ROLES.fill` and on the Colors foundations page beside the scrims they pair with.

**Changed from.** Every solid fill had a paired `--on-*` token except the scrim, so text on a scrim had no system answer and `Overlay.stories.tsx` hardcoded `color: "white"`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-02.

- [overlay-scrim-ink](#overlay-scrim-ink) makes the `Overlay` scrim set these tokens as the colour of its content.
- [scrim-value](#scrim-value) gives `--ds-scrim` one value, the 0.6 black alpha, in both appearances, where the dark appearance first used a 0.9 black alpha.
- [scrim-focus-ring](#scrim-focus-ring) closes the open focus ring case and corrects the 2.84:1 figure first recorded for it.
- [focus-ring](#focus-ring) replaces the scrim's focus ring with the accent ring and deletes `--ds-stroke-focus-hairline`.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`--ds-on-scrim` and `--ds-on-scrim-light`, the foreground for content drawn on a scrim (2026-09-02).** Every solid fill in this system has had a paired `--on-*` since 2026-06 (`theme.css`). The scrim was the one that did not, so text on a scrim had no system answer and `Overlay.stories.tsx` hardcoded `color: "white"`, a raw literal in a layer whose first rule is that components never hardcode a colour. **The values are DERIVED, not picked, which is what makes them defensible.** A scrim is a monotone alpha at 0.6 or darker, and that clamps the composite to one side whatever image sits beneath, so a worst-case bound exists even though the media is unknown. `--ds-scrim` is a black alpha in both appearances (`black-a8` light, `black-a11` dark). Its worst case is the light appearance over pure white media, compositing to `#666666`, where **white reads 5.74:1**. `--ds-scrim-light` is a white alpha with no `.dark` override. Its worst case is over pure black media, compositing to `#999999`, where **`#21201c` reads 5.72:1**. Both clear WCAG 1.4.3 AA for normal text at 4.5. **Two tokens rather than one, because the scrims are opposites:** white on `--ds-scrim-light` measures **1.00:1**. **The contract has a limit, stated rather than implied:** both guarantees hold only while the scrim alpha stays at or above 0.6, and below roughly 0.53 each falls under 4.5. `--ds-scrim` is marked mutable in `semantic.css`, so softening it forfeits this. **`#21201c` is a literal, not an alias to `--warning-contrast`**, which carries the same value today: the per-accent collision blocks re-pin that one, so aliasing would couple the scrim to the warning family. **What these do NOT certify:** a focus ring or a control border on a scrim, which is WCAG 1.4.11 at 3:1. Measured, `--ds-stroke-focus-hairline` resolves `#202020` in the light appearance and reads 2.84:1 against the worst-case scrim composite, so `GUIDELINES.md` §9 records that case as uncertified and open. **Why a token rather than documentation:** scrim content is structurally un-gateable by axe, which abstains when it cannot resolve the background it composites against, and a scrim always sits over an image. A named role and a written number are the only checks that reach this case, here or in any consumer's app. **The permanently-dark `<Theme>` idiom stays** the sanctioned mechanism for a whole scrim SURFACE the system owns (Thumbnail's remove ✕, Lightbox's chrome). These tokens serve a foreground on a scrim you cannot wrap, which is the consumer's case, since `Theme` is deliberately unexported. Registered in `DS_ROLES.fill` and on the Colors wall beside the veils they pair with, so nobody reads one without the other again. **[Update 2026-09-24 ([scrim-focus-ring](#scrim-focus-ring)): the focus-ring case is closed. Overlay's scrim re-points `--ds-stroke-focus-hairline` to these same inks, so the ring reads at least 5.74:1 and 5.72:1 at the worst media, against the 3:1 of WCAG 1.4.11. The 2.84:1 recorded above was the best case for a dark ring on the dark scrim, not the worst, which is 1.00:1 near #505050, and the dark appearance on the light scrim failed the same way near #d5d5d5. A control border on a scrim is still not certified by these.]**

### interaction-state-alphas

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `TOKENS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-25.

**An interactive state lays a Radix alpha over the rest fill, and never moves the fill to another step or invents a shade.**

**What you see.** A hover, press or open state lays one of Radix's own alpha steps, `--black-a*`, `--white-a*`, or an accent or gray alpha, over the rest fill, through a `--ds-*` role, and only while the interaction lasts. The polarity of the overlay follows the label, so the label's contrast rises during the interaction.

**Choosing the step.** The step is the alpha whose change on the rest fill lies closest to Radix's own hover from step 9 to step 10. It is chosen by that rule, not by eye.

**Rejected.** A move to another solid step, and a colour blended between two steps, which would be a value the system invents.

**Applies to.** The solid `Button` and `IconButton` first ([text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast)). Every other state rule that still switches a solid step moves to this rule when it is next touched. On 2026-09-25 those were the classic `Kbd` as a link, the `Lightbox` control disc, the `FileInput` dropzone, solid `Code` and the high-contrast menu highlight.

**New roles.** A new state role is an alias of a Radix alpha, never a pinned value. The system uses the tokens Radix defines until a mechanism that generates tokens exists.

**Guidance.** The maintainer ruled this on 2026-09-25, during the fix to the solid button hover, and plans a mechanism that generates tokens dynamically at a later stage.

**Changed from.** A hover or press state moved the fill to another solid step.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-25.

- [contrast-by-alpha-stacking](#contrast-by-alpha-stacking) extends the alpha stack to every part without text that falls short of its contrast floor.
- [textless-part-fills](#textless-part-fills) moves solid `Code` to the overlay, so a linked chip keeps its fill on hover.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Interactive states stack a Radix alpha over the rest fill, and never switch to another step or invent a shade (2026-09-25).** Ruled by the maintainer during the fix to the solid button hover. A hover, press or open state changes contrast by laying one of Radix's own alpha steps (`--black-a*`, `--white-a*`, or an accent or gray alpha) over the rest fill, through a `--ds-*` role, and only while the interaction lasts. It does not move the fill to another solid step, and it never uses a colour blended between two steps, because that is a value the system would invent. The overlay's polarity follows the label, so the label's contrast rises during the interaction. The step is chosen by rule, not by eye: the alpha whose change on the rest fill lies closest to Radix's own step 9 to step 10 hover. The solid Button and IconButton are the first adopters ([text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast)). The other state rules that still switch a solid step are Kbd classic as a link, the Lightbox control disc, the FileInput dropzone, solid Code and the high-contrast menu highlight, and they move to this rule as each is touched. This leans on Radix's defined tokens for now, and the maintainer plans a dynamic token-generation mechanism later, so a new state role is an alias of a Radix alpha, never a pinned value.

### contrast-by-alpha-stacking

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `ACCESSIBILITY`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-25.

**When a colour falls short of its contrast floor, the fix stacks on the element's own colour the lightest Radix black or white alpha that clears the floor, and a large fill that carries text is the one exception.**

**Applies to.**

- the hover and press states ([interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas))
- the part edges ([part-fill-edge](#part-fill-edge), [radio-cards-band-edge](#radio-cards-band-edge), [indicator-mark-edges](#indicator-mark-edges))
- the scrim ring ([light-scrim-focus-ring](#light-scrim-focus-ring))
- the focus ring ([focus-ring](#focus-ring))
- every later fix to a part without text

**Floor.** A part without text clears WCAG 3:1 and APCA Lc 30.

**Exception.** The solid Button, IconButton and Code chip fill ([text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast)) and the parts that match it in light ([textless-part-fills](#textless-part-fills)) move to the colour's own deeper Radix step.

**Why.**

- A black alpha over a bright fill muddies its hue. A thin ring or edge hides that, and a whole button does not.
- The fill must stay one colour value that works as a fill, a border, a text colour or a stroke, and a stack needs a second layer drawn on top.

**Guidance.** The maintainer chose, on 2026-09-25, one pattern for every subtle element, and weighed a stack on the fills that carry text before keeping the deeper step.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-25. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Contrast is kept by stacking a Radix alpha, and a fill that carries text is the one exception (2026-09-25).** Ruled by the maintainer, who asked which way the system keeps contrast and chose one pattern for every subtle element. When a colour falls short of its contrast floor, the fix stacks on the element's own colour the lightest Radix black or white alpha that clears the floor. The hover and press states ([interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas)), the part edges ([part-fill-edge](#part-fill-edge), [radio-cards-band-edge](#radio-cards-band-edge), [indicator-mark-edges](#indicator-mark-edges)), the scrim ring ([light-scrim-focus-ring](#light-scrim-focus-ring)) and the focus ring ([focus-ring](#focus-ring)) all work this way, and every later fix to a part without text follows it. A part without text clears WCAG 3:1 and APCA Lc 30. **The one exception is a large fill that carries text:** the solid Button, IconButton and Code chip fill ([text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast)) and the parts that match it in light ([textless-part-fills](#textless-part-fills)) move to the colour's own deeper Radix step. Two reasons keep it. A black alpha over a bright fill muddies its hue, which a thin ring or edge hides and a whole button does not. And the fill must stay one colour value that works as a fill, a border, text colour or a stroke, where a stack needs a second layer drawn on top. The maintainer weighed a stack on these fills too and kept the deeper step.

### apca-contrast-mode

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `ACCESSIBILITY`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-27.

**The WCAG and APCA contrast mode stays, and it exists for the four brands whose warning label cannot clear both floors in its own vivid colour.**

**Why it exists.** On gold, amber, yellow and lime brands the warning family shifts to orange ([brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate)). The label on the solid orange-9 warning fill then clears one standard only:

| Label ink | WCAG | APCA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dark ink | 5.47:1 | Lc 45.8 |
| White | 2.97:1 | Lc 60.8 |

**What stays.**

- the `contrast` prop on `Provider`, `wcag` by default
- the Contrast control in the Storybook toolbar
- `src/tokens/contrast.css`
- the Colors page check that holds `contrast.css` to the APCA polarity
- every WCAG and APCA check

**Scope.** Across 27 colours in both appearances, the APCA mode changes the label on the solid warning fill on these four brands in the light appearance, and nothing else. No shipped component painted text on the solid warning fill on 2026-09-27, so the choice reaches a consumer who does.

**Guidance.** The maintainer ruled, on 2026-09-27, to keep orange-9 and the contrast mode. The maintainer rejected orange-11, a deeper step that clears both floors, because it loses the vividness of the colour.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-27.

- [status-dot-edges](#status-dot-edges) closes a gap this ruling recorded in passing: the warning status dot read under 3:1 against the page in light, and it now stacks its own edge, `--warning-dot-edge`.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The WCAG and APCA contrast mode stays, and it exists for the four brands whose warning label cannot clear both floors in its own vivid colour (2026-09-27).** Ruled by the maintainer. On gold, amber, yellow and lime brands warning shifts to orange ([brand-status-collision-gate](#brand-status-collision-gate)), and the label on the solid warning fill clears one standard only: dark ink on orange-9 reads 5.47:1 and APCA Lc 45.8, and white reads 2.97:1 and Lc 60.8. Measured over 27 colours in both appearances on six text-on-fill pairs, 324 readings, the APCA mode changes these four pairs in light and nothing else. A deeper step clears both floors: orange-11 with white reads 4.51:1 and Lc 75.8 in light, and orange-11 with dark ink reads 8.07:1 and Lc 62.3 in dark on gold, yellow and lime, while dark amber on orange-10 with black reads Lc 55.2. The maintainer rejected the deeper step because it loses the vividness of the colour, and kept orange-9. So the `contrast` prop on Provider, the Contrast control in the Storybook toolbar, `contrast.css` and the Colors page check that holds `contrast.css` to the APCA polarity all stay, every WCAG and APCA check stays, and toggling between the two modes matters only for these four colours. No shipped component paints text on the solid warning fill today, so the choice reaches a consumer who does. **Found on the way, recorded and not fixed:** the warning status dot reads 1.23 to 2.9:1 against the page in light on all 27 colours, under the 3:1 a part without text owes. **[Update 2026-09-27 ([status-dot-edges](#status-dot-edges)): the warning dot stacks its own edge, `--warning-dot-edge`, and reads 3.04:1 and Lc 55.3 or more against the page, the subtle recess, a card and a panel in light, so this gap is closed.]**

## Accessibility rulings (made during implementation, verified in tests)

### warning-contrast-ink

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `ACCESSIBILITY`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Text on the solid warning fill takes a fixed near-black, `#21201c`, in both appearances.**

**What you see.** `--warning-contrast`, and `--on-warning` through it, is `#21201c` in light and in dark, and reads about 10:1 on the amber step 9 fill in both.

**Why.** Amber step 9 stays bright in dark, while `--amber-12` turns light, so the step 12 ink read 1.30:1 on the warning fill in dark.

**Changed from.** The provided `theme.css` set `--warning-contrast: var(--amber-12)`, which was unreadable on the warning fill in dark.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [apca-contrast-mode](#apca-contrast-mode) keeps the APCA contrast mode, in which `--warning-contrast` is white in light on gold, yellow, amber and lime brands, whose warning fill moves to orange.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Dark-mode warning-contrast bug fixed.** The provided `theme.css` set `--warning-contrast: var(--amber-12)`, which flips to light in dark mode while amber-9 stays bright → 1.30:1 (unreadable). Pinned to a fixed near-black `#21201c` → ~10:1 in both modes.

### warning-text-tolerance

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** No date recorded.

**Warning text on the page passes at 4.49:1, a tolerance of 0.05 under the 4.5:1 text minimum.**

**What you see.** `--ds-text-warning` reads `--warning-11`, which is amber-11 under the default warning family, and it computes 4.49:1. The value stays as Radix ships it.

**Why.** Step 11 is the step Radix tunes for accessible text.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** In force. No date was recorded for this ruling.

- [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) extends the tolerance to the step 11 of every scale a brand shift can route warning or success text through, with a floor of 4.39:1 against the page, and later holds `--ds-text-link` to the same floor.
- [soft-fill-text-exception](#soft-fill-text-exception) records that the floor was measured on the page background, so it does not cover text on a soft status tint.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`--ds-text-warning` (amber-11) accepted at a 0.05 tolerance** (computes 4.49; amber-11 is Radix's tuned accessible-text step). No edit to the provided file.

### focus-return-on-close

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-08-19.

**Every modal surface returns focus to the element that opened it, and the system supplies that restore where Radix does not.**

**What you see.** Close a `Dialog`, `AlertDialog`, `Lightbox`, `CommandPalette` or `MobileNav` with Escape or its close button, and focus lands on the element that held it before the surface opened. This holds whether the surface opens from an exported `Trigger` or from an `open` prop the consumer holds.

**Why.** Radix's modal `Dialog.Content` returns focus only to a rendered `Dialog.Trigger`. A surface driven from an `open` prop registers no trigger, so Radix cancels the focus scope's own restore, focus lands on `<body>`, and the page fails WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order.

**Mechanism.** One internal hook, `src/components/ui/useReturnFocus.ts`, captures the opener in `onOpenAutoFocus`, which Radix dispatches before it moves focus into the panel, and returns an `onCloseAutoFocus` that focuses the opener again. When the opener is no longer in the document, the handler does nothing and Radix's own behaviour stands, and a consumer handler that prevents the default still wins.

**Not covered.** `Popover`, `DropdownMenu`, `HoverCard`, `ContextMenu` and `Tooltip` expose a `Trigger` and need no repair. `Typeahead` and `PowerSearch` never move focus out of their input.

**Rejected.**

- A layout effect on the open flag as the capture point. A `Content` wrapper mounts with the page, because Radix gates the content below it, so the effect reads `<body>` once and never runs again.
- A `triggerElementRef` repeated in each component: five copies of a mechanism whose ordering constraint is invisible at each call site.
- Exporting the hook: a consumer cannot build a modal surface here, because `Theme` is not exported.

**Changed from.** Focus landed on `<body>` after `Lightbox`, `CommandPalette` or `MobileNav` closed, and after a `Dialog` or `AlertDialog` closed whose `open` state the consumer held.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-08-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Close-focus is restored by us, not by Radix, on every modal surface opened from a prop (2026-08-19).** Radix's modal `Dialog.Content` does not return focus to the element that had it. It runs `onCloseAutoFocus: composeEventHandlers(props.onCloseAutoFocus, (event) => { event.preventDefault(); context.triggerRef.current?.focus() })`, where `triggerRef` is populated only by a rendered `Dialog.Trigger`. A surface driven from an `open` prop registers no trigger, so the `preventDefault` cancels the focus scope's own restore and nothing replaces it: focus lands on `<body>`, failing WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order. **Measured before the fix**, on the shipped build: `document.activeElement` was `<body>` at every sample from 300ms to 2.4s after both Escape and the close button, with the opener still in the DOM. **Scope, verified rather than assumed:** `Lightbox`, `CommandPalette` and `MobileNav` all drive the raw Radix Dialog from a prop and all three were affected. `Dialog` and `AlertDialog` are correct when a consumer uses the exported `Trigger`, and carry the same hole when the consumer holds `open` themselves, which is the ordinary shape when the opener is a menu item, a row action or a keyboard shortcut. `Popover`, `DropdownMenu`, `HoverCard`, `ContextMenu` and `Tooltip` are **not** affected: they expose a `Trigger`, and `Typeahead` and `PowerSearch` never move focus out of their input. **Fix:** one internal hook, `src/components/ui/useReturnFocus.ts`, returning both halves. It captures the opener from **`onOpenAutoFocus`**, which Radix dispatches before it moves focus into the panel, and hands back an `onCloseAutoFocus` that focuses that element again. The handler **declines** rather than fires when the opener has been unmounted meanwhile, leaving Radix's own behaviour untouched, and a consumer handler that prevents the default still wins. **A React effect is the wrong capture point and this is recorded because it looked right.** The first implementation used a layout effect on the `false` to `true` edge, reasoning that the focus scope autofocuses from a passive effect so every layout effect in the commit precedes it. That reasoning holds, and the implementation still failed, for an unrelated reason: in a `Content` **wrapper** there is no such edge. React renders `<Dialog.Content>` as a child of `Dialog.Root` whether the dialog is open or not, because the gating happens inside Radix below the wrapper, so the wrapper mounts with the page, its effect reads `<body>`, and it never runs again. It passed in `Lightbox`, whose component holds the flag, and failed in `Dialog`, which is exactly the split a single component's test would have hidden. The event is the one capture point correct for both. **Rejected:** repeating a `triggerElementRef` in each component (five copies of a mechanism whose ordering constraint is invisible at each call site), and exporting the hook (a consumer cannot build a modal surface here anyway, since `Theme` is unexported, so publishing it would advertise a route that does not exist). **Locked by** `RestoresFocusOnClose` in the Lightbox, CommandPalette and MobileNav behaviour suites and `RestoresFocusWithoutTrigger` in the Dialog suite; the existing `Behavior` story already covered the `Dialog.Trigger` path, which is the one case Radix handles.

### wcag-claim-scope

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `DOCUMENTATION`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**The WCAG 2.2 AA claim is scoped, and `GUIDELINES.md` section 9 states what is verified and what is not.**

**Why.** The claim becomes a promise to other people when the package publishes, so a reader must not have to guess where it ends.

**Verified continuously.**

- axe over every story in the light and the dark appearance lane, apart from the registered opt-outs
- the contrast assertions in `src/foundations/_assert.ts`
- the guard lane

**Not verified.**

- No assistive technology pass. No screen reader was driven over any component, so every claim about a role, a name or an announcement rests on the primitive and on axe, and axe hears nothing.
- The accent axis. A story renders at one point in the globals space, so the suite sweeps appearance and leaves the accent at its default, as `.storybook/preview.tsx` states.

**Gap.** No guard sweeps the accents on a rendered component, so a contrast defect that appears on some accents only stays a measurement rather than an invariant. The guard that would close it is an accent sweep contrast probe in the browser lane, with its exceptions in a register and a reverse arm, so a new failure and a fixed exception both fail the probe.

**Changed from.** The WCAG 2.2 AA claim carried no written scope, so a reader could assume verification that never ran.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17.

- [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) closes the third gap this entry named. Text on a hovered solid accent fill read 2.59 to 2.79:1 on six accents at dark appearance, measured on 2026-09-17, and now reaches 4.5:1 at rest and on hover.
- [soft-fill-text-exception](#soft-fill-text-exception) records text on a soft semantic fill as a further measured exception in the same posture.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The WCAG 2.2 AA claim is SCOPED, and the scope is written down (2026-09-17).** The claim becomes a promise to other people at publish, so what was verified and what was not are both stated in `GUIDELINES.md` §9 rather than left to a reader to assume. **Verified continuously:** axe in two appearance lanes over every story bar the registered opt-outs, the contrast assertions in `src/foundations/_assert.ts`, and the guard lane. **NOT verified, and each is named:** (1) **No assistive-technology pass has been run.** Nothing in the repository records a screen reader being driven over any component, so every role, name and announcement claim rests on the primitive's own guarantees plus axe, which cannot hear anything. The claim is scoped rather than waiting on an AT pass. (2) **The accent axis is not swept by any suite.** `preview.tsx` says so deliberately: a story renders at one point in the globals space, so the suite sweeps APPEARANCE and leaves accent at the default. Which is exactly how (3) went unseen. (3) **Text on a hovered solid accent fill dips below the 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill at dark appearance, on six of twenty-seven accents.** Measured 2026-09-17 in real Google Chrome, rasterized through a canvas pixel because a wide-gamut display returns `color(display-p3 …)` that no `rgb()` regex parses: `--accent-contrast` over `--accent-10` gives blue **2.79**, green **2.76**, jade **2.74**, teal **2.64**, grass **2.62**, cyan **2.59** — against the 3.0 large/bold provision of that floor. At rest the same six clear it (3.00–3.26), and at LIGHT appearance every one of the twenty-seven clears it at both rest and hover, so this is dark-appearance hover only. **Both steps are Radix's own** (`--accent-10` is its hover step, `--accent-contrast` its solid foreground), so the pairing is inherited rather than introduced here — which is why it is recorded as a scoped gap and not as a regression. **Not fixed in this ruling, deliberately:** every available fix changes how a hovered primary button LOOKS on six accents (hold `--accent-9` through hover at dark, take a different step, or flip the foreground), and that is a design decision with its own review, not a footnote to a documentation change. **Mechanism gap, named rather than left implicit:** there is no guard over this, because no lane sweeps accents, so the numbers above are a measurement and not yet an invariant. The guard that would make it one is an accent-sweep contrast probe in the browser lane carrying the six-name set as a registered exception with a reverse arm, so neither a seventh accent falling below nor a fix that clears one can pass unnoticed. Until it exists, this entry is the record.

### popover-accessible-name

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**`Popover.Content` must carry an accessible name, and its type refuses a panel without one.**

**Rule.** `PopoverContentProps` accepts `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` or both, and a panel with neither is a compile error. A panel with a visible title may reference that title with `aria-labelledby`.

**Runtime check.** In a development build the panel warns when its name is an empty string, the case a template literal can produce and the type cannot catch, and the warning names WCAG 4.1.2.

**Why.** Radix sets `role="dialog"` on the panel, and a dialog without a name fails WCAG 4.1.2: a screen reader announces "dialog" and nothing else.

**Not covered.** Components built on the raw `@radix-ui/react-popover` never pass through this wrapper:

- `Typeahead` and `PowerSearch` set `role="none"` on the panel, because the form controls inside it carry the semantics, so the panel takes no name.
- `DateInput` and `DateRangeInput` keep `role="dialog"` and name the panel "Choose date" and "Choose date range".

**Precedent.** The rule follows [chat-log-scroller](#chat-log-scroller), where `ChatMessageList` requires its region name in the type and checks for the empty string at runtime.

**Changed from.** The type and the runtime both accepted an unnamed panel, while the `Popover.tsx` docblock claimed a labelled dialog. A composition scenario with a `MultiSelect` inside a `Popover` exposed the gap when axe reported `aria-dialog-name`. Every call site in the repository already passed `aria-label`, so the change broke none.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`Popover.Content` requires an accessible name, in the type (2026-09-17).** Radix hardcodes `role="dialog"` on the panel, and a dialog with no accessible name is a WCAG 4.1.2 failure: a screen reader announces "dialog" and nothing else. `Popover.tsx` has claimed "a labelled `role="dialog"`" in its docblock since it was written, for a panel that obliged nobody to label it — the type accepted an unnamed Content and the runtime accepted one too. **Found by composition, not by audit.** Every unit-level story happened to pass a name, so nothing was ever red; the gap surfaced when a scenario page put a `MultiSelect` inside a `Popover` and axe reported `aria-dialog-name` on the panel. That is the argument for the composition suite in one finding. **Fix, on [chat-log-scroller](#chat-log-scroller)'s precedent** (`ChatMessageList` made its region name required in the type and kept a runtime check for the empty string): `PopoverContentProps` now takes `aria-label` OR `aria-labelledby`, as a union that permits both and rejects neither being present, so omitting a name is a compile error. A `useEffect` catches the case the type cannot — the empty string a template literal hands over — and says which WCAG criterion it fails. **Non-breaking as landed:** all three call sites in the repo already passed `aria-label`, so this promoted a convention that was already being followed to a contract that cannot be forgotten. **Deliberately NOT applied to the non-dialog pattern.** `Typeahead` and `PowerSearch` build on the RAW `@radix-ui/react-popover` and suppress the role outright with `role="none"`, because there the inner form controls carry the semantics and a name on the container would be noise. Those never pass through this wrapper. `DateInput` and `DateRangeInput` also use the raw primitive, keep Radix's `role="dialog"` and already name it ("Choose date", "Choose date range"), so the three raw-primitive users were audited rather than assumed. **The name is a prop, not a heading scrape:** a panel with a visible title may point `aria-labelledby` at it, which is why both routes are accepted rather than just `aria-label`.

### soft-fill-text-exception

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**Text on a soft semantic fill is a scoped exception with measured values, not a case of the large or bold text provision.**

**What you see.** The soft `Badge` and `Callout` keep Radix's step-11 text on the weak status fill. Their story files scope the strict 4.5 axe rule off the toned specimens and name this ruling as the reason.

**Why the provision does not apply.** WCAG large text is 24px at regular weight or 18.66px at weight 700. A `Badge` renders 12px at weight 500 at every size step and `Callout` body text renders 14px at weight 400, so neither qualifies.

**Measured.** In light appearance the four tones read 4.10 to 4.43, under the strict 4.5, and in dark they read 7.72 to 10.35. The weak fill costs about 0.4 to 0.5 against the page background, where [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) and [warning-text-tolerance](#warning-text-tolerance) set the 4.39 floor for step-11 text.

**Why the paint stays.** These are Radix's own values for step-11 text on the step-a3 fill, and a change repaints every soft `Badge` and `Callout`. That is a design decision with its own review, in the same posture as [wcag-claim-scope](#wcag-claim-scope).

**Open options.** For that design decision:

- step-12 text, which breaks the convention that step 11 is the accessible text step
- a lighter weak fill, which weakens the tone signal
- 4.5 in dark appearance only, with light stated as the gap

**Gap.** No test lane sweeps this pairing, so the values are measurements rather than invariants. A guard belongs in the browser lane, asserting the four tones in both appearances against a registered set with a reverse arm.

**Changed from.** Two story files and a Decision card on the Callout page justified the scope-off with the large or bold provision for text on a solid fill, which this text never met. That provision belonged to the 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill, and [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) retired the floor on 2026-09-25.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Text on a SOFT semantic fill is a measured exception, NOT an application of the solid-fill large/bold provision (2026-09-17).** Three places claimed it was: `Badge.stories.tsx` ("the documented ~4.1:1 AA-3.0 tier", citing the solid-fill floor and [warning-text-tolerance](#warning-text-tolerance)), `Callout.stories.tsx` (the same, at ~4.1–4.4:1), and a reader-visible Decision card on the Callout page ("Text on a soft semantic fill sits at the AA-3.0 (large/bold) provision"). **The provision does not apply, and it is measurable that it does not.** WCAG large text is ≥24px at regular weight, or ≥18.66px at bold (≥700). Measured in real Chrome: a `Badge` renders **12px at weight 500** at every size step, and `Callout`'s body text **14px at weight 400**. Neither qualifies on either axis, so the 3.0 tier that genuinely large/bold solid-fill labels earn under the 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill cannot be borrowed here. That floor's own guardrail says exactly this in the other direction: "don't put small, regular-weight text on a step-9 fill." **What the pairing actually measures**, step-11 text on the weak fill (alpha step 3) composited over the page background, rasterized through a canvas pixel because a wide-gamut display reports `color(display-p3 …)`: LIGHT — error **4.43**, info **4.15**, warning **4.14**, success **4.10**. DARK — warning **10.35**, success **7.85**, error **7.74**, info **7.72**. On the page background instead of the tint, all four clear in light (4.50–5.08), which is the point: **the weak fill costs roughly 0.4–0.5 ratio points**, and the 4.39 floor [brand-collision-shift-table](#brand-collision-shift-table) and [warning-text-tolerance](#warning-text-tolerance) set for step-11 text was measured on the page background, never on a tinted one. So light appearance is the whole problem, and three of the four tones sit under 4.39 there while error clears 4.39 but misses the strict 4.5. **The exemption is what kept this green.** Both story files scope the strict-4.5 axe rule off on the toned specimens, so nothing was ever red, and the justification recorded beside the scope-off was the provision that does not apply. An exemption carrying a wrong reason is worse than one carrying none, because it reads as settled. **Ruling: the paint stays, the justification changes.** These are the values Radix's own step-11-on-step-a3 pairing produces, they are within 0.4 of the strict threshold rather than near the 3.0 tier, and moving them repaints every soft Badge and Callout in the system — a design decision with its own review, not a footnote to a documentation correction. So this is recorded as a SCOPED EXCEPTION with its measured numbers, in the same posture as [wcag-claim-scope](#wcag-claim-scope), and the three claim sites now say that rather than citing a provision. **Fix options, for whoever takes the design decision:** step-12 text instead of step-11 (darker, and it breaks the "11 is the accessible-text step" convention the whole token layer rests on), a lighter weak fill (less tint, weaker tone signal), or accepting 4.5 only in dark and stating light as the gap. **Mechanism gap, same as [wcag-claim-scope](#wcag-claim-scope)'s:** no lane sweeps this pairing, so these are measurements rather than invariants. A guard belongs in the browser lane, asserting the four tones in both appearances against a registered expected set with a reverse arm.

### scenario-axe-carve-outs

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**A scenario page may exempt itself from the axe `color-contrast` rule only by citing the rulings that justify it, and a guard checks each citation.**

**Applies to.** The composition fixture, `src/scenarios/_composition.stories.tsx`, the one scenario page that still runs axe. The showcase recreations run no axe at all ([showcases-and-fixture](#showcases-and-fixture)).

**The rule.**

- The fixture may exempt `color-contrast` and no other axe rule.
- Each exemption sits in the `SCENARIO_CONTRAST_EXEMPT` register in `src/foundations/axe-scope.node-check.ts`, with the rulings it cites and a measured reason.
- Every cited ruling must match an entry heading in `docs/DECISIONS.md`, so a citation no reader can follow fails the build.
- The register and the live exemptions must agree in both directions.

**Why.** Contrast belongs to a token pairing, so a composition page adds no information about it. Every contrast finding on the scenario pages was a ruled token value that failed on its own component page too, and a suite kept red by findings it cannot add goes unread. What a composition page alone tests is structure, and that half still runs.

**Cost.** A new contrast defect on the fixture is not caught there. The component's own page, where `color-contrast` stays on, and the token guards still catch it.

**Changed from.** The ruling of 2026-09-03 barred every axe exclusion on the composition pages and sent their findings to a report. Over fifteen days that rule found twelve `color-contrast` violations, each a ruled token value, and one structural defect, the unnamed `Popover` panel that [popover-accessible-name](#popover-accessible-name) closed.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17.

- [showcases-and-fixture](#showcases-and-fixture) splits the scenario pages into showcases with axe off and one composition fixture, which keeps this rule unchanged.
- [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) settles the solid-fill contrast question this ruling left open for the maintainer, and replaces the 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A scenario-page axe carve-out is permitted only by CITING a ruling, and a guard checks the citation (2026-09-17).** Amends the ruling of 2026-09-03, which was that the composition pages carry no axe exclusions at all and their findings go to a report. **That rule earned the amendment by working.** Held for fifteen days it produced exactly one harvest: twelve `color-contrast` violations across five pages, in both appearance lanes, and **nothing else of any kind** — no structural finding, no naming gap, no focus defect, no live-region collision. The one structural defect the suite ever found, an unnamed `Popover` panel, is closed by [popover-accessible-name](#popover-accessible-name) and is now a compile error. **Why that result narrows the rule rather than vindicating it.** Every one of the twelve is a token-level value already measured and ruled — soft semantic fill ([soft-fill-text-exception](#soft-fill-text-exception)): success 4.10, info 4.14 ×2, warning 4.17, error 4.42 ×2; solid semantic fill (the 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill): white on `error-9` at 3.91 in both appearances; solid accent fill on a page that re-skins to cyan (the same floor, and [wcag-claim-scope](#wcag-claim-scope) for the hover): 3.00 ×2, 3.42, and 2.58 at dark hover. Each reproduces on the component's own page, where `color-contrast` stays ON, and against the token guards. Contrast is a property of a token PAIRING, so a composition page adds no information about it; what a composition page uniquely tests is STRUCTURE, and it passed that half green. A suite kept permanently red by findings it cannot uniquely contribute is a suite nobody reads, which was the stated risk in the original ruling's own wording. **The mechanism, in `src/foundations/axe-scope.node-check.ts`:** a `SCENARIO_CONTRAST_EXEMPT` register maps each page to the rulings it stands on plus a measured reason, and three arms check it rather than believe it — every live carve-out is registered and every register entry is still live (the rot arm, both directions); a scenario page may scope off `color-contrast` and **nothing else**, so a second rule cannot be added quietly; and **every cited ruling must resolve to a real entry in `DECISIONS.md`**, matched as an entry heading rather than a mention in prose, so a citation nobody can follow fails the build. That last arm is the whole point: it converts "no exclusions" into "no UNJUSTIFIED exclusions". **The cost, stated rather than buried:** a NEW contrast defect introduced on one of those five pages would not be caught there. It would still be caught on the component's own page and by the token guards, which is what makes the trade affordable. The sixth page, Docs shell, needs no carve-out and keeps the rule on. **Still open, deliberately:** the SOLID tier's decision. `_internal/Button contrast` already measured the two obvious fixes and rejected both — darkening the fill two steps collapses dark appearance to 1.89, and forcing the high-contrast fill deletes the brand from the system's most important control — and renders the one option left, adopting large-text type at 18.66px/700, which no Radix button step offers (step 4 is 18px, 0.66 short), so taking it means adding a step. That is a decision for the maintainer, with a specimen ready, not a defect to fix in passing.

### focus-criterion-numbers

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `DOCUMENTATION`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-17.

**The focus ring evidences WCAG 2.4.7 and contributes to 1.4.11, 2.4.11 rests on separate evidence, and 2.4.13 is not claimed.**

| Criterion | Name and level | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2.4.7 | Focus Visible, A | The focus ring |
| 1.4.11 | Non-text Contrast, AA | The ring's contrast of 3:1 or more, as one contribution |
| 2.4.11 | Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA | The system ships no sticky and no fixed page chrome |
| 2.4.13 | Focus Appearance, AAA | Not claimed, because its perimeter and area test never ran |

**Consumer obligation.** An app that makes the header sticky pairs `--ds-appshell-header-height` with `scroll-padding-top` on its scroll container.

**Why.** The wrong number reached readers in `GUIDELINES.md` and in `dist/DECISIONS.md`, so the correction is recorded in place rather than made silently, as [soft-fill-text-exception](#soft-fill-text-exception) did for a misapplied provision. The names and levels were checked against the W3C Understanding pages on 2026-09-17.

**Changed from.** An earlier ruling that deferred focus-ring contrast, and `GUIDELINES.md` section 9 after it, cited 2.4.11 as the criterion for the neutral hairline ring under the name Focus Appearance, which belongs to 2.4.13.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-17.
