**What you see.** `gutter?: LayoutPadding` defaults to `"5"`, which is `--ds-space-24`. Steps `"0"` to `"6"` resolve to 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24 and 32px, the same spacing they give on a `Layout`.

**Mechanism.** A `data-gutter` attribute resolves to the `--ds-appshell-gutter` variable, the way `Layout` resolves its own `data-padding`.

**Why.** A flush, edge-to-edge application cannot have the 24px gutter, and the mail-client recreation had to design around it. The `Layout` scale serves both, so the system keeps one spacing vocabulary.

**Not covered.** The rail and the header keep their own padding, so `gutter="0"` makes the content flush and not the whole chrome. A density control for the whole shell would be a separate decision.

**Changed from.** The shell hardcoded `padding: var(--ds-space-24)` on `main`, with no way to change it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-18. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`AppShell` takes a `gutter`, because the 24px pad around `main` had no escape (2026-09-18).** The shell hardcoded `padding: var(--ds-space-24)` on `main`. That gutter is right for most applications and is what the `variant` ladder was designed against, but a flush, edge-to-edge app cannot have it. **Found by the mail-client recreation**, which adopted the shell and then had to design AROUND the gutter. **Fix: `gutter?: LayoutPadding`, defaulting to `"5"`.** It reuses `Layout`'s own padding scale rather than minting a second spacing vocabulary, so `"0"` through `"6"` mean the same spacing on the shell as they do on a Layout, and `--ds-space-24` is exactly step 5 — the default is the value that already shipped. Resolved through a `data-gutter` attribute to a `--ds-appshell-gutter` var, matching how `Layout` resolves its own `data-padding`, so the mechanism is one a reader of either file already recognises. **Verified:** default renders 24px unchanged, and all seven steps resolve (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32). **Not done here:** the rail and header keep their own padding, so `gutter: "0"` flushes the CONTENT and not the whole chrome. That is the correct scope for a prop named for the content gutter, and a shell-wide density knob would be a different decision.

### scroll-area-box-sizing

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`, `LAYOUT`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-18.

**`.rt-ScrollAreaRoot` takes `box-sizing: border-box`, so a padded `ScrollArea` keeps the width it is given.**

**Why.** Radix's ScrollArea Root declares no `box-sizing` and so takes the `content-box` default, unlike every other surface, which Radix's reset puts on `border-box`. A Root at `width: 100%` with `padding: 12px` rendered 24px wider than its parent, and an ancestor with `overflow: hidden` cut the content with no scrollbar to reveal it.

**Where the fix lives.** On `.rt-ScrollAreaRoot`, not at call sites, because an author at a call site sees clipped content rather than its cause and narrows the width instead.

**Found by a sweep.** After the recreations surfaced three defects ([seam-ownership](#seam-ownership), [select-affix-width](#select-affix-width), [empty-state-size](#empty-state-size)), cheap probes ran over every docs page and recreation. They asked whether a seam is drawn twice, a deeper heading renders larger than a shallower one, content is cut with no ellipsis, the document scrolls sideways, or a control stretches far past its content in a flex row.

**Lesson.** A probe not tested against a known-good page measures its own bug. The first seam probe reported 116 doubled seams, and once it required the two strokes to overlap vertically, 7 remained, all of them page composition.

**Gap.** Recorded on 2026-09-18 and not fixed here: the project board recreation clips 11px at its bottom, where a horizontally scrolling ScrollArea reserves its scrollbar gutter inside the viewport and the columns' natural height overruns it. The fix bounds the column height, which is a layout change.

**Changed from.** The ScrollArea Root kept the `content-box` default, and a padded one overflowed its parent by its padding.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-18. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A padded `ScrollArea` did not honour its own width, and a sweep found it (2026-09-18).** Radix's ScrollArea Root declares no `box-sizing`, so it inherits the UA default of `content-box` — unlike every other surface here, which Radix's own reset puts on `border-box`. Nothing shows until someone pads one: `width: 100%` plus `padding: 12px` renders **24px wider than the parent**, and because the overflow lands on an ancestor with `overflow: hidden` the content is cut with no scrollbar to reveal it. **Measured:** a bare Root at `width: 100%` inside a 300px parent rendered 324px; with `box-sizing: border-box`, 300px. The code-editor recreation's assistant panel was clipping 24px of its transcript this way, silently. Fixed on `.rt-ScrollAreaRoot` rather than at the call sites, because a call site cannot see the cause: the author sees clipped content and reaches for a smaller width. **Found by a suite-wide sweep, which is the point of this entry.** After three defects surfaced by building the recreations ([seam-ownership](#seam-ownership) seams, [select-affix-width](#select-affix-width) Select, [empty-state-size](#empty-state-size) EmptyState), five cheap probes were run over 145 rendered pages — 137 docs pages plus the eight recreations — asking: is any seam drawn twice, does any deeper heading render larger than a shallower one, is content cut by an `overflow: hidden` with no ellipsis intent, does the document scroll sideways, is any control stretched far past its content in a flex row. **The sweep's own first version was wrong and that is worth recording:** it reported 116 doubled seams by comparing x positions without requiring the two strokes to overlap vertically, so every docs Do/Don't card stacked down the page "collided" with the table above it. Requiring 50% vertical overlap took 116 to 7, and all 7 are a card border coinciding with a specimen placed flush inside it — page composition, not a component. A probe that has not been falsified against a known-good page is measuring its own bug. **What the sweep actually earned:** this entry, plus two markup defects on the analytics recreation — KPI values marked up as `h2` (a bare number in the document outline, rendering at 28px above the page's own `h1` at 24px) and a second `EmptyState` needing [empty-state-size](#empty-state-size)'s new `size`. **Left recorded, not fixed:** 11px clipped at the bottom of the project board, where a horizontally scrolling ScrollArea reserves its scrollbar gutter inside the viewport and the columns' natural height overruns it by exactly that. Removing the height declaration was tried and measured as a no-op, so the real fix bounds the column height and is a layout change rather than a tweak.

### kbd-default-variant

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**`Kbd` defaults to Radix's flat `soft` variant instead of the raised `classic` keycap.**

**What you see.** Every `Kbd` renders as a flat chip, a `gray-a3` fill with no shadow. `variant` passes through, so `classic` stays available for a raised key chosen on purpose.

**Why.** Radix's `classic` imitates a physical keycap with six inset shadows and a drop shadow. This system uses that look nowhere else: `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 8 builds elevation from flat rungs, and the shadow ladder never fakes a bevel.

**Tokens.** `soft` is a skin Radix ships, so the change picks a different shipped skin and invents none. `Kbd` stays in the family that reuses the Radix skin and declares no `--ds-*` roles, beside `Separator` and `CheckboxVisual`.

**Changed from.** `Kbd` took the Radix default, `variant="classic"`, a raised key with a bevel.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`Kbd` defaults to the FLAT key, not Radix's raised one (2026-09-19).** Radix Themes defaults `Kbd` to `variant="classic"`: six stacked inset shadows plus an outer drop shadow, imitating a physical keycap. This system uses that language nowhere else — §8 spends its entire elevation budget on three flat rungs and the shadow ladder never fakes a bevel — so a raised key reads as borrowed from somewhere else. **Fix: default `variant="soft"`, and pass `variant` through** so `classic` stays available for anyone who wants the raised key deliberately. `soft` is Radix's OWN flat chip (a `gray-a3` fill, no shadow), so this changes WHICH shipped skin is chosen rather than inventing one, which keeps `Kbd` in the "reuses the Radix skin, declares no `--ds-*` roles" family alongside `Separator` and `CheckboxVisual`. **Observable change:** every `Kbd` in the system loses its bevel. That is the point, and it is why this is a ruling rather than a page fix.

### resize-handle-seam

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**The resize handle is the seam itself, 1px of layout, and its grab zone is an overlay that takes no space.**

**What you see.** Panels with fills of their own meet the hairline on both sides of a `ResizeHandle`, with no stripe of the page background between surface and seam.

**Mechanism.** The element is the hairline (`--ds-stroke-weak`), 1px wide or tall. A `::before` overlay reaches `--space-1` past the track on each side as the grab zone, the same inner-element pattern the grab pill uses, and since it belongs to the handle, the handle's pointer and keyboard handlers receive its events as before.

**Why in the component.** The same stripe showed on three seams of one page, so the cause was the component, not the page. The page carries no stray padding, and negative margins on one drawer would hide the stripe there and leave it on the other seams.

**Changed from.** `ResizeHandle` was a 9px element that painted a 1px track through `background-clip: content-box`, with a transparent `padding-inline: var(--space-1)` grab zone on each side. That padding showed the background behind the handle, so each adjacent surface sat 4px off the hairline.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The resize handle is the seam, not a spacer beside it (2026-09-19).** `ResizeHandle` was a 9px-wide element painting a 1px track through `background-clip: content-box`, with `padding-inline: var(--space-1)` either side as the grab zone. That padding is TRANSPARENT, so it showed whatever sat behind the handle — the Layout body's own background — rather than the surfaces either side of it. Two panels with their own fills therefore never met their seam: each sat 4px off the hairline, reading as a gap between the surface and the edge. **Measured on the code-editor recreation at dark, 1440x900, uiSize small:** the Problems drawer started 4px after the hairline (bg-base #111113 through y711-714 before the surface at y715), and the same stripe appeared on the project rail (x277-280) and the assistant panel (x1003-1006). Three seams, one cause — systemic to the component, not to the page. **Fix: the element IS the hairline and takes 1px of layout, so the surfaces meet it; the grab zone moves to a `::before` overlay extending `--space-1` past the track without occupying space.** Same inner-element pattern the grab pill already used. The pointer and touch target is unchanged because the pseudo-element belongs to the handle, so the handle's own pointer and keyboard handlers receive those events exactly as before. **Fixed in the component, not the page:** the page carries zero stray padding, and negative margins on one drawer would have hidden a systemic stripe on two other seams and left the page internally inconsistent.

### side-nav-section-divider

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**`SideNav.Section` takes `divided`, which draws a hairline above the section where whitespace alone no longer separates two groups.**

**What you see.** A divided section that is not the first draws a 1px `--ds-stroke-weak` border on its block start, with `--ds-space-12` of margin above and padding below it, inset to the inline padding of the rail.

**When to use it.** Between adjacent lists of the same shape, such as a conversation history with Today above Previous 7 days. A two-section rail with a heading on each reads clearly on whitespace, so `divided` is off by default.

**Why on the component.** A `Separator` placed in a page does not travel, so every other `SideNav` would still group by whitespace alone. A border belongs to the section that sets `divided`, survives a reorder and follows the padding of the rail.

**Why the spacing.** A hairline tight under a heading reads as the underline of that heading, not as a boundary.

**Changed from.** Sections grouped by an 8px margin alone, and dense rows of the same shape read as one list with uneven spacing.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`SideNav.Section` can draw its own boundary, because whitespace stopped carrying one (2026-09-19).** Sections grouped by an 8px margin alone. With dense rows of the same shape — a conversation history rail, TODAY above PREVIOUS 7 DAYS — that reads as one list with uneven spacing rather than two groups. **The fix is on the component**, because a `Separator` dropped into the page does not travel: every other `SideNav` in the system would still group by whitespace alone. That is why `divided` lives on `SideNav.Section` and the page uses it instead. **Opt-in, not default:** a two-section rail with a heading on each is legible on whitespace, and a rule there is noise. It is for adjacent lists of the same shape, which is when whitespace stops being enough. **A `border-block-start` rather than a Separator element**, so the rule belongs to the section that asked for it and cannot be orphaned by a reorder, and so it inherits the rail's inline padding instead of spanning edge to edge. `:not(:first-child)` because the first section has nothing above it to separate from. The extra block spacing is part of the fix: a hairline tight under a heading reads as that heading's underline rather than as a boundary.

### container-narrowing

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**A container that narrows never scrolls sideways: labels truncate to one line, and prose reflows.**

**Rule.** `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 8b holds it.

- A horizontal scrollbar is a defect unless it is deliberate: a code surface whose lines must not wrap, a data table that needs a two-dimensional layout, or a shelf that is itself a horizontal scroller.
- A container that narrows gets a real minimum width.
- Titles, nav rows, list items, tabs, breadcrumbs and filenames truncate to one line.
- Paragraphs, message bodies and descriptions reflow.

**Why.** A single-line label that wraps sets its container's min-content width to its longest unbreakable word, so one long filename can set the minimum width of a whole panel and produce the horizontal scrollbar. Truncated labels make a minimum width honest.

**Consequence.** The 1.4.12 ellipsis allowance in section 9 holds only where a mechanism reveals the full text, so more truncation means more places that owe a `Tooltip` or a destination that carries the full text.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered narrowing. A resizable panel showed a horizontal scrollbar even where its content reflowed.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19.

- [per-component-line-budget](#per-component-line-budget) gives `Outline` a `labelLines` budget that defaults to one line, and keeps the choice with each component.
- [truncating-label-width](#truncating-label-width) stops a truncating label from setting its whole string as the minimum width of its row, so the ellipsis engages as the container narrows.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Narrowing is ruled: no horizontal scroll, truncate labels, reflow prose (2026-09-19).** Two defects on the same recreation share one rule. On a resizable panel, a reflow is of no use when a horizontal scroll appears anyway, so a container that narrows gets a minimum width it reflows to and never scrolls sideways. On the rail beside it, titles and lists in a resizable container truncate by default rather than wrap, and text blocks reflow. **They are cause and effect.** A single-line label that wraps sets its container's min-content width to its longest unbreakable word, so one long filename can set the minimum width of a whole panel — which is what produces the horizontal scrollbar. Truncating the labels is what makes a minimum width honest. **Ruled in `GUIDELINES.md` §8b:** a horizontal scrollbar is a defect unless deliberate (a code surface whose lines must not wrap, a data table needing two-dimensional layout, a shelf that IS a horizontal scroller); a container that narrows gets a real minimum width; titles, nav rows, list items, tabs, breadcrumbs and filenames truncate to one line; paragraphs, message bodies and descriptions reflow. **Consequence carried forward:** §9's 1.4.12 ellipsis allowance holds only where a mechanism reveals the full text, so truncation-by-default increases the number of places that owe a `Tooltip` or a carrying destination.

### optical-icon-weight

**Tags.** `FOUNDATIONS`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**Optical weight is its own axis, so a sparse glyph steps to `bold` until its row reads evenly.**

**What you see.** Phosphor's `regular` is one stroke weight, not one perceived weight. A glyph built from small disconnected marks, such as `DotsThree`, `DotsSixVertical` or `Minus`, carries far less ink than one built from continuous strokes, so beside dense glyphs it reads faint.

**Rule.** Judge the row, not the glyph, and step a sparse glyph to `bold` until the row reads evenly, as section 4 of `docs/GUIDELINES.md` states. An overflow menu is a `MoreMenu`, which ships `DotsThreeVertical weight="bold"`, never a hand-built `IconButton` around the same glyph.

**Why.** On the AI assistant scenario, a three-dots kebab beside a share icon was barely visible, because the page wrapped its own `IconButton` around the glyph and lost the compensation `MoreMenu` carries.

**Guard.** `src/foundations/sparse-glyph-weight.node-check.ts` asserts three things:

- every sparse glyph in `src/` declares an explicit `weight`
- the list of sparse glyphs still matches real code
- `MoreMenu` still ships its bold default, because its loss would turn every `MoreMenu` light at once and the first check would not fail on it

**Not covered.** The guard reads source, not pixels, because a bounding box does not measure optical weight. Whether a row reads evenly stays a judgement for review. The scan blanks comments and string literals first, so text about a glyph, such as a docblock or a props-table row, never counts as a render of one.

**Changed from.** The bold compensation lived only inside `MoreMenu`, and no rule or guard named it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Optical weight is its own axis, and a sparse glyph needs a step up (2026-09-19).** Phosphor's `regular` is one STROKE weight, not one PERCEIVED weight: a glyph built from small disconnected marks carries far less ink than one built from continuous strokes. On the assistant recreation, a three-dots kebab beside a share icon was barely visible. **`MoreMenu` already had the answer and the page had walked around it.** The component ships `DotsThreeVertical weight="bold"` precisely for this; the page hand-rolled an `IconButton` around the same glyph and lost the compensation. So the page fix is to USE `MoreMenu`, which it should have done anyway for an overflow menu, and the system fix is to stop the compensation being a secret the component keeps. **Ruled in `GUIDELINES.md` §4:** judge the ROW, not the glyph, and step a sparse one to `bold` until the row reads evenly. **Mechanism: `sparse-glyph-weight.node-check.ts`** asserts every sparse glyph in `src/` declares an explicit weight, that the named list still matches real code, and that `MoreMenu` still ships its bold default — that last arm because the default lives in one place and its loss would take every `MoreMenu` light at once, which the first arm would never see. **It reads source, not pixels, and that boundary is deliberate:** optical weight is not measurable from a bounding box, so the guard holds the mechanical half and leaves "does this row read evenly" to review, which is where a judgement belongs. **Two false-positive classes had to be taught out of it first**, and both are the same mistake in different clothes — a docblock saying `pass icon={<DotsThree/>}` and a props-table row carrying `def: "<DotsThreeVertical/>"` are text ABOUT a glyph, not a render of one, so the scan blanks comments and string literals before matching.

### per-component-line-budget

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**A line budget is a prop of each component, and `Outline` takes `labelLines`, which defaults to one line.**

**What you see.** An `Outline` entry truncates to one line and carries a `title` with its full text, so the 1.4.12 ellipsis allowance of `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 9 holds.

**Mechanism.** `Outline` uses the name and the implementation of `Item`'s `labelLines`, shared from `src/utils/truncation.ts`, so `1` means the same thing in both components.

**Scope.** The budget is per component and never global, so `Provider` carries no truncation setting and none is to be added. Whether a list truncates depends on the width of its container and on what its entries say, so the decision stays at each call site.

**Applies to.**

- `Item` carries `labelLines` and `descriptionLines`, and a string label defaults to one line, so `TreeList`, `SideNav` and `List` truncate through it.
- `Outline` carries `labelLines`.
- `Breadcrumbs`, `DataList` and `Tabs` render label rows without one, and are the next candidates if a narrow container makes them wrap.

**Changed from.** `Outline` rendered its own link, and `.rt-ds-outline-link` declared no wrapping rule, so on the code editor the rail header truncated while the outline below it wrapped.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A line budget is a PER-COMPONENT prop, and `Outline` gains one (2026-09-19).** On the code editor, the rail header truncated while the outline below it wrapped. Truncation is the ruled default ([container-narrowing](#container-narrowing)), so the gap is a property for wrapping versus truncation, and the set of components that lack one. `Item` already carries that property, and where else it belongs is the useful part. `Item` has carried `labelLines` / `descriptionLines` since it was written, and it defaults a STRING label to one line — which is why `TreeList`, `SideNav` and `List` all truncate correctly: they compose `Item`. `Outline` does not compose `Item`; it renders its own link, and `.rt-ds-outline-link` declared no wrapping rule at all. That is the whole defect. **Fix: `Outline` takes `labelLines`, defaulting to 1**, using the same name and the same implementation as `Item` so `1` cannot come to mean two different things in two components. The implementation moved to `src/utils/truncation.ts`, shared rather than copied, because two copies of four CSS longhands is exactly how that divergence starts. Entries also carry a `title`, which is what keeps §9's 1.4.12 ellipsis allowance honest — truncation is only permitted where a mechanism reveals the full text. **Scope, ruled explicitly: this is NOT a global setting.** Each component sets truncation or wrapping for its own rows, and no global setting does. So there is no `Provider` knob and none should be added. The shared module is an implementation detail that keeps the vocabulary consistent; the DECISION stays at each call site, which is right, because whether a given list truncates depends on how wide its container is and what its entries say. **Where else it applies:** `Item` and its composers already have it; `Outline` now does; `Breadcrumbs`, `DataList` and `Tabs` render label rows without one and are the next candidates if a narrow container ever makes them wrap.

### panel-background

**Tags.** `COLOUR`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**Panels are solid: `Provider` passes `panelBackground="solid"` to the Radix theme.**

**What you see.** Every Card, panel and menu surface is opaque, so content that scrolls behind one stays hidden.

**Why.** Radix Themes defaults to `panelBackground="translucent"`, which resolves `--color-panel` to an alpha wash, a 3.5% light wash in dark mode. Content behind a panel smeared through it, which read as a flicker and as a lighter band at a scroll container's edges, in dark mode only. The token layer already holds a raised surface opaque (`--ds-bg-raised`), so the translucent render contradicted it.

**Override.** `Provider` spreads its other props after this one, so a consumer who wants the translucent look passes `panelBackground="translucent"`.

**Changed from.** Panels rendered translucent, Radix's default, and content scrolled through them in dark mode.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Panels are SOLID; Radix shipped them translucent and content scrolled through them (2026-09-19).** Radix Themes defaults `panelBackground="translucent"`, which resolves `--color-panel` to an alpha wash — measured `#d8f4f609` in dark, and the Card fill computed as `rgba(216, 244, 246, 0.035)`. Every Card, panel and menu surface was therefore see-through, so content scrolling BEHIND one smeared through it. It showed two ways, both dark-mode only: a section that appeared to be flickering, and a lighter gradient at the scroll container edges. Dark-only is the tell — a 3.5% light wash over near-black is obvious and over white is invisible. **It also contradicted our own token layer**, which already says a raised surface is opaque (`--ds-bg-raised: var(--gray-2)`), so the system described one thing and rendered another. This is the "translucent-panel token + opaque backstop" item that has sat in the Phase 2 committed list since the beginning. **Fix: `Provider` passes `panelBackground="solid"`.** `rest` spreads after it, so a consumer who genuinely wants the translucent look still can. **Verification is worth recording because the first attempt was wrong in the SAFE direction:** a per-row luminance scan across the scroll edge reported a 0.0/255 delta between the two modes, which looked like proof the theory was wrong. It was sampling a region with no card in it. Reading the Card's `::before` fill directly showed `rgba(216,244,246,0.035)` against `rgb(24,25,27)`. A null result from a probe aimed at the wrong element is not evidence of absence.

### scrim-value

**Tags.** `TOKENS`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**`--ds-scrim` is `--black-a8`, an alpha of 0.60, in both light and dark.**

**Why.** A black alpha is the same in either appearance, so a dark override compensates for nothing. At 0.90 the veil hid the media under it.

**Measured.** White text on the scrim over pure white media, the worst case, reads 5.74:1 at 0.60 against a floor of 4.5:1. At 0.90 it read 17.49:1, nearly four times the headroom the floor requires.

**Guarded.** A regression test holds the scrim alpha between about 0.55 and 0.75. Below the floor, text on the scrim fails contrast. Above the ceiling, the scrim becomes a blackout.

**Changed from.** `--ds-scrim` was `--black-a8` (0.60) in light and `--black-a11` (0.90) in dark, through a `.dark` override.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **One scrim value serves both appearances (2026-09-19).** `--ds-scrim` was `--black-a8` (0.60) in light and overridden to `--black-a11` (0.90) in dark. Both are BLACK alphas, which are identical in either appearance, so the override was a choice rather than a compensation for anything. The dark hover reveal hid the media: a 90% black veil over a photograph leaves no photograph. **Measured against the obligation the token actually carries:** white text on the scrim over worst-case white media reads **5.74:1 at 0.60** and **17.49:1 at 0.90**, against a 4.5 floor. The dark override was buying nearly four times the required headroom and paying for it by erasing the media. The override is deleted; 0.60 now serves both, which is also the value the contrast analysis beside the token was written against. **Guarded with a floor AND a ceiling**, because this token has a defect in both directions: under ~0.55 the text on it fails contrast, over ~0.75 it stops being a scrim and becomes a blackout.

### avatar-group-overlap

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**The avatar-group overlap is 20% of the box, a number derived from the width of two initials.**

**What you see.** Each avatar after the first overlaps the one before it by 20% of the box, `calc(var(--ds-avatar-box) * -0.2)`, so both letters of every two-letter pair stay readable at every size.

**Derivation.** Two letters at the `--avatar-fallback-two-letters-font-size` ratio of 0.44 occupy about 58% of the box, centred, so their ink runs from 21% to 79%. The next disc must start at or after 79%, which caps the overlap at 21%, and 20% is that bound with a little room. A change to the 0.44 ratio moves this number with it.

**Cost.** The stack is looser than before. A stack whose initials cannot be read carries no information, so density yields.

**Changed from.** The overlap was 40% of the box, chosen so the stack read as one unit. It covered the second letter of every two-letter pair, 7.6px of ink at the large size, so "RK DM SO HB" read as "RI DI SC HI".

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The avatar-group overlap is derived from the initials, not chosen (2026-09-19).** The overlap was `-0.4` — 40% of the box — picked so the stack "reads as one cohesive unit". It ate the second letter of every two-letter pair. Measured at the large tier: a 40px disc with 16px of overlap leaves 24px visible, while the initials' ink is 23.2px centred, so its right edge lands at 31.6px and **7.6px sits under the next avatar**. "RK DM SO HB" rendered as "RI DI SC HI". It is proportional, so it was equally wrong at every tier; it was noticed at large because the glyphs are bigger, and reasonably read as the initials being off-centre. They were centred to within 0.3px — the overlap was covering them, which is a different defect with a different fix. **The derivation, so the number is not taste:** two letters at the measured `--avatar-fallback-two-letters-font-size` ratio of 0.44 occupy ~58% of the box, centred, so the ink runs from 21% to 79%. The next disc must start at or after 79%, capping overlap at 21%; 20% is that bound with a little room. Change the 0.44 ratio and this must move with it. **Cost accepted:** the stack is looser than it was. A stack whose initials cannot be read is not carrying information, so density loses.

### chrome-heading-lane

**Tags.** `SIZING`, `TYPOGRAPHY`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**A heading inside chrome takes the `chromeHeading` lane, one step above the text lane, and never a literal Radix step.**

**What you see.** `chromeHeading` resolves to steps 2, 3 and 4, which is 14, 16 and 18px, at the small, medium and large tiers. It sits below a page heading and above the body beside it.

**Applies to.** A heading inside a small surface, such as a card title or a panel header. A `ClickableCard` title takes the lane by default, and `EmptyState` reads lanes in place of the literal steps `"2"` and `"3"`.

**Why.** A literal step cannot move, so a pinned title stays one size while the global size changes around it. The `heading` lane, 20, 24 and 28px, is a page-title ladder and is too large inside a small surface: on a 264px kanban column it made one card nearly twice as tall.

**Guard.** `size-lanes.node-check.ts` asserts that no lane is inert between small and large, that `chromeHeading` is exactly one step above `text` at every tier and below `heading`, and that `control` never drifts from `text`. It asserts steps and not pixels, because the mapping from step to pixel belongs to Radix.

**Changed from.** `ClickableCard.headingSize` defaulted to `"3"`, so a card title measured 16px at every tier. `EmptyState` pinned `"2"` and `"3"`, which put a 14px title under a 16px description at the large tier.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19.

- [size-lane-hook](#size-lane-hook) exports `useSizeLane`, so a heading a consumer composes can take `chromeHeading` as `ClickableCard` does.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A heading inside chrome gets its own lane; literals were making components tier-inert (2026-09-19).** Across six recreations, a new global size left almost every rendered size as it was. The cause was the same shape every time: something took a LITERAL Radix step instead of a lane, and a literal cannot move. Two SHIPPED components did it in their own source. `ClickableCard.headingSize` defaulted to `"3"`, so a card title measured 16px at small, medium and large. `EmptyState`'s ladder hardcoded `"2"` and `"3"` ([empty-state-size](#empty-state-size)), which additionally **inverted at the large tier: a 14px title under a 16px description**, a component contradicting its own hierarchy, and worse than the defect [empty-state-size](#empty-state-size) set out to fix. **Why they pinned, and why unpinning alone is the wrong fix.** The `heading` lane is a PAGE-title ladder (5/6/7 = 20/24/28px) and is measurably wrong inside a small surface: on a 264px kanban column, putting card titles on it took four cards from 174/156/188/156px to **336/264/296/228px**, one filling a third of the viewport. So the pins were escaping a real problem, and deleting them without choosing a lane just swaps an inert title for a broken layout. **Fix: a fifth lane, `chromeHeading`, at text + 1 step — 2/3/4 = 14/16/18px.** Subordinate to a page heading, superior to the body beside it, and at `small` byte-identical to the literals it replaces, which is what made it safe to land on shipped components. The +1 offset is the same device `CONTROL_MEMBER_STEP` already uses within a lane ([toggle-group-box](#toggle-group-box)). Verified: `ClickableCard` now renders 14/16/18 across the tiers, and `EmptyState`'s inversion is gone (title 14/16 against description 12/14). **Mechanism: `size-lanes.node-check.ts`** asserts the policy table directly — every lane steps, none is inert between small and large, `chromeHeading` is exactly text+1 at every tier and strictly below `heading`, and control never drifts from text. It deliberately does NOT assert pixels: the step-to-px mapping is Radix's, and pinning it here would fail on a vendor upgrade that changed nothing about our policy.

### display-size-lane

**Tags.** `SIZING`, `TYPOGRAPHY`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**A hero metric takes the `display` size lane, steps 7, 8 and 9 of Radix's display ramp, so it grows with the size tier.**

| Tier | `heading` lane | `display` lane |
|---|---|---|
| `small` | 20px | 28px (step 7) |
| `medium` | 24px | 35px (step 8) |
| `large` | 28px | 60px (step 9) |

**What you see.** At `small` the lane renders the 28px that the pinned value rendered before, so the default tier does not change and the lane grows only above it. With the page title on the `heading` lane and the value on `display`, a metric outranks the title at every tier.

**Why.** No lane fit a hero number. Unpinned `Text` takes the text lane at 12, 14 and 16px, and the `heading` lane would cut the value from 28px to 20px at the default tier, while a pinned value stayed 28px as its tile padding grew from 16px to 32px, the defect of [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane) in mirror image.

**Large tier.** 60px at `large` is deliberate: the large tier exists to make things larger, and a hero metric has the most licence to grow.

**Guard.** `size-lanes.node-check.ts` asserts that `display` stays above `heading` at every tier, because a lane at or below it would be redundant.

**Changed from.** The analytics dashboard pinned its KPI values at `Text size="7"`, 28px at every tier, and a pinned 28px value sat above a pinned 24px `h1`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A hero metric is display type, and the system had no rung for it (2026-09-19).** The analytics dashboard renders its KPI values at `Text size="7"` — 28px, frozen. Measured small against large on one tile: label 14/14, value 28/28, delta 14/14, footnote 12/12, while the tile padding went 16px to 32px and the tile height 178px to 210px. **The page's single most prominent number was inert while the box around it inflated**, the mirror image of the board-card defect in [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane). **Unpinning was not available**, and that is the finding. `Text` unpinned takes the text lane (12/14/16), so the hero number would render 12px at small. The largest lane the system had was `heading` at 20/24/28, and putting the value there cuts it 28px to 20px at the DEFAULT tier — a 29% reduction to the most prominent element on the page, and exactly the regression [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane) was careful to avoid. So the pin was not laziness; there was no correct lane to take. **Fix: a `display` lane at 7/8/9 = 28/35/60px.** It takes Radix's own display ramp rather than inventing one, and `small` is step 7, precisely what the pin rendered — so adopting the lane is free at the default tier and only opens up above it. 60px at `large` is deliberate: the large tier exists to make things larger, and a hero metric has the most licence to take it. **It also resolves a second-order inversion** the `MetricRow` comment had half-fixed: with the page title on the page lane (20/24/28) and the value on display, the metric outranks the title at every tier rather than only at small. Previously a pinned 28px value sat above a pinned 24px `h1`. Guarded by `size-lanes.node-check.ts`, which now also asserts `display` stays strictly ABOVE `heading`, because the moment it does not the lane is redundant and the KPI is inert again.

### size-lane-hook

**Tags.** `SIZING`, `INSTALL`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**`useSizeLane(lane)` is public, so a hand-composed element can follow the global size, and no setter is exported.**

**What you see.** The package exports `useSizeLane`, `useUISize` and the `SizeLane` type. `useSizeLane(lane)` returns the Radix step for that lane at the active tier, so a hand-composed `Heading` inside a card can take `chromeHeading` exactly as `ClickableCard` does.

**Why.** Every sized component resolves its lane through `useResolvedSize`, which was private. A hand-composed element could only write a literal, and a literal does not move when the global size changes, the most common defect in this system. The system's own social-feed recreation needed the private import to follow [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane), which a consumer could not copy.

**Read only.** No setter is exported. The tier belongs to `Provider`, and a subtree that could change it would make the global size unpredictable for everything below.

**Not exported.** `useResolvedSize` stays internal, because it carries the explicit-size override and the missing-Provider warning, which are internal contracts.

**Changed from.** Lane resolution was private, so a consumer could not participate in `uiSize`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The size lanes are public; a consumer could not participate in `uiSize` (2026-09-19).** Every sized component here resolves a lane through `useResolvedSize`, but that resolution was PRIVATE. Anything hand-composed therefore had no way to ask what step the active tier wants, and the only thing left to write was a literal — which cannot move. That is the mechanism behind the single most common defect in this system: the global size changes and the composition does not. **Our own showcase pages hit the wall first:** the social-feed recreation routed three composed headings through `useResolvedSize` to satisfy [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane), an import that is not public API, so the page did something a consumer could not copy. A design system whose own pages need a private import to follow its own size policy has published the policy without the means to obey it. **Fix: `useSizeLane(lane)` is exported**, alongside `useUISize` and the `SizeLane` type. It returns the Radix step for the active tier, so a hand-composed `Heading` inside a card can take `chromeHeading` exactly as `ClickableCard` does. **Read-only by design, and the omission is the decision:** there is no exported setter. The tier belongs to `Provider`, and a component that could change it for its subtree would make the global size unpredictable for everything below. **Not `useResolvedSize` itself:** that one carries the explicit-size override and the missing-Provider warning, which are internal contracts a consumer has no business in. The public surface is the narrow question — what step does this lane want right now — and nothing else.

### top-nav-bar-height

**Tags.** `SIZING`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**The TopNav bar height follows the global size tier, 56px, 60px and 64px at small, medium and large.**

**Why.** Every control inside the header, the search field, the nav links, the icon buttons and the avatar, grows with the global size, so a bar of fixed height would hold controls that outgrow it. A literal cannot move, the same defect class as [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane) and [display-size-lane](#display-size-lane), here in the token layer rather than a component prop.

**Derivation.** The bar is the nav row ladder of 32px, 36px and 40px, the rungs `SideNav` uses ([control-box-per-step](#control-box-per-step), [nav-row-ladder](#nav-row-ladder)), plus a fixed 24px of chrome gutter.

**Default.** `small` resolves to 56px, the value the literal rendered, so the default tier is unchanged and the ramp opens only above it, the constraint the two lane rulings held to.

**Mechanism.** `--ds-topnav-bar` keys on `data-ui-size`, which `Provider` writes on the theme root and `typography.css` reads, so a tier-keyed value takes the existing mechanism rather than a second one.

**Applies to.** The `TopNav` component, never one page. A local height fix on a page would leave every other `TopNav` consumer with a header that ignores the size they set.

**Changed from.** The bar was a fixed 56px at every size.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The TopNav bar was a hardcoded 56px and did not ride the tier (2026-09-19).** Every control inside the header — the search field, the nav links, the icon buttons, the avatar — grew with the global size, and the bar containing them did not. The bar scales with the controls inside it, so a header never holds a fixed height while the inputs inside it grow. A literal cannot move, which makes this the same defect class as [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane) and [display-size-lane](#display-size-lane), expressed in the token layer instead of a component prop. **Derived, not picked:** the bar is the nav-row ladder (32/36/40 — the same rungs `SideNav` uses, per the [control-box-per-step](#control-box-per-step) box law) plus a fixed 24px of chrome gutter, giving **56/60/64**. `small` resolves to 56, exactly what the literal rendered, so the default tier is byte-identical and the ramp only opens above it — the same constraint [chrome-heading-lane](#chrome-heading-lane) and [display-size-lane](#display-size-lane) held to. Keyed on `data-ui-size`, which `Provider` already writes on the theme root and `typography.css` already reads, rather than inventing a second mechanism for a tier-keyed value. **A component fix, never a page fix:** nudging the height locally would have left every other consumer of `TopNav` with a header that ignores the size they set.

### status-glyph-line-box

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**The `ChatToolCalls` status box is one line box tall, so its glyph centres on the first line of its row at every size.**

**What you see.** The glyph centres on the first line at small and medium. At large every row sits 0.5px off, alike, because a 16px glyph cannot centre on a half pixel in a 19px line.

**Mechanism.** `min-height: 1lh` on the status box is the row's own line box, because the component sets font size and line height per `data-size`, so the box tracks the size by construction. Under `[data-align="start"]` the box takes `align-self: flex-start` and sits on the first line.

**Why.** An earlier fix used `min-height: inherit` with `align-self: stretch`, and neither half did anything. `inherit` copies the same property from the parent, here a `min-height` of `auto`, and `stretch` stretches an item to its flex parent, which was itself only as tall as the glyph.

**Guard.** A measurement of a defect is not evidence of its remedy. `regression-cover.node-check.ts` requires a measured ruling to carry a check able to fail.

**Changed from.** The status box stayed 16px tall in a 24px line box. Measured before this fix, error rows sat 0, 2 and 3.5px off their first line at small, medium and large, so they disagreed with their neighbours.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The first status-glyph fix was inert, and the glyph was still off its line (2026-09-19).** `ChatToolCalls` still drew its status glyph slightly off its first line at every tier, and the first status-glyph fix is the reason. That fix reached for `min-height: inherit` plus `align-self: stretch`, and **neither half did anything**. `inherit` copies the SAME property from the parent, never a different one, so a rule intending "inherit the parent's line-height" actually inherited the parent's `min-height`, which computed to `auto`. And `stretch` stretches a flex item to its flex PARENT, which here is `.rt-ds-item-start` — itself only glyph-tall. The status box stayed 16px inside a 24px line box. **Measured before the fix**, glyph centre against first-line centre: **0 / -2 / -3.5px** at small / medium / large on error rows, and **+0.5px on EVERY row at large**, because a 16px glyph cannot centre on a half pixel inside a 19px text rect. The mechanism is now one declaration: `min-height: 1lh` on the status, which **is** the row's own line box because the component already sets font-size and line-height per `data-size`, so the box tracks the tier by construction rather than by a token somebody has to remember to keep in sync. `[data-align="start"]` then only needs `align-self: flex-start` to sit on the first line. **After: 0px at small and medium, a uniform 0.5px at large** — uniform being the point, since the visible defect was error rows disagreeing with their neighbours. **The lesson worth more than the fix:** the first status-glyph fix shipped with a measurement of the DEFECT and none of the REMEDY. A before-number is not evidence that an after-number changed. `regression-cover.node-check.ts` now enforces that a measured ruling carries something able to go red.

### select-anchoring

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**`Select` anchors its listbox below its trigger with popper positioning, like every other floating surface.**

**What you see.** The panel opens 4px below the trigger with no horizontal offset, at least as wide as the trigger, with `data-side="bottom"`.

**Why.** Radix's default `position="item-aligned"` floats the panel so the selected option lands over the trigger, a native macOS menu idiom that reads as breakage on the web. Measured on the analytics dashboard header, the panel covered its own trigger, sat 20px to its right and ran 20px narrower than it. `Dialog`, `Popover`, `DropdownMenu`, `ContextMenu`, `HoverCard` and `Tooltip` are all popper-positioned.

**Mechanism.** The wrapper locks `position="popper"` beside the locked `variant="solid"`, because an unanchored listbox is a defect, not a matter of taste. The width floor needs no rule of its own: Radix's `.rt-SelectContent:where([data-side])` already sets `min-width: var(--radix-select-trigger-width)`, and only popper content carries `data-side`.

**Motion.** Popper positioning adds `rt-PopperContent`, which the shared motion block times with a 260ms exit, and that exit left the closed listbox mounted and focusable inside a subtree Radix marks `aria-hidden`. The motion rule excludes `.rt-SelectContent` and silences its animation names, so the panel appears and disappears with no motion, as before.

**Not covered.**

- Whether a `Select` that opens beside its trigger should slide is a motion decision of its own, with an exit-focus problem to solve first.
- `Typeahead`'s panel is deliberately wider than its input.
- No other floating surface shares the default, because only Radix's `Select` has an item-aligned mode.

**Changed from.** `Select` used Radix's default item-aligned positioning, the sole exception among floating surfaces, and no ruling chose it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`Select`'s listbox was not anchored to its own control (2026-09-19).** **Measured on the analytics dashboard header:** the open panel sat **4px ABOVE its trigger's top edge** (covering the control it belongs to), **20px to its right**, and rendered **170px wide against a 190px trigger** — three independent ways of telling the reader that the control and its options are not the same object. The cause is Radix's default `position="item-aligned"`, which floats the panel so the SELECTED option lands over the trigger. That is a native-macOS-menu idiom, it reads as breakage on the web, and every other floating surface this system ships — `Dialog`, `Popover`, `DropdownMenu`, `ContextMenu`, `HoverCard`, `Tooltip` — is popper-positioned by construction. **`Select` was the sole exception, and nobody chose it.** Now locked at the wrapper alongside `variant="solid"`, for the same reason that one is locked: an unanchored listbox is a defect, not a taste. **After: dx 0, a 4px gap below the trigger, panel width equal to trigger width, `data-side="bottom"`.** **THE FIX IS ONE SWITCH, AND THE FIRST DRAFT SHIPPED A SECOND ONE THAT DID NOTHING.** That draft also set `min-width: var(--radix-select-trigger-width)` inline to cure the narrow panel. Red-probing it — delete the line, expect the guard to trip — left the suite GREEN, which is how the dead weight was caught. Radix's own stylesheet already carries that exact declaration under `.rt-SelectContent:where([data-side])`, and `[data-side]` exists **only** on popper-positioned content. The narrow panel was therefore never a second bug: item-aligned content has no `data-side`, so it never matched the rule that would have floored it. This is the repo's standing override rule earning its keep — probe the cascade before adding a declaration, because most of the time the existing selector already wins. Checked the other floating surfaces for the same latent default: none share it, because only Radix's `Select` has an item-aligned mode. `Typeahead`'s panel is deliberately wider than its input and is not covered by this. **THE SWITCH HAD A SIDE EFFECT THIS RULING DOES NOT CLAIM, AND IT IS EXCLUDED RATHER THAN KEPT.** Popper-positioned content carries `rt-PopperContent`, which the motion block in `components.css` times, and Radix supplies per-side slide names to match. So anchoring silently gave `Select` an exit animation it had never had. With a 260ms exit the closed listbox stays MOUNTED for the duration, focusable, inside the subtree Radix marks `aria-hidden` while the menu is modal: **eight story assertions went red on axe's `aria-hidden-focus` rule**, naming a `role="listbox" data-state="closed"` node with a `data-side`. The motion rule now excludes `.rt-SelectContent` and the vendor's animation-names are silenced on it, so the panel appears and disappears with its trigger exactly as it always did. **Whether a Select that now opens BESIDE its trigger should slide is a real question, and it is a motion decision on its own merits with an exit-focus problem to solve first.** It is not something an anchoring fix gets to decide by accident.

### data-list-overflow

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`, `LAYOUT`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**A `DataList` declares one overflow policy on its root, and every value in the list obeys it.**

**What you see.** The root takes `overflow="wrap" | "truncate"`. A truncated value keeps its full text in a derived `title`, so the ellipsis loses nothing. A value that must differ states it at the call site with `truncate` on `DataList.Value`.

**Default.** `wrap`, which is Radix's existing `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, so every shipped instance renders unchanged.

**Narrow widths.** The root is a `container-type: inline-size` query container, so the layout follows the panel width, not the viewport, which does not move when a user drags a resize handle.

- At 256px the label column releases Radix's 120px floor.
- At 15.3em the label and value stack. The `em` unit follows the type, so the stack begins near 245px at the large size and near 184px at the small size.

**Why.** On the agent-run Run details rail, some values wrapped and one ended in an ellipsis, three rows with two behaviours, because the component held no policy. Truncation against wrapping is decided per component, and one list is one component.

**Not covered.** A query container cannot take its size from its own contents, so a `DataList` inside a shrink-to-fit box is the case where this limit would show. Every shipped instance sits in a block-level or fixed-width parent.

**Changed from.** `DataList` had no overflow policy, so each value wrapped or truncated according to its own content and column width, and the label gutter kept one width at every panel size.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A `DataList` had no overflow policy, so one list showed two behaviours (2026-09-19).** On the agent-run Run details rail, some values truncated and some wrapped, ad hoc. Nothing in the component decided the question, so each value did whatever its own content and column width produced: `orion-3.5-large` wrapped to two lines, `ephemeral-vm-04` wrapped, `agent/billing-sdk-migration` ellipsised. Three rows, two behaviours, no rule a reader could learn. **The policy is now declared ONCE, on the root:** `overflow="wrap" | "truncate"`, and every value in that list obeys it. A value that genuinely must differ is a per-ITEM opt-in the caller states deliberately, and a truncated value keeps its full text reachable through a derived `title`, so nothing is lost to the ellipsis. This is the house rule about truncation versus wrapping — decided per component, never globally — pushed down one level, because a single list is a single component and had been deciding it per row by accident. **The default is `wrap`, and that was measured rather than assumed:** it is exactly Radix's existing `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, so every shipped instance renders byte-identical. **The gutter now answers the CONTAINER, not the viewport:** the gutter between the label and the value kept one width at every panel size, and no breakpoint applied to the panel's width. A resizable panel makes a media query the wrong instrument outright — the viewport does not move when the user drags a handle. The root is a `container-type: inline-size` query container, so the label column releases Radix's flat 120px floor at **256px** and the pair STACKS at **15.3em**, both derived from measured content rather than picked: the first is where the value column drops under a usable measure, the second is expressed in `em` so it rides the type and the stack begins earlier at large (about 245px) and later at small (about 184px). **Verified:** all six rail rows on one line with full text in `title`, and at 320 / 282 / 230px the label column reads 120 / 58 / stacked. **One consequence worth knowing:** a query container cannot be sized by its own contents, so a `DataList` inside a shrink-to-fit box is the shape that would surface it. Every shipped instance sits in a block-level or fixed-width parent and measured identical.

### nesting-treatments

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**Each nesting relationship takes one treatment: embedded content takes a bordered surface, and a reply takes a connector rail.**

**Embedded content.** A quoted post or a link preview by someone else is a bordered surface, because it is a separate object whose edges the reader can see. It leads with its author, as a top-level post does.

**Continuation.** A reply in the same thread is a connector rail with no border, because it continues the same conversation and is not a new object.

**What you see.** On the social feed recreation, a 2px rail and an outlined `Card`, each used for one relationship. The quoted post and the link preview share the outlined `Card`, and the quote and the top-level post share one identity row. A quote carries no action row and no counts, so nothing inside an embed looks like a control on the post that contains it.

**Left rule.** A left rule never serves both readings. `Blockquote` is for a passage quoted inside prose, so the feed does not use it, and the mail reply trail does.

**Changed from.** The feed used three treatments: a bordered card for a link preview, a 2px connector rail for a reply, and a `Blockquote` with a 4px accent left rule for a quoted post. The quote put its body first and its byline underneath.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **One nesting treatment per relationship, and the feed had three (2026-09-19).** On the social recreation, the nested item looked different from the post beside it, its treatment did not show how the two related, and no rule set that treatment. The page rendered a link preview as a bordered card, a threaded reply as a 2px connector rail, and a quoted post as a `Blockquote` whose 4px accent left rule sat forty pixels from that connector rail and meant the opposite thing. Worse, the quote put the BODY first and the byline underneath, so a reader met a wall of text with no idea whose it was. **THE RULE: the treatment names the relationship.** Embedded content by someone else — a quoted post, a link preview — is a BORDERED SURFACE, because it is a separate object whose edges the reader can see, and it therefore leads with its author exactly as a top-level post does, since it IS a post, just contained. Continuation of the same thread — a reply — is a CONNECTOR RAIL with no border, because it is the same conversation carrying on rather than a new object. **A left rule may not serve both.** The quoted post was rebuilt onto the same outlined `Card` the link preview already renders, so a reader learns one visual idea instead of two, and the post identity row was extracted into one component shared by the top-level post and the quote, which makes "a quoted post leads with its author exactly as a top-level post does" true in code rather than by coincidence. The quote carries no action row and no counts: nothing inside an embed should look like a control acting on the post that contains it. **After: two devices on the page, a 2px rail and a 6px-radius bordered card, each used for exactly one relationship.** `Blockquote` left the feed entirely, which is correct — it is for a passage quoted inside prose, not for an embedded post with an author and a timestamp — and moved to the mail reply trail, which is that case exactly.

### action-bar

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**An action bar sits at the foot of the surface it acts on, spans its full width and stays on screen.**

**The rule.**

- It sits flush at the foot of the surface it acts on and spans that surface's full width.
- A top hairline from `--ds-stroke-*` separates it from the content.
- Its padding comes from the space scale.
- It sits outside the scroll region, so its primary action is always on screen.

**Construction.** An action bar is built on `ButtonGroup`, the channel every action row in this system uses and the only one that anchors the solid primary under `buttonOrder`. On the mail recreation, the thread's bar and the draft's commit row are one construct used twice.

**Rejected.** `Toolbar`, which is a cluster of related tools with roving-tabindex focus ([toolbar-slots](#toolbar-slots)). A commit row is not a toolbar.

**Changed from.** On the mail recreation, the thread's Forward and Reply pair sat in plain content flow with no chrome, so it left the screen as the message scrolled. The compose row had the same flaw.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19.

- [action-bar-states](#action-bar-states) makes the thread bar and the composer two states of one region, so only one commit row shows at a time.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **An action bar spans the foot of its surface, and is never two loose buttons (2026-09-19).** Measured on the mail recreation: the thread's Forward/Reply pair sat in ordinary content flow with no chrome at all, so it **scrolled away with the message**, and under `primary-last` it pinned to the far edge of a 990px band with nothing anchoring it. The compose row had the same non-construction. **THE RULE: an action bar sits flush at the foot of the surface it acts on, spans that surface's full width, carries a top hairline from `--ds-stroke-*` to separate it from the content, takes its padding from the space scale, and stays out of the scroll region so its primary action is always on screen.** Both rows are now one construct used twice, which is the whole point: they looked like different things because they were built as different things. **Verified at three tiers: 49 / 57 / 65px, both bars identical in height, width and padding, both still governed by the global `buttonOrder`.** Built on `ButtonGroup` rather than `Toolbar`, deliberately: `ButtonGroup` is the channel every action row in this system already runs through and the only one that anchors the solid primary per `buttonOrder`, whereas `Toolbar` is a cluster of related TOOLS with roving-tabindex focus ([toolbar-slots](#toolbar-slots)), and a commit row is not a toolbar. Send is not a tool.

### measure-cap-scope

**Tags.** `TYPOGRAPHY`, `LAYOUT`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**A reading-measure cap belongs to prose whose width the reader cannot change, and a pane the reader resizes takes none.**

**Why.** A measure cap exists because long lines are hard to track, and it is the right default for editorial prose at a width the reader does not control. A resize handle answers the same question, so a pane with both a handle and a cap overrides the width the reader chose.

**What you see.** The mail reading pane carries no cap. Its body fills the pane and reflows to wherever the reader leaves the handle. `--ds-text-measure` stays in force wherever no resize handle exists.

**Measured.** At a 1920px viewport, before the change, the 65ch cap stopped the body 358px short of a 990px content box sized by the reader.

**Gap.** `Callout` caps its own text inline at `--ds-text-measure`, and a page cannot override an inline style without `!important`, which the system bans. A Callout inside a resizable pane keeps the cap until `Callout` changes. On 2026-09-19 the thread summary in the mail pane was such a Callout, 574px wide inside the 990px box.

**Changed from.** The mail reading body took the 65ch cap like any prose and left the right third of the pane empty.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A measure cap belongs to prose the reader cannot resize (2026-09-19).** The mail reading pane left its right-hand third empty: the body did not fill the pane, and a pane the reader resizes takes no fixed reading width. The general rule is worth more than the fix. A measure cap exists because long lines are hard to track, and it is the RIGHT default for editorial prose whose width the reader does not control. **A pane the user drags is the opposite case: they have already chosen the measure, and the cap overrules them.** Measured at 1920: the body was capped at 65ch and stopped **358px short** of a pane the user had sized to 990px of content box. The cap is removed for that surface and the body fills, reflowing to wherever the handle is left. `--ds-text-measure` stays in force everywhere no handle exists. **This is not "caps are bad".** It is that a cap and a resize handle are two answers to the same question, and shipping both means the app quietly ignores the one the user gave. **Not yet applied consistently within that pane:** the thread-summary `Callout` still caps its own text inline at 65ch, so at 1920 it reads 574px inside a 990px box. A page cannot override an inline style without `!important`, which is banned, so closing that gap is a `Callout` change and is recorded rather than done here.

### checkbox-target-size

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-19.

**`Checkbox` breaches the 24x24 pointer target floor at every size, and at `small` it breaches the spacing exception too. The breach is recorded and not fixed.**

**Rule.** `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 9 sets the floor: an interactive target is at least 24x24.

**Measured.** On 2026-09-19 the `Checkbox` anatomy measured 20x20, and 16x16 inside `CheckboxGroup`. On the mail recreation the row checkbox measured 14x14 at small, 16x16 at medium and 20x20 at large.

**Why it fails.** WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion (SC) 2.5.8 allows an undersized target when a 24px circle centred on it touches no other target's circle, and that exception holds in the component's own stories, where checkboxes sit far apart. On the mail list a 14x14 checkbox sits beside a 24x24 star with centres 23.0px apart, one pixel short, so any dense row that pairs a checkbox with a second control fails, which covers most tables the system serves.

**Proposed fix.** An expanded hit area, a transparent `::after` or block padding that takes the target to 24x24 while the painted square stays where it is, so nothing moves and `small` stays byte-identical. A bigger box is the wrong fix, because it moves every shipped layout.

**Not covered.** `Radio` and `Switch` raise the same question and were not measured. The fix belongs in `Checkbox`, reaches every consumer and changes interaction on a control in nearly every form, so it needs a ruling by the maintainer before it lands.

**Changed from.** No ruling recorded the breach. The spacing exception of SC 2.5.8 carried the checkbox in the component's own stories.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-19. No later ruling amends or fixes it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`Checkbox` breaches the 24x24 pointer floor, and at `small` it breaches the spacing exception too (2026-09-19, RECORDED, NOT FIXED).** `GUIDELINES.md` §9 states the floor as law: interactive targets are at least 24x24. **The system's own `Checkbox` does not meet it at any tier.** Measured on `system-choice-checkbox--anatomy`: **20x20**, and inside `CheckboxGroup` **16x16**. On the mail recreation the row checkbox measures **14x14 at small, 16x16 at medium, 20x20 at large**. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA) allows an undersized target when a 24px circle centred on it touches no other target's circle, and **that exception is what has been carrying this** — it holds in the component's own stories, where the checkboxes are far apart. **It fails on the mail list.** Each row pairs a 14x14 select box with a 24x24 star, centres **23.0px** apart against the 24px the exception requires: eight rows, short by one pixel, at the DEFAULT tier. At large the same pair measures 20x20 beside 32x32 and clears it. So the page that finally exposed this is not the page at fault: any dense row pairing a checkbox with a second control reproduces it, which is most tables this system is for. **Why it is recorded rather than fixed here:** the remedy belongs in `Checkbox` and reaches every consumer of it. The fix is not a bigger box — the visual square is correct and enlarging it would move every shipped layout. It is an expanded HIT AREA: a transparent `::after` or block padding that takes the target to 24x24 while the painted square stays exactly where it is, so nothing moves visually and `small` stays byte-identical. The same question applies to `Radio` and `Switch` and neither has been measured yet. Needs a ruling by the maintainer before it lands, because it is a system-wide interaction change on a control that appears in nearly every form.

### truncating-label-width

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**A truncating label carries `contain: inline-size`, so its row narrows with its container and the ellipsis shows.**

**What you see.** On a narrow rail a row narrows to the rail's width, its label ends in an ellipsis, and the trailing status mark stays inside the viewport. No text is cut mid-glyph.

**Why.** A flex item's `min-width: auto` floors it at its min-content, and a label that does not wrap has its whole string as min-content, so one label holds the whole row at its full text width. `min-width: 0` does not reach this. Size containment in the inline axis removes the string from the label's intrinsic width, so the row takes the rail's width.

**Applies to.** The truncating text only: a TreeList row label or description that Item clamps, and an Outline entry. The chevron, the icon and the trailing mark still set a minimum, so the one-glyph status mark is never what the clipping removes.

**Measured.** At a 150px rail, before: 62px of overflow, no label ellipsed and no status mark visible. After: 8px of clearance at 150, 200 and 272px, and both status marks inside the viewport at every width. The resting width does not change.

**Changed from.** A label too long for a narrow rail held its row at full width, `ScrollArea` clipped the row through a letter, and the trailing status mark was the first thing cut.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A truncating label reported its whole string as an intrinsic width, so the row never shrank and the panel cut it mid-glyph (2026-09-20).** On the code editor's explorer and outline rails, elements were clipped with no sign of the hidden text, which does not count as truncation, and the right-aligned status indicator moved when the sidebar was resized. **Measured at 1600x1000, narrowing the rail:** at 272px the widest row ended at 264 inside a 272 viewport and fitted; at 200px the row stayed **212 wide, 12px past the viewport**; at 150px it stayed 212 wide, **62px past**. Throughout, the label reported `scrollWidth 102 === clientWidth 102`, so **the ellipsis it already carried never fired**. The row simply refused to shrink, and `ScrollArea` clipped it through a letter. It also breached the rail's own declared 208px floor. **The cause is intrinsic sizing, not a missing `overflow` rule.** A flex item's `min-width: auto` floors it at min-content, and a nowrap label's min-content is its ENTIRE string, so one label anywhere in the chain pins the whole row at its full text width no matter how narrow the container gets. The fix is `contain: inline-size` on the truncating text: the label stops publishing its string as an intrinsic contribution, the row inherits the rail's width, and the ellipsis engages. **Scoped to the text only, deliberately** — the chevron, the file icon and the trailing marker still contribute a minimum, which is what keeps the one-character git status letter from being the first thing cut. That is the harder half: a status marker is the row's state, it is one glyph wide, and it must never be what the clipping eats. **After, at the same three widths: 8px of clearance at all three (never overflowing), 0 / 2 / 8 labels ellipsed, and 2 of 2 status marks inside the viewport at every width.** Before, at 150px: 62px of overflow, 0 labels ellipsed, 0 marks visible. The resting width is untouched.

### action-bar-states

**Tags.** `LAYOUT`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**A control that opens a surface is replaced by that surface, so an action bar and the surface it opens are two states of one region, never two bars.**

**What you see.** In the mail recreation the thread bar and the composer are one region with three states, and each state shows exactly one commit row:

- Draft open: the draft's commit row only.
- Draft closed: the thread's Reply and Forward row only.
- Draft minimised: the thread's Reply and Forward row, with a collapsed dock above it.

**Fewer controls at rest.** The summary `Callout` is a closed `Collapsible`, recipient chips are plain text, and To, attachments and scheduling sit behind progressive disclosure.

**Why.** A button that starts an action has no purpose once that action is under way, so no mail client stacks the two rows.

**Applies to.** Every recreation of a familiar kind of interface. The test is whether the page matches what a daily user of that kind of app expects next, not whether each part looks right on its own.

**Changed from.** [action-bar](#action-bar) built the thread's Forward and Reply bar and left the composer's Save draft and Send bar below it, so two commit rows sat stacked. The pane showed eighteen interactive controls at rest, and no line of the message, at 1440 by 900.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **An action bar and the surface it opens are two states of one region, never two bars (2026-09-20).** This kind of interface never carries two button bars at once, because a mail client removes its reply button when the user starts to write. The page read right at a glance and, a few seconds later, did not match what a reader expects. [action-bar](#action-bar) built the thread's Forward/Reply bar correctly and left the composer's Save draft/Send bar below it, so the reader saw **two competing commit rows stacked**. No mail client stacks the two, because a button that starts an action has no purpose once that action is under way. **THE RULE: a control that opens a surface is replaced by that surface, not stacked above it.** The thread bar and the composer are now one region with three states. Open draft shows the draft's commit row only. Closed or minimised shows the thread's Reply row only, with a collapsed dock above it when minimised. **Verified by driving all three in Chrome: composer open gives Send and no Reply, discard gives Reply and no Send and no textarea, Reply restores the composer and removes Reply.** Exactly one commit affordance in every state. **The mismatch is measurable:** the pane showed eighteen interactive controls at rest with not one line of the message visible at 1440x900. The summary `Callout` became a closed `Collapsible`, recipient chips became plain text, and To, attachments and scheduling moved behind progressive disclosure. The test for this class of defect is whether the page matches what a daily user of this kind of app expects next, not whether each part looks right on its own.

### component-shadowing

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**No file outside the component layer may declare a component the system ships, and a source check fails when one does.**

**Guarded.** `component-shadow.node-check.ts` fails when a file outside `src/components/ui/` declares a top-level name equal to a shipped component's registered name or one of its exports. The check reads source, because a shadow renders without error and leaves nothing to measure at runtime.

**Why.** Inside a file that shadows a component, the name resolves to the local copy, so every reader sees the system's component in use and gets the wrong result. That is worse than never using the component, and it is the failure the reuse rule in `AGENTS.md` exists to prevent.

**Case.** The analytics scenario declared its own `function Toolbar()` with `align-items: flex-end`, so its compare switch group, 20px tall against 32px controls, sat 6px off the shared centre line. The shipped `Toolbar` centres its members and supplies the role, the group dividers and the control tier. With the shadow deleted, every member centre agrees at every tier. The compare control is now a surface `Select` named "Comparison".

**Changed from.** Nothing checked whether a page redefined a shipped component, and the analytics scenario carried a local `Toolbar` that looked like the system's.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20. No later ruling amends it.

- Revised on 2026-10-02: the Case part names the compare control as a surface `Select`, which replaced the `ToggleButton` that read "Compare".

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A page redefined a component the system ships, and nothing noticed (2026-09-20).** The analytics filter bar was not centred vertically, and its compare control, a labelled `Switch` 227.6px wide, took a large share of the row in a shape that filter bars do not use. **Measured:** every control in the bar centred on 54px except the compare switch group, which is 20px tall against 32px controls and centred on **60**. The bar was `align-items: flex-end`. **The root cause is not the 6px.** The page declared its own `function Toolbar()` and hand-rolled the row, while the system ships a `Toolbar` that already sets `alignItems: "center"` and would have been right first time. Inside that file the name `Toolbar` resolved to the local copy, so every later reader saw a page apparently using the system's component and getting the wrong result. **That is worse than never reaching for it**, and it is the exact failure "reuse before you invent" exists to prevent. The shadow is deleted and the bar is the shipped component, which also supplies the role, the group dividers and the control-tier cascade. **After: every member centre agrees at every tier (39 / 43 / 48 at small / medium / large).** The compare control moved from a 227.6px labelled `Switch` to a 77.9px `ToggleButton` reading "Compare", with the rest of the sentence in `VisuallyHidden` so the accessible name is still "Compare to previous period" and the pressed state survives without colour. **The mechanism, which matters more than the page:** `component-shadow.node-check.ts` now fails if any file outside `src/components/ui/` declares a top-level name matching a shipped component's registered name or exports. It was written before the fix landed, went red naming this exact line, and went green when the shadow was deleted. A shadow is invisible at runtime by construction, so source is the only place it can be caught.
>
> The Case part before the revision of 2026-10-02:
>
> **Case.** The analytics scenario declared its own `function Toolbar()` with `align-items: flex-end`, so its compare switch group, 20px tall against 32px controls, sat 6px off the shared centre line.
