The shipped `Toolbar` centres its members and supplies the role, the group dividers and the control tier. With the shadow deleted, every member centre agrees at every tier, and the compare control is a `ToggleButton` that reads "Compare", with an accessible name of "Compare to previous period".

### reorder-capability

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**Reorder is a capability, the headless hook `useReorder`, not a component, and its one piece of new UI is `DragHandle`.**

**The hook.** More than one component needs drag and drop, so the behaviour lives in the library, after the `useResizable` precedent, which `ResizeHandle` and `Layout` consume. `useReorder` returns prop getters the caller spreads, so any markup adopts it, and one hook drives a plain vertical list and a multi-column board with no special cases. It moves items within a group and across groups. Pure index math lives in `src/utils/reorderMath.ts`, as `resizableMath` does for resizing.

**DragHandle.** The grip glyph, the box, the focus ring and the ARIA wiring, with every behaviour from the hook, the confinement [file-input](#file-input) set for new UI.

**Feedback.** The minimal reorder pattern:

- The element under the pointer shows `grab`, and the whole document shows `grabbing` for the length of a drag.
- The held item keeps its slot as a ghost at `opacity: 0.4` with a dashed outline, so the original order stays readable.
- A separate indicator marks the exact landing slot, for the keyboard route too, and covers the end of a group and an empty group.
- `useReorder().groups` returns the committed order, not a live preview, and changes once, on the drop, when `onReorder` fires. A count badge holds still while an item moves.

**Rejected.**

- A new runtime dependency such as dnd-kit or react-dnd.
- The HTML5 drag API, which has no keyboard story, poor touch support and an unstyleable drag image. The capability runs on Pointer Events.
- The maximal pattern, where the list opens a real gap, because it leaves unclear how to abort with nothing changed, which would undercut the Escape-to-cancel contract of [reorder-single-pointer-path](#reorder-single-pointer-path).
- `!important` for the cursor. The card link's pointer comes from the user-agent rule `a:-webkit-any-link`, so one author declaration settles it, and the document-wide grabbing state uses `html[data-ds-reorder-dragging] .radix-themes *` at (0,2,1) to clear the item rule at (0,2,0).

**Gap.**

- The indicator is a horizontal line and the shipped axis is vertical within a group, so a horizontal list would get it on the wrong axis.
- The ghost opacity of 0.4 can make an item that is already low in contrast faint, and it is the number most likely to need tuning.
- As built on 2026-09-20, the indicator painted as an outer `box-shadow` on the item, so an item with its own `box-shadow` lost it while the marker showed.

**Changed from.** The system carried three drags, `ResizeHandle`, `Lightbox` pan and `Slider`, and no way to reorder anything, though the project board implied drag and drop. The first version of the hook, on the same day, gave no feedback, and its `groups` returned the live preview order.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20.

- An amendment dated 2026-09-20, recorded in this entry, adds the feedback and changes `groups` from the preview order to the committed order.
- [textless-part-fills](#textless-part-fills) paints the reorder marker in `--accent-indicator`.
- [indicator-mark-edges](#indicator-mark-edges) stacks `--accent-part-edge` on the drop line and its end dot.
- [drop-target-dash](#drop-target-dash) stacks a Radix alpha on the dashed edge of the empty drop slot.
- [published-aschild-props](#published-aschild-props) refuses `asChild` on `DragHandle`, which emitted no button with it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Reorder is a capability, not a component (2026-09-20).** The project board implied drag and drop, and no interaction pattern for it was defined anywhere. The system carried three drags — `ResizeHandle`, `Lightbox` pan and `Slider` — and no way to reorder anything. Measured on the board before this: no `draggable` attribute, no grab cursor, no handle glyph, nothing. The archetype promised an interaction the implementation never had, which is the failure [action-bar-states](#action-bar-states) records, one level higher. The drag-and-drop interaction lives in the library, because more than one component needs it. So the capability is a headless hook, `useReorder`, following the `useResizable` precedent where the behaviour is the library's and `ResizeHandle` plus `Layout` are merely its consumers. It returns prop-getters the caller spreads, so any markup adopts it: the docs prove that by driving a plain vertical list and a multi-column board **from the same hook with no special-casing**. It handles moves within a group and across groups, because a kanban needs the second and a sortable settings list needs only the first. **The one piece of net-new UI is `DragHandle`**, deliberately tiny at 59 lines: the grip glyph, the box, the focus ring and the ARIA wiring, with every behaviour coming from the hook. That confinement is the [file-input](#file-input) precedent. **Pure index math lives in `src/utils/reorderMath.ts`** with 32 unit tests, mirroring `resizableMath`, which also kept every file inside the 400-line cap (318 / 278 / 139 / 59) and every function inside 100. **No new runtime dependency**: no dnd-kit, no react-dnd. The HTML5 drag API was rejected outright because it has no keyboard story, poor touch support and an unstyleable drag image; this is Pointer Events. **AMENDED 2026-09-20, THE FEEDBACK WAS MISSING AND THAT IS MOST OF THE PATTERN.** The first version worked and gave no feedback. Three defects were found: the cursor showed the link pointer, a drag showed nothing while it lasted, and a drop gave no sign of where the item would land. All three measured true. The item computed `cursor: grab`, but `ClickableCard`'s stretched link overlay computes `pointer` and covers the whole card, so the finger is what a reader ever saw; `document.body` stayed `auto` through a drag, so there was no grabbing hand at all; the held card got a background tint and nothing else, with `opacity: 1`, `transform: none` and `box-shadow: none`; and no element anywhere carried a drop position. Of the two legitimate reorder patterns recorded in `REFERENCES.md`, we took the MINIMAL one: the held item keeps its slot as a ghost so the reader retains the original order, and a separate indicator marks the precise landing slot. The maximal pattern, where the list opens a real gap, was rejected because it leaves unclear how to abort the operation without changing anything, which would undercut the Escape-to-cancel contract [reorder-single-pointer-path](#reorder-single-pointer-path) records. **After, measured on the board:** the element under the pointer computes `grab`, `document.body` computes `grabbing` for the duration, the held card stays at its own y with `opacity: 0.4` and a dashed outline, and the indicator moves between slots as the pointer crosses them (`data-ds-reorder-drop=before` at one slot, `after` at another). **The indicator serves the keyboard route too**, because a keyboard user needs the same answer to where this is going, and it handles the two cases insertion markers always get wrong: the end of a column and an empty column. **The cursor fix was a cascade fight won on specificity, not `!important`:** the winner was the USER-AGENT rule `a:-webkit-any-link { cursor: pointer }`, with no author rule matching the card link at all, so one author declaration settles it, and the document-wide grabbing state needs `html[data-ds-reorder-dragging] .radix-themes *` at (0,2,1) to clear the item rule at (0,2,0). **ONE SHIPPED CONTRACT CHANGED, AND A CONSUMER CAN SEE IT:** `useReorder().groups` used to return the live PREVIEW order and now returns the COMMITTED order, because under the minimal pattern the preview is expressed by the indicator rather than by moving anything. Every call site in this repo was checked and none depended on the old reading, but a downstream consumer rendering `groups` mid-drag would have seen items move and now will not. The visible consequence on the board is deliberate: a column's count badge no longer ticks as you arrow, because a number claiming a move that has not happened is a lie the drop indicator already answers better. It changes once, on the drop, which is when `onReorder` fires. **THREE KNOWN GAPS, recorded rather than quietly carried.** (1) The indicator is a HORIZONTAL line and the shipped axis is vertical-within-group, so a horizontally laid out list would get it on the wrong axis. There was no line at all before, so this is a gap and not a regression. (2) The ghost is `opacity: 0.4`, judged on a board card and a plain row; an item that was already low-contrast will get faint, and this is the number most likely to need tuning. (3) The indicator is painted as an outer `box-shadow` on the item, because Radix's `Card` has already spent both of that element's pseudo-elements. An item declaring its own `box-shadow` on the element itself would lose it for the frames the marker is there. No shipped component does that; a hand-rolled one could.

### reorder-single-pointer-path

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-20.

**The reorder capability offers a single-pointer path, because a keyboard alternative satisfies WCAG 2.1.1 and never 2.5.7.**

**Why.** [dragging-movement-gaps](#dragging-movement-gaps) records `ResizeHandle` and `Lightbox` as WCAG 2.5.7 failures, and a third drag with only a keyboard alternative would make a pattern of it. 2.5.7 asks for a single-pointer alternative to the drag itself, as `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 9 states.

**Routes.** `useReorder` runs one lift, move and drop state machine, reachable three independent ways:

- Keyboard: Space lifts, an arrow key moves the pending slot, Space drops, and Escape cancels and restores the original order.
- A single pointer: a click lifts the item, and a click on a destination places it, with no drag at all.
- A pointer drag.

The click route is the same machine, not an addition beside it.

**Announcements and state.** The existing singleton `useAnnounce` speaks each lift, move, drop and cancel with the item and its position, such as "position 3 of 5", because "moved" alone gives a screen reader user nothing. The accessible name, an `aria-describedby` key map and the live announcements carry the state. `aria-grabbed` is deprecated and unsupported, so it is not used.

**Target and motion.** The handle measures 24x24, 32x32 and 40x40 across the tiers, so it clears the pointer floor at the smallest step. Motion clamps to 1e-05s under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

**Testing.** `element.click()` does not exercise the single-pointer route, because the machine runs on Pointer Events. A synthetic click reports a false negative, and a real `page.mouse.click` exercises the path.

**Changed from.** No earlier ruling covered this.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-20.

- [reorder-capability](#reorder-capability), amended the same day, keeps the order unchanged until the drop, so an arrow key moves the drop indicator rather than the item.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The reorder capability owes a single-pointer path, and it has one (2026-09-20).** [dragging-movement-gaps](#dragging-movement-gaps) already records `ResizeHandle` and `Lightbox` as WCAG 2.5.7 failures, so shipping a third drag with only a keyboard alternative would have made a pattern of it. **`GUIDELINES.md` §9 states the distinction people get wrong: a keyboard equivalent satisfies 2.1.1 and NEVER 2.5.7**, which asks for a single-POINTER alternative to the dragging movement itself. `useReorder` therefore runs one lift-move-drop state machine reachable three independent ways, and the click route is not a bolt-on but the same machine. **Verified in the test browser against the real page.** Keyboard: focus the handle, Space lifts and announces "Lifted Full name, position 1 of 5", ArrowDown reorders live and announces "Full name, position 2 of 5", Space drops and announces "Dropped Full name, position 2 of 5". Escape cancels and **the original order is restored**, announced "Cancelled. Full name, position 1 of 5" — asserted by comparing the array before the lift with the array after the cancel, not by trusting the message. Single pointer: a real click on the handle lifts, a real click on a destination places, and the item moved from position 1 to position 3 **with no drag at all**. Announcements come from the existing singleton `useAnnounce` rather than a second live region. Position is stated in human terms, "position 3 of 5", because "moved" alone tells a screen-reader user nothing. The handle measures **24x24 / 32x32 / 40x40** across the tiers, so it clears the pointer floor at the smallest step, which is more than `Checkbox` currently manages ([checkbox-target-size](#checkbox-target-size)). Motion is clamped to 1e-05s under `prefers-reduced-motion`. `aria-grabbed` is deprecated and unsupported and is deliberately not used: state is carried by the accessible name, an `aria-describedby` key map, and the live announcements. **A caveat for whoever tests this next:** `element.click()` does NOT exercise the single-pointer route, because the machine listens to Pointer Events. A synthetic click reports a false negative, and a real `page.mouse.click` is what exercises the path.

### measured-surface-census

**Tags.** `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-21.

**A claim about what the component surface does is measured by compiling and rendering it, never by reading the source.**

**Why.** A census read by eye was wrong three times out of five. `src/foundations/radix-surface.node-check.ts` records an earlier hand count of 67 wrapped and 36 unwrapped that miscounted the same five components, and a second hand count was the case for widening `asChild`.

**Method.**

- A type probe, `"asChild" extends keyof ComponentProps<typeof X>`, compiles over every exported name.
- Each name renders three times in two engines, and the depth of the slotted element is compared against an anchor. The first tag in the markup gives false positives and misreads a name whose child is already the root.
- The type question and the render question are asked apart, because they disagree for real components.

**Measured.** At commit `671fa8b`, on 2026-09-21, over 194 component names: 43 carry `asChild` in the type and 28 reach the root, and one forwards without the type. Of the 194, 28 already forward, 108 are blocked, 8 crash and 50 cannot forward by structure: 28 portals, 19 with no element of their own and 3 with several root elements. The registry then counted 106 ported entries. [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error) rules on the eight crashes.

**Changed from.** The component surface was counted by reading the source.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-21. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A census read by eye was wrong three times out of five, and the repo already had a record of the same mistake (2026-09-21).** A hand count of the component surface was the case for widening `asChild`. **`src/foundations/radix-surface.node-check.ts` records the SAME method failing before**, a hand census of "67 wrapped, 36 unwrapped" that was internally consistent, confidently stated, and miscounted the same five components. Reading source by eye is the method that has now failed twice on the same question. **THE RULE: a claim about what the component surface does is measured by compiling and rendering it, never by reading it.** The replacement measurement compiles a type probe of the form `"asChild" extends keyof ComponentProps<typeof X>` over every exported name, then renders each name three times in two engines and compares the DEPTH of the slotted element against an anchor, because reading the first tag in the markup produces false positives and also misreads the nineteen names whose child is already the root. **The two questions disagree for real components**, so they are asked separately: forty-three names carry `asChild` in the type and only twenty-eight reach the root, and one name forwards without being typed. Measured at 671fa8b over 194 distinct component names: **28 already forward, 108 blocked, 8 crash, 50 structurally cannot**, the last splitting into 28 portals, 19 with no element of their own, and 3 rendering several root elements. The entry-level reconciliation returns the registry's ported total of **106**.

### aschild-or-type-error

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-21.

**`asChild` either works or is a type error, and never a crash.**

**Why.** Radix `Slot` requires exactly one element child, so a component that forwards `asChild` to an element it renders several children into throws `React.Children.only` at render. Eight names crashed this way, and `Toolbar.Root` published `asChild`, so a TypeScript consumer reached the crash from code that compiled cleanly.

**Gained the seam.** Radix `Slottable` serves a component whose own content belongs inside the consumer's element.

- `EmptyState` gives its root to the consumer's element and keeps its icon, title, description and actions inside it.
- `ButtonGroup` reads the cluster from the slotted element's own children and orders it there.
- `Toolbar.Root` renders one element that carries `role="toolbar"`, the roving focus, the orientation and the layout.

**Refused.** Four components declare `asChild?: never` and remove the prop before the spread, the idiom `ClickableCard` shipped first. Each renders more than one child into its own root and spends `children` on a label or a body, so support would need a new prop to hold the slot target. [badge-scope](#badge-scope) already stripped the prop from `Badge` and `Token`, but it still arrived from an untyped spread and threw.

**Criterion.** A component can take the seam when it has exactly one root element to give the consumer and the transfer preserves its contract. Seam ownership under [seam-ownership](#seam-ownership) is no reason to refuse: `Slot` concatenates `className` and merges `style` shallowly, so the component's classes land on the consumer's element and the seam still paints. `Layout`, `AppShell`, `ResizeHandle` and `SideNav` each render one root element and pass this test.

**Changed from.** Eight components crashed with `React.Children.only` when given `asChild`, one of them through a published prop.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-21.

- [api-seam-criterion](#api-seam-criterion) adds a first test: a seam needs a named consumer need, and the structural test here is necessary but not sufficient.
- [published-aschild-props](#published-aschild-props) applies the `asChild?: never` idiom to four more components whose published prop broke the control.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **`asChild` crashed on eight names, and one of them was reachable from a clean compile (2026-09-21).** Radix `Slot` requires exactly one element child, so a component that forwards `asChild` to a Radix element it renders several children into throws `React.Children.only` at render. **`Toolbar.Root` is the serious one: `asChild` sat in its published props, so a TypeScript consumer reached a runtime crash from code that compiled cleanly.** A crash is a defect independent of any decision about widening the seam, and these were fixed before the seam question was reopened. **THE RULE: `asChild` either works or is a type error, and never a crash.** Three components gained the seam through `Slottable`, which is the Radix mechanism for a component whose own content belongs INSIDE the consumer's element: `EmptyState` hands over the block and keeps its icon, title, description and actions within it, `ButtonGroup` reads the cluster from the slotted element's own children and orders it there, and `Toolbar.Root` renders one element carrying `role="toolbar"`, the roving focus, the orientation and the layout. Four refuse instead, declaring `asChild?: never` and destructuring the prop away before the spread, which generalises the idiom `ClickableCard` already shipped as `Omit<CardProps, "asChild" | "title">`. **Each of the four renders more than one child into its own root and each already spends `children` on a label or a body, so supporting the seam would mean inventing a prop to hold the slot target.** [badge-scope](#badge-scope) had already decided `Badge` and `Token` strip the prop; the defect was that it still arrived from an untyped spread and threw rather than being ignored. **Seam ownership is NOT a reason to refuse.** Owning a hairline under [seam-ownership](#seam-ownership) does not justify refusing `Layout`, `AppShell`, `ResizeHandle` or `SideNav`, because `Slot` merges `className` by CONCATENATION and `style` shallowly, so a component's classes land on the consumer's element and the seam still paints. All four render exactly one element at the root position. The criterion is structural instead: **exactly one root element to hand over, and handing it over preserves the contract.**

### aschild-handover-warning

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-21.

**A consumer who passes an element through `asChild` assumes the system's guarantees for it, so the seam warns about the loss and never repairs it.**

**The hazard.** `Slot` merges `{ ...slotProps, ...overrideProps }` with the override props taken from the child, so for anything other than an event handler, `className` or `style`, the consumer's value wins. A consumer's own `role`, `tabIndex` or `aria-*`, or a non-interactive element in place of an interactive one, silently voids what the system publishes: WCAG 2.2 AA conformance, the 24 by 24 pointer floor, the focus ring, and the roles and keyboard models inherited from Radix. The rendered page shows nothing.

**Rejected.** Reapplying the system's props after the merge. It would make `asChild` mean that the consumer's props hold except the ones the system silently reclaims, a second silent failure in the other direction, and it would no longer be composition. Ariakit's `render` prop, the nearest alternative, uses the same precedence, so passing an element means passing its props in every API that offers it.

**Two mechanisms.** Neither one covers the other.

- `checkAsChild` in `src/foundations/asChildContract.ts` runs during render behind `DEV_WARN`, through the `warnOnce` layer of [container-size-seeding](#container-size-seeding). It reads values a static pass cannot: a `role` computed at runtime, a child assembled elsewhere, two children or none, and a legitimate `Slottable` composition it must not report.
- The `ds-check` rule `aschild-nonint` reads consumer source, so it covers code that never ran in development, and it fails a consumer's CI where a console warning goes unread.

**Gap.** Neither mechanism catches a child that is a component, because at runtime that child is a function and in source it is only a name, and neither reports a guess. Closing the gap needs a read of the resolved node through a ref after mount.

**Changed from.** Nothing warned when a consumer's props replaced the system's through `asChild`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-21.

- [focus-ring](#focus-ring) replaces the neutral focus hairline this ruling listed among the guarantees with the accent focus ring.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Handing over the element hands over the guarantees, so the seam warns and never repairs (2026-09-21).** `Slot` merges `{ ...slotProps, ...overrideProps }` with `overrideProps` derived from the CHILD, so for anything that is not an event handler, `className` or `style`, **the consumer's value wins**. A consumer passing their own `role`, `tabIndex` or `aria-*`, or swapping an interactive element for a non-interactive one, silently voids what this system publishes: WCAG 2.2 AA conformance, the 24x24 pointer floor, the neutral focus hairline, and the roles and keyboard models inherited from Radix. **Nothing about the rendered page shows it.** Prior art settles that this is not a Radix quirk to design around: Ariakit's `render` prop, the nearest alternative shape, merges `style`, `className`, `ref` and event props and lets every other prop on the rendered element OVERRIDE the component's, which is the same precedence. **Handing over an element means handing over the props, in every API that offers it.** So re-applying the system's props after the merge was considered and REJECTED: it would make `asChild` mean "your props are honoured, except the ones we quietly take back", which is a second silent failure pointed the other way, and it would not be composition any more. **THE RULE: the seam makes the loss loud and early, and never pretends the swap is safe.** Two mechanisms, neither subsuming the other. `checkAsChild` in `src/foundations/asChildContract.ts` runs during render behind `DEV_WARN`, reusing the `warnOnce` layer [container-size-seeding](#container-size-seeding) established rather than repeating it, and sees VALUES a static pass cannot: a `role` computed at runtime, a child assembled elsewhere, a shape defect of two children or none, and a legitimate `Slottable` composition it must NOT report. A fifth `ds-check` rule, `aschild-nonint`, reads consumer source and sees CODE THAT NEVER RAN, including a feature-flagged branch or a page nobody opened in development, and it fails a consumer's CI where a console warning is read by nobody. **Neither catches a child that is a COMPONENT**, since one holds a function and the other a name, and both decline to guess rather than warn wrongly. That gap is named in both, and closing it needs a post-mount ref read of the resolved node. Proven both ways: `<Toolbar.Root asChild><nav role="navigation">` draws the named warning that "navigation" wins and `role="toolbar"` is dropped, and the same `nav` without a `role` draws nothing.

### api-seam-criterion

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-21.

**A component gains a seam only when a named consumer needs one, never to make the surface uniform.**

**The rule.** Before the structural test of [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error), write one concrete sentence that names what a consumer needs to do and how this seam answers it. If that sentence cannot be written, the component stays as it is.

**Why.** The structural test, one root element to pass to the consumer and a contract that holds after the handover, says whether a seam can exist and not whether it should. A seam is a release valve for a consumer, and a match with a system pattern never justifies a seam that no consumer would seek.

**The cheaper valve.** Where a tag serves the need, `as` comes before `asChild`, because `as` swaps the tag with no prop merge and carries none of the [aschild-handover-warning](#aschild-handover-warning) hazard. `as` takes a closed union of the tags the component's CSS supports, never an open `ElementType`, as `Item` does.

**Applied.** No measured component earned `asChild`. `as` was recommended for `ChatLayout`, `ChatMessage` and `ChatSystemMessage`, which sit inside a document structure the consumer owns. The `Breadcrumbs` candidate was withdrawn after measurement: inside another `nav` it draws no axe violation and exposes two distinctly named landmarks.

**Changed from.** [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error) gave the structural test alone, so a seam that could exist met no test of whether it should.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-21.

- [chat-layout-tag](#chat-layout-tag) tests each recommendation again before building it: `ChatLayout` takes `as` with `"div" | "main" | "section"`, and `ChatMessage` and `ChatSystemMessage` do not.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A seam is earned by a named consumer need, never by making the surface uniform (2026-09-21).** The criterion: a seam exists only as a release valve that a consumer needs to work with the system, and a match with a system pattern never justifies a seam that a consumer would not find useful or look for. [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error) gave a STRUCTURAL test, one root element to hand over and a contract that survives the handover. That test is necessary and it is not sufficient, because it answers whether a seam CAN exist rather than whether it SHOULD. **THE RULE: before the structural test, name in one concrete sentence what a consumer is trying to do that this seam is the answer to. If the sentence cannot be written, the component is left alone.** Applied to the 66 measured names where the seam is technically reachable, the answer is almost always to do nothing: of the 40 one-level names, **zero** earned `asChild`; of the 24 deeper names, **zero** earned `asChild`. That is the criterion working rather than failing. The corollary is that **the cheaper valve is preferred where it serves the need**: `as` swaps the tag with no prop merge, so it carries none of the [aschild-handover-warning](#aschild-handover-warning) hazard, and a consumer who needs a `main` rather than a `div` wants a tag rather than an element handover. `Item` is the shipped precedent and its shape is the one to copy, a CLOSED union of the tags whose CSS the component survives rather than an open `ElementType`. Three components are recommended for `as` on a stated need and none for `asChild`: `ChatLayout`, `ChatMessage` and `ChatSystemMessage`, which are content placed inside a document structure the consumer owns, so the tag depends on that structure rather than on the component. A recommendation was also WITHDRAWN under measurement rather than asserted: `Breadcrumbs` inside another `nav` draws zero axe violations and exposes two distinctly named landmarks, so the candidate need dissolved.

### aschild-depth

**Tags.** `COMPONENTS`, `CONTRIBUTING`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-21.

**The `asChild` depth number measures where the consumer's children land, not where a consumer reaches, and no component needs flattening.**

**What the number means.** The measurement reported 24 names that hold the slotted element 2 to 7 levels deep. A consumer who asks for the seam on `ChatLayout` asks for the root to be their own element. The 7 levels are what `Slottable` would have to cross, not the thing swapped.

**Demonstrated.** At full depth a plain root `Slot` throws the crash of [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error), because the root renders the log, the session line and the dock. `Slottable` on `children` puts the consumer's `main` at the root with `rt-ds-chat-layout` and keeps the composer, the `role="log"` tab stop and the imperative handle, but drops the transcript, because `children` is the transcript. With the transcript moved to a named prop the seam works, the transcript still 6 levels down, and all 7 levels stay.

**The real obstacle.** All 24 names spend `children` on their own content, so no free slot exists, at 2 levels or at 7. The cost of a slot seam is a silent break: an existing `<ChatLayout>{messages}</ChatLayout>` would render an empty conversation with no crash, no warning and no type error.

**Recommendation.** `as="main"` gives the same root element with no API change, no break and none of the hazard in [aschild-handover-warning](#aschild-handover-warning).

**Changed from.** The depth number read as a mark of the riskiest group of components, and raised two questions: whether a consumer edits an element seven levels in, and whether a seven-level component could be flattened and still work.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-21. No later ruling amends it. [chat-layout-tag](#chat-layout-tag) gives `ChatLayout` the `as` prop this ruling recommends.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **The depth number measures where the consumer's children land, not where a consumer reaches, and nothing needed flattening (2026-09-21).** The measurement reported 24 names burying the slotted element 2 to 7 levels inside, and the reasonable reading of that was the riskiest group. That reading raised two questions: whether a consumer modifies an element seven layers in, and whether a seven-layer component could be flattened and still work. The number supports neither question, and the correction is the useful part. A consumer does not modify an element 7 layers in. A consumer asking for the seam on `ChatLayout` is asking for the ROOT to be their element, and the 7 layers are what `Slottable` would have to reach past rather than the thing being swapped. **Demonstrated by building it at the full depth, not by reasoning:** a naive root `Slot` throws the [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error) crash, because the root renders the log, the session line and the dock. `Slottable` on `children` puts the consumer's `main` at the root carrying `rt-ds-chat-layout`, with the composer, the `role="log"` tab stop and the imperative handle all intact, **and the transcript gone**, because `children` WAS the transcript. Moving the transcript to a named prop makes the seam work completely, with the transcript still 6 levels down the identical chain. **All 7 layers stayed. Flattening was never required.** The real obstacle is not depth at all: all 24 of these names spend `children` on their own content, so there is no free slot, and that obstacle is identical at 2 layers and at 7. The caution was right for a reason other than the one first given, because the cost is not structural collapse, it is that an existing `<ChatLayout>{messages}</ChatLayout>` would render an empty conversation with no crash, no warning and no type error, which is the worst shape a breaking change can take. `as="main"` gives the same root element with no API change, no breakage and none of the [aschild-handover-warning](#aschild-handover-warning) hazard, which is why it is the recommendation.

### published-aschild-props

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-21.

**A published prop that does not do what its name says is an accessibility defect, so a component honours `asChild` or refuses it as a type error.**

**What you see.**

- `Popover.Anchor` binds to the `@radix-ui/react-popover` primitive that Radix Themes itself imports, checked by object identity so the two cannot drift apart, and it keeps the consumer's element.
- `Callout`, `DragHandle`, `MobileNavToggle` and `ToggleButton` declare `asChild?: never` under [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error).

**Exception.** `AspectRatio` keeps `asChild`. The consumer's `img`, `video` or `iframe` becomes the inset content box, with the component class ahead of its own, and the outer box stays because it holds the ratio. Its docblock names which of its two elements the prop replaces.

**Why.** Six components carried `asChild` in their public props and never put the consumer's element in place of their root. Rendered on 2026-09-21, five failed with no error and a clean compile:

- `Callout` lost its `rt-CalloutRoot` element, and with it the tone fill, the urgency border and `role="alert"`.
- `DragHandle`, `MobileNavToggle` and `ToggleButton` emitted no `button` element, so the control was not focusable, not operable by keyboard and not named to a screen reader.
- `Popover.Anchor` erased the consumer's subtree, because the system's wrapper bound to the Radix Themes re-export.

**Changed from.** Six components published `asChild` without honouring it.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-21. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Six components published `asChild` and four of them broke the control rather than ignoring the prop (2026-09-21).** The type probe found six names carrying `asChild` in their public props that never put the consumer's element where their own root stood, and rendering them showed the defect was worse than a silent drop. **`Callout` lost its `rt-CalloutRoot` element entirely, taking the tone fill, the urgency border and `role="alert"` with it.** `DragHandle`, `MobileNavToggle` and `ToggleButton` each emitted **no `button` element at all**, leaving an `svg` or a layout `span` wearing the button's classes and ARIA, which is a control that is not focusable, not activatable by keyboard and not named to a screen reader. **`Popover.Anchor` erased the consumer's entire subtree**, and it did so on a shipped path, because the system's own wrapper bound to the Radix Themes re-export rather than to `@radix-ui/react-popover`, so anchoring silently did nothing for `DateInput`, `DateRangeInput`, `Typeahead` and the `TopNav` flyouts. All of it compiled clean and none of it raised an error. **THE RULE: a published prop that does not do what its name says is an accessibility defect, not a documentation gap.** `Popover.Anchor` is repaired by binding to the primitive Radix Themes itself imports, verified by object identity so the two cannot drift apart. The other four declare `asChild?: never` under the [aschild-or-type-error](#aschild-or-type-error) idiom. `AspectRatio` is the one deliberate exception and keeps the prop: the consumer's `img`, `video` or `iframe` genuinely becomes the inset content box with the component class concatenated ahead of its own, and the outer box cannot be handed over because that box IS the ratio. Its docblock now names which of its two elements the seam gives you.

### table-accessible-name

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-22.

**`aria-label` on `Table.Root` names the table, because the system renders it as a visually hidden `<caption>`.**

**Rule.** Where an author's first attempt is predictable, the system makes that attempt work rather than teach a different spelling.

**What you see.** Radix renders `Table.Root` as a wrapper `div` that carries every consumer prop, around a `ScrollArea`, around the `table`. The system takes `aria-label` and renders it as a `<caption>` inside `VisuallyHidden`, the first child of the `table`, so the `table` carries the name and the wrapper carries none.

**Visible caption.** The `caption` prop renders a visible `<caption>`, placed by `captionSide` with the CSS `caption-side` and painted `--ds-text-weak`. `aria-label` beside `caption` is a type error, because the system can honour only one name.

**Not accepted.** `aria-labelledby` cannot become a caption, because a caption cannot reference an id. Its type is a string literal that states the fix, the rule of [published-aschild-props](#published-aschild-props) applied to a new prop.

**Rejected.** A reimplementation of the Radix root that puts `aria-label` on the `table`. It copies `rt-TableRootTable`, a vendor internal that `docs/GUIDELINES.md` section 10 puts off contract.

**Changed from.** `aria-label` on `Table.Root` named the scroll container, and the `table` had no accessible name, a WCAG 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 failure that raised no warning.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-22. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A data table was anonymous in the accessibility tree, and the fix is to make the instinctive call work (2026-09-22).** Radix Themes renders `Table.Root` as a wrapper `div` carrying every consumer prop, wrapping a `ScrollArea`, wrapping the `table`. So `<Table.Root aria-label="Quarterly revenue">` named a SCROLL CONTAINER and left the `table` with no accessible name, which for a table with headers is a WCAG 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 failure. Nothing warned, and the markup looked correct. **THE RULE: where an author's first attempt is predictable, make that attempt work rather than teaching a different spelling.** `aria-label` on `Table.Root` is what a person and an agent both write first, so it is now intercepted and rendered as a visually hidden `<caption>`, which is the one element a consumer prop can reach, since Radix places `children` directly inside the `table` and a `caption` is valid as its first child. Measured: the caption lands first inside the `table` and the wrapper carries no name. **Reuse rather than invention, in both directions.** The mechanism is the HTML `caption` element rather than a new ARIA pattern, the hiding is the shipped `VisuallyHidden`, the placement is Radix's own `caption-side`, and the paint is `--ds-text-weak`, so nothing new was added to the token layer and no vendor internal was copied. Reimplementing Radix's root to put `aria-label` on the `table` directly was REJECTED, because copying `rt-TableRootTable` is a vendor internal and GUIDELINES section 10 puts those off contract. **What cannot be honoured is refused at compile time rather than dropped at runtime**, which is [published-aschild-props](#published-aschild-props)'s rule applied forward instead of retroactively: `aria-labelledby` cannot become a caption because a caption cannot reference an id, so its type is a string literal that STATES THE FIX, and `aria-label` together with `caption` is a type error because the system can honour only one. A defect fixed by adding a second silent no-op would not have been a fix.

### scrim-focus-ring

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**A surface that paints a fixed backdrop under controls seeds its own focus ring, so a ring on a scrim holds contrast over any media.**

**What you see.** On the `Overlay` scrims the focus ring is the system's accent ring, with its stack chosen for the veil. `.rt-ds-overlay-scrim` sets `--ds-stroke-focus-stack` to `--accent-ring-stack-scrim`, and `[data-scrim="light"]` sets it to `--accent-ring-stack-scrim-light`, beside the `color` that [overlay-scrim-ink](#overlay-scrim-ink) sets.

**Why.** Both scrim veils keep their colour in either appearance ([scrim-value](#scrim-value)), and the page ring follows the appearance, so a page ring on a scrim can match the veil and vanish. On 2026-09-24 the page ring of that date fell to 1.00:1 on each scrim at its worst media value.

**Applies to.** Any later surface that paints a fixed backdrop under controls. A consumer who paints their own scrim redeclares the ring on it the same way, through the token seam in section 10 of `docs/GUIDELINES.md`.

**Limit.** The stack is measured against the veil over media, not against an opaque plate placed inside the scrim, the same limit the scrim's ink carries ([overlay-scrim-ink](#overlay-scrim-ink)).

**Enforced by.** `_internal/Focus` `ScrimRingContrast` focuses a control in a real `.rt-ds-overlay-scrim` and sweeps the ring over media from 0 to 255 for every accent, both appearances and both scrims.

**Changed from.** The scrims set no ring, so the page ring, `gray-12`, painted on both veils. The recorded worst case of 2.84:1 in [scrim-foreground-tokens](#scrim-foreground-tokens) was the best case for a dark ring on the dark scrim, and this ruling closes that open item.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24.

- [light-scrim-focus-ring](#light-scrim-focus-ring) rings a focused Button or IconButton on the light scrim in a deep shade of its own colour.
- [focus-ring](#focus-ring) makes every ring the accent with a Radix alpha stacked on it. The scrim now sets only that stack, and the dark scrim ring is no longer white.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A focus ring on a scrim takes the scrim's paired ink (2026-09-24).** The system ring `--ds-stroke-focus-hairline` is `gray-12`, which flips with the appearance, while both scrim veils keep their colour in either appearance since [scrim-value](#scrim-value). So on `Overlay`'s scrim the page ring could equal the scrim composite. Swept over grey media 0 to 255 under the 0.6 veil, the page ring read 1.28 over black, 1.30 over mid grey and 2.85 over white on `--ds-scrim` in the light appearance, with a worst of **1.00:1 at media near #505050**, and 2.45, 1.38 and 1.16 on `--ds-scrim-light` in the dark appearance, with a worst of **1.00:1 near #d5d5d5**. The other two cells passed at 4.95 and 5.75. Rendered on the Overlay page before the fix, the focused Play button read 1.51:1 on the dark scrim in the light appearance, and the light-scrim Play button read 1.11:1 outside its edge in the dark appearance. **The earlier record of 2.84:1 was the best case for a dark ring on the dark scrim, not the worst.** It reused [scrim-foreground-tokens](#scrim-foreground-tokens)'s worst case for white text, and a dark ring does worst at the crossover, where it vanishes. **The fix is two declarations.** `.rt-ds-overlay-scrim` sets `--ds-stroke-focus-hairline: var(--ds-on-scrim)` beside the `color` [overlay-scrim-ink](#overlay-scrim-ink) already sets, and `[data-scrim="light"]` sets it to `var(--ds-on-scrim-light)`. The paired ink sits on the far side of the veil at every media value, so the ring now reads at least **5.74:1** on the dark scrim and **5.72:1** on the light one, in both appearances, and holds 3:1 down to a veil alpha of about 0.42, below [scrim-value](#scrim-value)'s floor. Token, selectors, width and offset are unchanged from the first neutral focus ring and [validation-focus-paint](#validation-focus-paint): 2px at a 2px offset on a solid button, 2px at -1px on a surface one. **THE RULE: a surface that seeds its own ink seeds its own ring.** This is the first scoped re-point of a semantic role in `components.css`, and it is the shape for any later surface that paints a fixed backdrop under controls. A consumer who paints their own scrim redeclares the ring the same way on it (the GUIDELINES §10 token seam). **One visible change:** in the light appearance a secondary button on the dark scrim shows a white rim just outside its light face. The inner half of that ring reads about 1.5:1 against the face, which WCAG 1.4.11 permits because the outer half carries the contrast. **Limit, stated:** a light opaque plate placed inside the scrim would carry a white ring, the same limit [overlay-scrim-ink](#overlay-scrim-ink)'s ink carries. **The Overlay page's dark-media stand-in painted `gray-12` to `gray-10`, which inverts,** so in the dark appearance the light-scrim specimen sat over a light poster. It is pinned to the light scale now and draws the same poster in both appearances. Guarded by `_internal/Focus` `ScrimRingContrast`, which sweeps a real `.rt-ds-overlay-scrim` over media 0 to 255 for every accent, both appearances and both scrims, and by two measured focus-ring rows on the Overlay page. Closes the open item in [scrim-foreground-tokens](#scrim-foreground-tokens) and amends [overlay-scrim-ink](#overlay-scrim-ink). The first neutral focus ring, [validation-focus-paint](#validation-focus-paint) and [scrim-value](#scrim-value) stand. **[Update 2026-09-25 ([focus-ring](#focus-ring)): the scrim no longer seeds its ring's ink. It re-points only the ring's stack, and the ring is the accent on both scrims.]**

### toast-under-modal

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**A toast raised under an open modal stays reachable to a screen reader and to the pointer.**

**Screen reader.** `ToastViewport` gives the `ol` of the rail the attribute `aria-live="off"`, the mechanism of Radix pull request 4127. A modal `Dialog` hides the rest of the page with the aria-hidden package, which skips every `[aria-live]` node and its ancestors, so Undo stays a button named "Undo" while the rest of the app stays hidden. The value "off" announces nothing, so the Radix status node still speaks once.

**Pointer.** `ToastViewport` portals its rail to `document.body` inside a nested `Theme`, so the `--ds-z-toast` of the rail stacks above the modal scrim, and a click on Undo runs Undo while the dialog stays open. The nested `Theme` carries `data-ui-size`, so the rail matches at every size tier.

**Container.** The `container` prop defaults to the body. The docs measurement host passes its own element, which keeps its specimens in frame.

**Gap.** A toast raised before the modal opened paints above the scrim but takes no pointer input, because the Radix DismissableLayer disables pointer events on every layer older than the modal. A click there closes the dialog and does not run Undo.

**Guard.** The UnderModal story in `_internal/Toast behavior` checks that Undo is a button named "Undo", that it is the hit target, and that a click on it runs Undo and leaves the dialog open.

**Changed from.** A toast raised inside a modal sat in an `aria-hidden` subtree, so Chrome marked its Undo button ignored (Radix issue 4115). It also painted under the scrim, because the root `Theme` of the Provider is a `z-index: 0` stacking context that caps `--ds-z-toast`, and a click on Undo closed the dialog.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. The pointer half landed the same day. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A toast raised under a modal stays reachable to a screen reader, and its pointer half waits on a ruling (2026-09-24).** A modal Dialog calls `hideOthers` from the aria-hidden package, so a toast raised from inside the modal sat in an `aria-hidden` subtree and Chrome marked its Undo button ignored at 250 ms and at 1,450 ms (Radix #4115, react-toast v1.2.17). **`ToastViewport` now passes `aria-live="off"` to the rail's `ol`**, the mechanism of Radix PR #4127: aria-hidden leaves every `[aria-live]` node and its ancestors alone, and "off" announces nothing, so Radix's own status node still speaks once. Measured on the rendered page, Undo reads as role button, name "Undo", not ignored, while the rest of the app stays hidden. The guard is `_internal/Toast behavior` → *UnderModal*, red when the attribute is removed. **The pointer half is PENDING.** The toast still paints under the scrim, because the Provider's root Theme is a `z-index: 0` stacking context that caps `--ds-z-toast`, and a click at Undo lands on the dialog's scroll layer and closes the dialog. A body portal fixes it, measured, but moves the rail out of the Toast Usage page's measurement host, so it waits on a block that also covers `Toast.stories.tsx`. **[Update 2026-09-24: the pointer half landed. `ToastViewport` now portals its rail to `document.body` inside a nested `Theme`, with a `container` prop that defaults to the body, so the rail's `--ds-z-toast` stacks above a modal's scrim. The docs measurement host passes `container={host}` to keep its specimens in the frame. Measured with a real mouse, a toast raised from inside an open modal paints bright above the scrim, and a click on Undo runs Undo while the dialog stays open. The nested Theme carries `data-ui-size` from SizeContext, so the rail's computed styles match HEAD in light, in dark and at the medium and large tiers. *UnderModal* now also checks that Undo is the hit target and that a click there runs Undo and leaves the dialog open. It went red when the portal was removed. One case remains: a toast raised before the modal opened paints above the scrim but takes no pointer input, because Radix's DismissableLayer turns pointer events off on every layer older than the modal. A click there lands on the dialog, closes it and does not run Undo.]**

### dialog-describedby

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**A Dialog or AlertDialog without a Description carries no `aria-describedby`.**

**What you see.** A dialog with a Title alone carries no `aria-describedby` and passes axe. A dialog with a Description keeps its accessible description, and a consumer's own `aria-describedby` still wins.

**Mechanism.** `Dialog.Description` and `AlertDialog.Description` are thin wrappers that register with their Content through a context. While none is mounted, Content passes `aria-describedby={undefined}`, the opt-out Radix provides. The registration runs in a layout effect, so the attribute is final before paint and before focus moves into the dialog on open.

**Why.** react-dialog v1.1.17 sets `aria-describedby` to its description id whether or not a Description renders (Radix issue 3007), so a Title-only dialog referenced an id that no element carried. axe v4.12.1 files that as needing review, never as a violation, so the axe lane could not fail on it. Radix prints no development warning for it either, because its `WarningProvider` in that version is a passthrough.

**Guarded.** *DescribedbyResolves* in `_internal/Dialog behavior` and in `_internal/AlertDialog behavior`.

**Changed from.** A Title-only Dialog or AlertDialog carried an `aria-describedby` that referenced no element, and a comment in `Dialog.tsx` claimed that Radix warned in development.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A dialog without a Description carries no `aria-describedby` (2026-09-24).** react-dialog v1.1.17 sets `aria-describedby` to its description id before spreading the consumer's props, whether or not a Description renders, so a Title-only Dialog or AlertDialog pointed at an id no element carried (Radix #3007). axe v4.12.1 files this as needs-review under `aria-valid-attr-value`, never a violation, so the axe lane could not fail on it. **`Dialog.Description` and `AlertDialog.Description` are now thin wrappers that register with their Content through a context, and Content passes `aria-describedby={undefined}`, Radix's own opt-out, while none is mounted.** The override sits before the consumer's props, so a consumer's own `aria-describedby` still wins (measured). The registration runs in a layout effect, so the attribute is final before paint and before the open auto-focus. Measured on the rendered page, a Title-only dialog carries no attribute and axe passes, and a described dialog keeps its accessible description. The Dialog.tsx comment that said Radix warns in dev is corrected, because the v1.1.17 `WarningProvider` is a passthrough. The guards are *DescribedbyResolves* in `_internal/Dialog behavior` and `_internal/AlertDialog behavior`, each red on three separate probes: no override, an override that never lifts, and a registration that never unregisters.

### select-option-numbering

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**`Select` numbers its own options with `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize`, because the Radix Select sets neither.**

**What you see.** `Select.Content` numbers every `[role="option"]` in the open listbox in DOM order when the listbox mounts, and again whenever its items change. An option that carries its own numbering keeps it.

**Why.** With no numbering, VoiceOver with Chrome announces a wrong count or none, as Radix issues #3962 and #4110 report.

**Guarded by.** The `Menu states` play holds five options at 1 of 5 through 5 of 5.

**Not covered.** `MultiSelect` options, recorded as a gap in [documentation-and-markup-gaps](#documentation-and-markup-gaps).

**Changed from.** Options in the open listbox carried no `aria-posinset` or `aria-setsize`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Select numbers its own options (2026-09-24).** Radix's Select sets no `aria-posinset` or `aria-setsize` on its options, and Radix #3962 and #4110 report that VoiceOver with Chrome then announces a wrong count or none. `Select.Content` numbers every `[role="option"]` in the open listbox in DOM order the moment the listbox mounts, and again whenever its items change. An option that carries its own numbering keeps it. Measured on the rendered listbox, four options went from no attributes to 1 of 4 through 4 of 4. The `Menu states` play asserts 1 of 5 through 5 of 5 and went red with the numbering removed.

### dropdown-assistive-click

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**DropdownMenu opens on the click that assistive technology sends.**

**What you see.** A click with no pointer press before it toggles the menu: VoiceOver's modifier key (VO) plus Space in Safari and Firefox, the browse-mode Enter of NonVisual Desktop Access (NVDA), and `element.click()`. A mouse press, Enter and Space each open the menu exactly once.

**Why.** Radix's menu trigger toggles on `pointerdown` and `keydown` only, so these clicks left the menu closed (Radix issues #1963 and #2700).

**Mechanism.** `DropdownMenu.Root` owns the open state and shares a toggle. `DropdownMenu.Trigger` toggles on a click unless a pointer gesture began it. The gesture mark clears one task after the document's next capture-phase `pointerup`, because a modal menu keeps that gesture's own click from the trigger.

**Applies to.** `DropdownMenu`, and `MoreMenu`, which inherits the fix with no code of its own.

**Changed from.** DropdownMenu and MoreMenu stayed closed on a click from VoiceOver, NVDA or `element.click()`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it. [tabs-open-on-navigation](#tabs-open-on-navigation) gives Tabs the same shape.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **DropdownMenu opens on the click assistive technology sends (2026-09-24).** Radix's menu trigger toggles on pointerdown and keydown only, so the click sent by VoiceOver's modifier key (VO) plus Space in Safari and Firefox, by NonVisual Desktop Access (NVDA)'s browse-mode Enter and by `element.click()` left DropdownMenu and MoreMenu closed (Radix #1963, #2700). `DropdownMenu.Root` owns the open state and shares a toggle, and `DropdownMenu.Trigger` toggles on a click unless a pointer gesture began it. The gesture mark clears one task after the document's next capture-phase pointerup, because a modal menu keeps that gesture's own click from reaching the trigger. MoreMenu inherits the fix with no code of its own. Measured on the rendered menus, a bare click, `element.click()`, a mouse press, Enter and Space each opened the menu exactly once, and a mouse open, Escape and a bare click reopened it. The `AssistiveClick` plays in `_internal/DropdownMenu behavior` and `_internal/MoreMenu behavior` went red with the click toggle removed, with the gesture check removed and with the mark never cleared.

### scroll-area-keyboard-stop

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COMPONENTS`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**A ScrollArea that overflows with only text inside is a keyboard stop, and a named one reads as a region.**

**What you see.** ScrollArea applies the three measures of [chat-log-scroller](#chat-log-scroller) by default:

- An overflowing viewport with nothing focusable inside takes `tabIndex={0}`, unless the caller passed a `tabIndex`.
- A viewport given `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` takes `role="region"`, unless the caller passed a role.
- A focusable viewport with no name warns once in development through `warnOnce`.

**Why.** Radix puts no tab stop, role or name on the viewport. Chromium 130 and later make such a scroller a tab stop exposed as a generic node, and in a browser without that behaviour the overflow is beyond keyboard reach.

**Not covered.** A scroller that holds a focusable element keeps no stop of its own, because the keyboard reaches it through that element.

**Guard.** The `TextOnlyStop` play in `_internal/ScrollArea behavior`.

**Changed from.** A bare text scroller carried no tabindex and read as a generic node.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24. No later ruling amends it.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A text-only ScrollArea is a named keyboard stop (2026-09-24).** Radix puts no tab stop, role or name on the ScrollArea viewport. Chromium 130 and later make a scroller with nothing focusable inside a tab stop on their own, exposed as a generic node, and a browser without that behaviour leaves the overflow out of keyboard reach. ScrollArea applies the three from [chat-log-scroller](#chat-log-scroller) by default. An overflowing viewport with nothing focusable inside takes `tabIndex={0}` unless the caller passed one, a viewport given `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` takes `role="region"` unless the caller passed a role, and a focusable viewport with no name warns once in development through `warnOnce`. Measured in the test browser, a bare text scroller went from no tabindex and a generic node to tabindex 0, and a named one reads as region "Release notes". The `TextOnlyStop` play in `_internal/ScrollArea behavior` went red on each of its four arms when the matching line was removed.

### forced-colours

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**Under Windows forced colours every control keeps a visible edge and a visible state, drawn in system colours.**

**Why.** Radix draws edges with inset box-shadow and marks as white on an accent fill, and forcing computes box-shadow to none and backgrounds to Canvas (CSS Color Adjust 1 section 3). Every control edge measured 1.00:1 in both system palettes, and checked and unchecked radios and switches rendered identical.

**Mechanism.** `src/tokens/forced-colors.css`, imported last in `src/tokens/index.css`, holds one `@media (forced-colors: active)` block under `.radix-themes` in three layers:

- Roles: the edge, state and disabled roles point to `ButtonBorder`, `Highlight` and `GrayText`.
- Edges: a real 1px edge returns where Radix used box-shadow, as an inset `::after` on Button, IconButton, the Select trigger and Callout so no box moves, and as a border on the TextField and TextArea roots in place of their reserved 1px padding.
- Marks: checked, on and selected states paint `Highlight` with a `HighlightText` mark.

**Measured.** Under emulation on 2026-09-24 every edge read about 21:1 against Canvas, a disabled edge 14:1 in `GrayText`, and state fills 11.3:1 in light and 9.1:1 in dark, with marks at the same ratio. The focus ring stays a `Highlight` outline, and outside forced colours the rendered geometry is byte-identical.

**Guard.** `_internal/Forced colors` enables emulation through the `cdp()` of Vitest Browser Mode and asserts every edge and state in both palettes.

**Gap.** Composite surfaces still draw their edge with box-shadow: Tokenizer, SegmentedControl, Slider, CheckboxCards, RadioCards and Card. A standalone StatusDot shows nothing under forced colours ([status-dot-edges](#status-dot-edges)).

**Changed from.** The system carried no forced-colours rules, so every control edge and every checked state vanished under forcing.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24.

- [focus-ring](#focus-ring) makes each carrier's own outline the whole ring under forced colours, painted `Highlight` at 2px.
- [neutral-part-stacks](#neutral-part-stacks) adds the Pagination dots: a `ButtonBorder` ring on every dot, a `Highlight` current dot and a `GrayText` disabled dot.
- [card-picker-focus-width](#card-picker-focus-width) widens the outline of a focused CheckboxCards or RadioCards card to 4px under forced colours.
- [token-pressed-state](#token-pressed-state) adds the pressed Token, which paints `Highlight` under `HighlightText`.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Windows forced colours keep every control edge and state (2026-09-24).** Under emulated `forced-colors: active` every control edge measured 1.00:1 in both system palettes, and checked and unchecked radios and switches rendered pixel-identical, because Radix draws edges with inset box-shadow and marks as white on an accent fill, while forcing computes box-shadow to none and forces backgrounds to Canvas (CSS Color Adjust 1 section 3). `src/tokens/forced-colors.css`, imported last in `src/tokens/index.css`, holds one `@media (forced-colors: active)` block under `.radix-themes` in three layers. The edge, state and disabled roles re-point to `ButtonBorder`, `Highlight` and `GrayText`. A real 1px edge returns where Radix used box-shadow, drawn as an inset `::after` on Button, IconButton, Select trigger and Callout so no box moves, and as a border on the TextField and TextArea roots that takes over their reserved 1px padding. Checked, on and selected states paint `Highlight` with a `HighlightText` mark. Measured after, every edge reads 20.99 to 21:1 against Canvas (disabled 14:1 in GrayText), state fills read 11.3:1 light and 9.1:1 dark with marks at the same ratio, the focus ring stays a Highlight outline, and outside forced colours the rendered geometry and screenshots are byte-identical. The guard `_internal/Forced colors` turns emulation on through Vitest Browser Mode's `cdp()` and asserts all of it in both palettes. Composite surfaces (Tokenizer, SegmentedControl, Slider, CheckboxCards, RadioCards, Card) still draw their edge with box-shadow and remain a gap.

### button-focus-ring-offset

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-24.

**A standalone button rings 2px outside its edge in every variant, and a button inside a field keeps its ring inside the edge.**

**What you see.** Every focused soft, ghost, outline and surface `Button` and `IconButton` takes `outline-offset: 2px`, the offset Radix gives solid and classic buttons. The ring is the accent focus ring that [focus-ring](#focus-ring) sets.

**Why.** Radix rings soft, ghost, outline and surface buttons at `-1px`, across the edge. On the Overlay page those rings sat flush against a light face at 1.4 to 1.6:1 and read as a border, not as focus.

**Exception.**

- A button inside a field (`[data-inset]`) keeps Radix's inset ring, so the ring stays within the input.
- A component rule that places its own ring wins, as the SideNav rail trigger at `-2px` does, because the rule in `components.css` sits at specificity (0,2,0).
- The Thumbnail remove control sits 2px inside a frame that clips its overflow, so it rings at offset 0 and fills that margin exactly.

**Changed from.** The first neutral focus ring kept Radix's offset for each variant when it changed the ring colour, so four variants rang across their edge.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-24.

- [input-focus-ring-offset](#input-focus-ring-offset) gives every input the same 2px gap.
- [focus-ring](#focus-ring) keeps the gap and draws the ring it places in the stacked accent.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **A standalone button's focus ring sits 2px outside its edge in every variant (2026-09-24).** Radix rings solid and classic buttons at `outline-offset: 2px` but soft, ghost, outline and surface at `-1px`, straddling the edge, and the first neutral focus ring kept that per-variant offset when it swapped the ring colour. On the Overlay page those straddling rings sat flush against a light face at 1.4 to 1.6:1 and read as a border, not as focus. **`components.css` now gives every focused soft, ghost, outline and surface Button and IconButton `outline-offset: 2px`, which amends the first neutral focus ring**, at specificity (0,2,0) so a component rule that places its own ring still wins, as the SideNav rail trigger's -2px does. A button inside a field (`[data-inset]`) keeps Radix's inset ring so it stays within the input. A Tab-focus sweep of every non-solid button across the component pages, dialogs, toasts and popovers found one clipped site, the Thumbnail remove ✕, which sits 2px inside a frame that clips with overflow hidden and lost its ring on the top and right, so it rings at offset 0 and fills that margin exactly. `_internal/Focus` → *RingGapOutsideEdge* focuses each variant at all three steps and reads the computed offset, and went red with the rule removed and again with the inset exclusion removed. **[Update 2026-09-25 ([focus-ring](#focus-ring)): the gap stands, and the ring it places is [focus-ring](#focus-ring)'s stacked accent.]**

### text-on-solid-fill-contrast

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-25.

**Text on a solid fill reaches WCAG 4.5:1 and APCA Lc 60 at rest, on hover and on press, and the fill takes a deeper step where step 9 does not reach both floors.**

**Why.** The old 3:1 floor treated a solid-fill label as large or bold text, but a button label renders at 12px and weight 500 at the default size, so it never qualified. White on step 9 read 3.00 to 3.91:1 on 15 of 27 accents.

**The fill.** The fill that carries text is its own role in `theme.css`, `--accent-solid` and `--error-solid`, read by `--ds-fill-accent` and `--ds-fill-error`. The solid `Button`, `IconButton` and `Code` chip paint from it, and a part given its own `color` takes the fill of a page in that colour.

**Per colour.**

| Colours | Ink | Fill |
|---|---|---|
| iris, indigo, violet, purple, plum, oxblood | white | step 9 |
| yellow, amber, lime, mint, sky | dark | step 9 |
| tomato, red, ruby, crimson, pink, blue, cyan, teal, jade, green, grass, brown, orange, gold, bronze, gray | white | step 11 of light, pinned as sRGB hex for both appearances |

The gray pin follows the neutral. Pink passes at step 10 by 0.001 and takes step 11 for the margin. Orange moves to white ink because its dark ink read APCA Lc 45.8 on step 9, and `--accent-contrast` stays dark for the glyphs Radix draws on orange step 9.

**Danger.** The danger fill follows the error family: red step 11 by default, ruby step 11 under a bronze brand, and oxblood step 9 where error moves to oxblood.

**Hover and press.** The fill keeps its rest colour and takes a Radix alpha on top: `--black-a2` under a white label, and `--white-a4` under the dark label of amber, lime, mint, sky and yellow. Press and an open menu trigger take the same overlay under the Radix press filter. The alpha is the one whose change on the rest fill lies closest to the Radix step 9 to step 10 hover ([interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas)).

**Rejected.**

- Step 12 of light as the hover. It turned near-black and read 1.14 to 1.61:1 against the dark page.
- A blend between two steps, a value the system would invent ([interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas)).

**Not covered.** The warning, success and info solids carry glyphs and not text, and stay at the 3:1 non-text floor, so text on them lies outside this ruling until they adopt the role. The error fill of a seeded brand keeps the Radix step 9 and is an open gap.

**Guard.** `ON_FILL` in `src/foundations/_assert.ts` holds the four text pairs at 4.5:1 and Lc 60 across 27 accents and both appearances, and `assertPairing` applies the Lc floor at every call site.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved, on 2026-09-25, the recommended treatment in both appearances, and rejected step 12 as the hover.

**Changed from.** Text on a solid fill was held to 3:1 as large or bold text, and every solid fill painted step 9.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-25.

- [textless-part-fills](#textless-part-fills) points the parts without text in the 16 deepened colours at `--accent-solid` in light, and gives the solid `Code` chip the pair of the button.
- [part-colour-parity](#part-colour-parity) gives a part with its own `color` the fill of a page in that colour, which closes the gap this ruling recorded for a button given the Radix `color` prop.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Text on a solid fill reaches WCAG 4.5:1 and APCA Lc 60, at rest and on hover, and the fill deepens where step 9 cannot (2026-09-25).** Approved by the maintainer as the Recommended column in both appearances, and it supersedes the 3:1 floor for text on a solid fill. That floor held solid-fill labels to AA 3.0 as large or bold text, but a button label renders 12px at weight 500 in the default lane, so it never qualified, and white on step 9 measured 3.00 to 3.91:1 on 15 of 27 accents with Danger at 3.91. The fill that carries text is now its own role in `theme.css`, `--accent-solid` and `--error-solid`, read by `--ds-fill-accent` and `--ds-fill-error`, and the solid Button and IconButton paint from it. Where the ink already passes both on step 9 nothing moves, which keeps white on iris, indigo, violet, purple, plum and oxblood and the dark ink on yellow, amber, lime, mint and sky. Everywhere else the ink is white and the fill is the colour's own light step 11, pinned as sRGB hex so the value is the same in both appearances, on tomato, red, ruby, crimson, pink, blue, cyan, teal, jade, green, grass, brown, orange, gold, bronze and gray, keyed on the neutral for gray. Pink passes at step 10 by 0.001 and takes step 11 for the margin. Orange's dark ink read APCA Lc 45.8 on step 9, so orange moved to white on orange-11 at 4.51, and `--accent-contrast` stays dark for the glyphs Radix draws on orange-9. Danger follows the error family, red-11 by default, ruby-11 under bronze, and oxblood-9 where error moves to oxblood. The hover keeps the rest fill and lays an alpha from Radix's own scale over it, `--black-a2` under a white label and `--white-a4` under the dark label of amber, lime, mint, sky and yellow, chosen because its median change on the rest fills (ΔE-OK 0.043 and 0.031) lies closest to Radix's own step 9 to step 10 hover (0.036), and press and an open menu trigger take the same overlay under Radix's press filter, so every label passes both floors on hover and press while the hover stays its own colour one small step on. The maintainer rejected light step 12 as the hover, because it turned near-black and sat 1.14 to 1.61:1 from the dark page, and a blend between two steps was rejected as an invented value ([interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas)). `ON_FILL` in `_assert.ts` asserts the four text pairs at 4.5 and Lc 60 across 27 accents and both appearances, and `assertPairing` applies the Lc floor at every call site. The status solids (warning, success, info) carry glyphs rather than text and stay at the 3.0 non-text floor, so text on them is not covered until they adopt the role. A seeded brand's error fill and a button given Radix's `color` prop keep Radix's step 9 and are recorded as open gaps.

### textless-part-fills

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-25.

**In light, a part without text takes the shade of its colour's buttons, the switch thumb takes a stroke where its track hides it, and solid Code paints the button's fill and ink.**

**Applies to.** The 16 colours whose text fill [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) deepens: gold, bronze, brown, orange, tomato, red, ruby, crimson, pink, blue, cyan, teal, jade, green, grass and gray. Every other colour keeps Radix's values.

**Parts.** In light, `theme.css` sets Radix's `--accent-indicator` and `--accent-track` to `--accent-solid`, so every checkbox, radio, switch track, slider range, progress bar and tab underline of one colour is the shade of its buttons. Radix's step 9 read 2.90 to 3.00:1 against the light page on cyan, teal, orange and grass, and the deeper fill reads 4.40 to 5.79:1. In dark the 16 keep Radix's step 9, which clears the dark page.

**System marks.** The CheckboxCards outline, the accent StatusDot, the Pagination dot, the Calendar today bar, the Outline bar and the reorder marker paint `--accent-indicator` in `components.css`, so a card shows one shade of its accent.

**Switch thumb.** The thumb stays white on every colour. Where it falls under 3:1 against its track, its 1px ring paints `--accent-thumb-stroke`, the lightest step of the same colour that clears 3:1 as painted.

| Appearance | Colours | Stroke |
|---|---|---|
| Light | amber, lime, mint, sky, yellow | `--accent-a11` |
| Dark | amber, lime, mint, sky, yellow | `--accent-7` |
| Dark | orange | `--accent-6` |

**Code and ink.** Solid Code paints `--ds-fill-accent` under `--on-accent`, at least 4.51:1 on all 27 colours, and a linked chip keeps that fill on hover under the [interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas) overlay. Orange's glyph ink follows its fill: Radix's white on light step 11, and `#21201c` on dark step 9.

**Guidance.** The maintainer approved, on 2026-09-25, the Code chip in the button colour, the Switch as it stood with a stronger stroke where the thumb fails, the deeper fill in light and Radix's step 9 in dark.

**Changed from.** Every part painted Radix's step 9, under 3:1 against the light page on four colours, and the system's own marks painted `--ds-fill-accent`, so a card showed two shades of one accent. Solid Code painted Radix's `--accent-a9` under `--accent-contrast`.

**Status.** Ruled 2026-09-25.

- [part-fill-edge](#part-fill-edge) closes the gap this ruling left on light amber, lime, mint, sky and yellow and on dark oxblood, with a 1px edge on the fill.
- [colour-prop-and-high-contrast](#colour-prop-and-high-contrast) extends these fixes to a part given Radix's `color` prop or `highContrast`.
- [part-colour-parity](#part-colour-parity) sets the part arm of the indicator and the track to the part's own `--accent-solid`, and adds oxblood to the base arm of the thumb stroke.

**Evidence.** The entry before the rewrite of 2026-10-01:

> **Parts without text follow the text fill in light, the switch thumb takes a stroke where a light track hides it, and solid Code paints the button's pair (2026-09-25).** Approved by the maintainer from the extension review page: the Code chip in the button colour, the Switch as it is today with a stronger stroke where the thumb fails, Option A in light and Option B in dark. In light, the 16 colours whose text fill [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) deepens (gold, bronze, brown, orange, tomato, red, ruby, crimson, pink, blue, cyan, teal, jade, green, grass and gray) point Radix's `--accent-indicator` and `--accent-track` at `--accent-solid` in `theme.css`, so every checkbox, radio, switch track, slider range, progress bar and tab underline of one colour is the shade of its buttons, and step 9, which sat at 2.90 to 3.00:1 against the light page on cyan, teal, orange and grass, rises to 4.40 to 5.79:1. In dark the same 16 keep Radix's step 9 (3.67 on gray, 4.55 to 6.31:1 on the rest). Orange's glyph ink follows its fill, Radix's own white on light step 11 (4.51:1) and `#21201c` on orange-9 in dark (5.47:1). The system's own marks that painted `--ds-fill-accent` (the CheckboxCards outline, the accent StatusDot, the Pagination dot, the Calendar today bar, the Outline bar and the reorder marker) paint `--accent-indicator` in `components.css`, so a card no longer shows two shades of one accent. The switch thumb stays white on every colour. Where it fell under 3:1 against its track, its 1px ring, Radix's `--accent-a4`, paints `--accent-thumb-stroke`, the lightest step of the same colour that clears 3:1 as painted: `--accent-a11` on amber, lime, mint, sky and yellow in light (3.19 to 4.20:1), and in dark, where no alpha step reaches it (2.11:1 at best), the solid scale, step 7 on amber, lime, mint, sky and yellow and step 6 on orange (3.14 to 4.03:1). Solid Code without its own `color` paints `--ds-fill-accent` under `--on-accent`, at least 4.51:1 and APCA Lc 74.9 on all 27 colours, and a linked chip keeps that fill on hover under the [interaction-state-alphas](#interaction-state-alphas) overlay. The PartsWithoutText play in `_non-text-contrast.stories.tsx` holds each part at 3:1 against the page, the thumb or its stroke at 3:1 against the track, the check and the radio dot at 3:1 on their fill, and one shade per colour, across 27 accents in both appearances. It names light amber, lime, mint, sky and yellow (1.31 to 1.54:1) and dark oxblood (2.06:1) as an open gap, because [textless-part-fills](#textless-part-fills) moves only the colours [text-on-solid-fill-contrast](#text-on-solid-fill-contrast) deepens.

### part-fill-edge

**Tags.** `ACCESSIBILITY`, `COLOUR`. **Ruled.** 2026-09-25.

**On the colours where a part without text falls under its contrast floor against the page, the part stacks a 1px Radix alpha edge on its fill.**

**Applies to.** The checked or indeterminate checkbox, the checked radio and switch track, the slider range, the progress bar, the active tab line of Tabs and of Tabs.Nav, the accent status dot and the selected CheckboxCards band.
